artigo.texto: Two years after fighting off a landfill proposal, Russell County residents questioned the new set of developers hoping to build a data center campus on a different parcel of a historic former coal mine site near the town of Cleveland. The developers are still waiting for approval of a power agreement and looking to attract a company to operate three or four data centers. Ground could be broken for the project by next fall, they told a crowd in Lebanon on Wednesday. Oasis Digital Properties developers discussed their timeline for the project, shared projected economic benefits and addressed environmental and quality-of-life concerns about the project. Virginia is the state with the most data centers, most located in the northern part of the state, but in recent years more proposals have come to the coalfields in far Southwest. About 100 people turned out for the forum held by the developers. The crowd included Cleveland residents and their neighbors in nearby communities, who took notes, asked questions and pushed back on details like the amount of water that would be used and how the noise would be controlled. Oasis entered into an option agreement with the Russell County Industrial Development Authority, which owns the land, in July 2025 to explore developing the site.The partnership opened a 36-month period for the company to “prove” its project to the authority, Ross Litkenhous, co-founder of Oasis, said during the forum. Litkenhous said in an interview on Friday that the agreement allows Oasis to purchase the property until July 2028, but it is “not going to move forward unless they have a project that makes sense.” The purchase price would be just under $3 million, he said. New details and some changes have emerged since Cardinal News’ initial story on the project in September. Water and power usage Appalachian Power told the Oasis team that the utility has 300 megawatts of untapped power capacity available at its Carbo plant, Litkenhous said in a September interview. The company is still waiting on this power purchase agreement to be finalized, he said Wednesday. He said Friday that he does not know when the agreement would happen, but it’s a key step toward moving forward with the project. He said that the cost of bringing that power to the site will not fall on customers and added that while power bills are going up across the board, “it will not be because of this data center.” Residents highlighted the rate increases Appalachian Power has already initiated and questioned how Litkenhous could guarantee the buildings’ increased usage wouldn’t have trickle-down effects. Previously, Litkenhous said that water consumption would depend on the clients that would ultimately occupy the buildings. He said at the meeting that Oasis has committed to using a closed-loop system to cool the buildings. Closed-loop cooling systems would reuse water but use more power, he previously said. He added Friday that there would still be regular water use anticipated for people working in the buildings. He said Wednesday that would likely fall between 5,000 and 10,000 gallons per day, per building, and that was less than a large office building. He said the water would not come from Lake Bonaventure, a 66-acre lake nearby. Oasis has not yet reached an agreement with the county’s public service authority, which the developers hope will provide the water, he said Friday. Pollution concerns Litkenhous said that as part of the project, Oasis will sign an agreement with the authority that will outline community benefits and parameters on development. Details will be shaped by feedback from the meeting, submitted public comments and another forum planned for the spring, he said. As part of the agreement, Oasis will commit to keeping the noise at an agreed-upon level, which would typically be between 55 and 60 decibels. He compared that level of sound to an electric dryer and said it would be measured at its property line. In addition to power from the grid, the data centers would also run backup generators on site intermittently, he said, including battery storage and tier four diesel generators, the emission standard required by state law. Potential stormwater runoff during construction and operations phases would be managed by a team of engineers, he said when questioned about impact to nearby Dumps Creek, which flows into the Clinch River. Litkenhous said Oasis would pay for any independent impact study if the county or authority calls for one. Noise, air and water pollution were front of mind for several speakers, as was whether any community benefit agreement could actually be enforced with the clients who would occupy the buildings. Nick Over, the co-founder of Oasis, said the agreement would carry with the land regardless of the final client, and Litkenhous said the county would be able to enforce its provisions. Consequences of any violations are yet to be determined, he said. Jennifer Chumbley, who lives on a neighboring farm, said noise travels in the mountains and asked whether it would reach her home in the middle of the night. On the Friday evening before the forum, Chumbley was part of a smaller group of people who met in a Cleveland community center to learn more about data centers and strategize before the forum. “My main question for you is this: Can you guarantee in writing, with 100% certainty, that this data center will not harm the health or well-being of our community or even one person who lives in it?” Chumbley asked the developers. “That’s the only question I have for you guys tonight.” Oasis developers answered some questions during the meeting, but wrote down several, including Chumbley’s, they said they would respond to later. Jobs and tax revenue The financial benefit of the potential data center campus is quantified by a projected $4.6 million in tax revenue per year, Litkenhous said during the meeting, a revision from the projection of $20 million per year that he gave in Septem

artigo.texto: Infrastructure is emerging as a standout investment trend heading into 2027, as spending on energy security and artificial intelligence fuels demand. Preqin data shows infrastructure fundraising rebounded sharply in the third quarter of 2026, with $62 billion raised across 21 funds, bringing this year's total to $101 billion across 65 funds. Rene Lubianski, managing partner, infrastructure at Brookfield Asset Management, said infrastructure is a "cornerstone" of the private markets giant's business during the group's third-quarter earnings call Nov. 6. The firm has raised roughly $50 billion in capital commitments across its infrastructure strategies over the past year. Earlier this month, Brookfield said the latest vintage of its flagship infrastructure strategy had received $26 billion in commitments, with $13 billion coming after the end of the quarter. "This puts us well on track to exceed our $30 billion target in early 2027," Lubianski said. "At that size, the fund would surpass the $28 billion raised for its predecessor to become the largest closed-end infrastructure fund ever raised. "If the current momentum continues, it could also become the largest closed-end private fund ever raised in any sector." 'A challenge and an opportunity' The fundraising surge is unfolding even as investors wait longer to exit existing infrastructure holdings. Portfolio companies owned by the 50 largest infrastructure general partners had an average holding period of 7.6 years in 2025, up from 6.1 years in 2021, according to Boston Consulting Group. Exit activity improved from the prior two years, although many transactions involved continuation vehicles and open-ended infrastructure funds, according to a BCG analysis published earlier this year. Looking ahead, institutional investors appear to have room to bulk up their infrastructure allocations. Goldman Sachs' latest annual 2026 Global Alternatives Survey — which polled some 225 institutional investors, including pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, insurance investors, family offices and other wealth managers between June and August — found that 43% of respondents have a more favorable outlook on infrastructure investment compared with a year ago, with 7% who were less favorable. Nearly half of investors, 49%, with a target allocation to infrastructure said they were under-allocated, compared with just 5% who were over-allocated, according to the study, published Oct. 21. "Geopolitical tensions and their effects on inflation, interest rates, and growth prospects continue to impact valuations and investors' ability to return capital. Those constraints coincide with extraordinary demand for private capital to finance the infrastructure supporting AI expansion — creating both a challenge and an opportunity," said Jeff Fine, global co-head of alternatives capital formation, Goldman Sachs Alternatives. Why infrastructure now J.P. Morgan Asset Management strategists said Nov. 12 that the sector stands to benefit from stronger government and corporate spending next year, while offering protection if that spending keeps inflation and interest rates elevated. Hugh Gimber, executive director and global market strategist at JPMAM, said infrastructure has some of the "strongest foundations" among alternative assets in the current economic environment. The sector has evolved over the past three years, Gimber noted, with data centers, communications networks, renewables and energy storage accounting for a growing share of investment alongside traditional assets such as transport and utilities, helping support returns. Power generation has been a standout, returning almost 40% a year over that period and 60% in the past year, according to JPMAM's 2027 Investment Outlook, published on Nov. 16. Defense and energy security concerns, coupled with the rise of AI, are also accelerating Europe's push for greater self-sufficiency — and the infrastructure needed to support it. "Infrastructure assets today are well geared to some of these stronger spending pushes," Gimber told media, including CNBC, at a recent macro outlook roundtable Nov. 12. "You have much more coming from digital, you have much more coming from renewables, and these tie in much better, particularly in Europe, to the self-sufficiency push that we see underway." Inflation protection JPMAM said a lasting resolution to the Middle East conflict could help ease inflationary pressures on economies next year. But if price pressures prove more persistent, infrastructure bets could also offer greater portfolio protection for investors. Karen Ward, managing director and EMEA chief market strategist at JPMAM, said renewed escalation in the conflict could push inflation higher, potentially triggering simultaneous falls in stocks and bonds. That risk strengthens the case for alternatives that can cushion portfolios against inflation shocks, she added. In an economy powered by higher spending, investors need protection against both recession and inflation — underscoring the need for a larger long-term allocation to alternatives, Ward said.

artigo.texto: Ford has started producing LFP battery cells at its BlueOval Battery Park Michigan facility in Marshall. The US$3 billion (RM12.4 billion) factory is owned and operated by Ford, but uses technology licensed from CATL. The first batch has been shipped to the Louisville plant in Kentucky for use in prototypes of the Fathom EV pick-up truck, which is planned for launch next year. Ford also plans to begin battery pack production at the Michigan facility in 2027, before the Fathom launches. The carmaker said in a release that the cells use a prismatic design and contain no nickel nor cobalt – helping cut production costs versus nickel-based battery chemistries – and that the “assembly lines can deliver 40 cells every minute, making it among the fastest LFP prismatic battery assembly lines outside of China.” Reuters quoted Ford advanced development projects VP Alan Clarke as saying that working with CATL was the fastest way to build affordable EVs in the US. “CATL being the biggest in the world, it means that they’re the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn how to produce LFP cells,” he said. Reuters reported in September that US transportation secretary Sean Duffy urged Ford CEO Jim Farley in a letter to sever ties with Chinese firms including CATL, Geely and BYD, and that China committee chair John Moolenaar said: “Ford should work with our nation’s allies, not our adversaries.” Ford replied in a statement that Duffy’s letter was a “wrongheaded attempt to capture headlines”, adding that “while others continue to import Chinese batteries, Ford is investing to build batteries here in America” and that “Ford owns the plant, controls the operation and employs the workforce.”

artigo.texto: Sungrow launches modular commercial energy storage range Mon, 23rd Nov 2026 (Today) Sungrow has launched a modular commercial and industrial energy storage portfolio that includes the PowerKeeper system and the new PowerKeeper Lite. The products are designed for commercial and industrial applications and can be paired with Sungrow's SHCX hybrid inverter series, including the SH50/80/100/110/125CX models and the SH30/40/50CX-P2 range. The launch expands Sungrow's offering in a market where businesses are seeking storage systems that can adapt to different site layouts, connect to varied grid conditions and reduce installation complexity. Organised under the "Keeper Family" brand, the portfolio centres on modular configurations across a power range of 50 kW to 125 kW and a capacity range of 50 kWh to 1,000 kWh. Safety focus PowerKeeper is positioned as the heavier-duty product in the line-up. Sungrow says the system uses a three-layer safety structure covering "proactive detection, instant interception, and physical containment". According to Sungrow, the system has undergone more than 700 tests from cell to system level. The company also highlighted features including 50 cm water-immersion protection, fire-spread prevention, resistance to triple-height drops and explosion venting. PowerKeeper is intended to address common issues in commercial and industrial storage projects, including site adaptation, installation, operation and maintenance, and performance in demanding grid environments. Sungrow also says the product uses energy management algorithms that can deliver an additional 10% to 30% in monthly revenue, although it did not provide further detail on the assumptions behind that figure. Installer design Alongside PowerKeeper, Sungrow introduced PowerKeeper Lite for the IP20 segment. The system is also compatible with Sungrow's existing SH50/80/100/110/125CX hybrid inverters and the SH30/40/50CX-P2 series. PowerKeeper Lite is designed for easier installation and servicing. Sungrow says the unit supports both vertical and horizontal layouts, allowing it to fit different indoor spaces. It also uses plug-in connections and wall-side cabling intended to reduce wiring work during deployment. For operation and maintenance, the system links to Sungrow's iSolarCloud remote diagnostics and control platform. On-site fault-finding is supported through an inverter viewing window and LED indicators at battery-pack level. The emphasis on installation reflects a broader issue in the commercial and industrial market, where deployment costs and site constraints can weigh heavily on project economics. Suppliers have increasingly focused on modular products that can be configured to suit space limitations and varied customer load profiles. Grid scale The Keeper Family is also intended for larger projects and more difficult grid conditions. According to Sungrow, the SHCX system can support direct parallel connection of up to 10 units, with on-grid and off-grid switching. It also includes virtual synchronous generator, or VSG, grid-forming functions. In microgrid use cases, Sungrow says battery storage can operate alongside diesel generators to meet changing demand while maintaining voltage and frequency stability. The portfolio supports a DC/AC ratio of 2.0 and charging at 1.6 times rated capacity. Sungrow also says a single unit can connect to photovoltaic modules at up to twice rated power, allowing excess solar generation to be stored rather than curtailed. Commercial and industrial energy storage has become an increasingly contested segment for suppliers of batteries, inverters and energy management software. Demand has risen as businesses seek to manage electricity costs, integrate more on-site solar generation and maintain supply through weaker or unstable grids. System flexibility has become a key selling point in that market, particularly in regions where industrial sites differ widely in available floor space, grid connection standards and backup power requirements. Products that can be scaled in smaller increments or installed in multiple orientations can reduce engineering changes and shorten deployment timelines. Speaking about the new line-up, Sungrow says the portfolio was built to cover a wide range of commercial and industrial scenarios. The company describes the products as combining modular design, simplified installation and broader grid adaptability across the range. "The PowerKeeper Family delivers comprehensive energy storage solutions across diverse C&I scenarios," Sungrow said.

artigo.texto: Want 24/7 clean power for data centers? Try giant heat batteries. Data center developers are scrambling to find enough electricity to power their energy-intensive facilities. Some are building their own fossil gas power plants. But that comes with tradeoffs — sky-high equipment costs, yearslong waits for backlogged turbines, and growing public backlash against their polluting plans. A new report from think tank Energy Innovation proposes a faster, cheaper, and cleaner route for powering off-grid data centers: giant heat batteries that are fueled by low-cost solar and wind. This “hybrid thermal power” approach can be cost-competitive with fossil gas in many parts of the country, said Eric Gimon, the report’s author and an Energy Innovation senior fellow. Even more important, it can deliver power within a year or two in places where renewable energy is under development, he said — much faster than the wait for a gas plant. “It’s a pretty simple solution that hyperscalers and developers can pursue,” Gimon said. “You can do off-grid that’s fast, clean, reliable, and affordable.” Nevertheless, Gimon said he’s unaware of a U.S. data center taking this approach today. That’s despite the availability of heat batteries from a number of different companies, including Antora, Brenmiller Energy, Electrified Thermal Solutions, and Rondo Energy. These energy storage systems use electricity to heat rocks, bricks, or other materials to temperatures exceeding 1,000 degrees Celsius (1,832 degrees Fahrenheit). The systems can retain that heat for hours, days, or even weeks at a time, and then dispatch it later. Most thermal storage systems installed today supply industrial process heat for everything from food processing to cement production. But they can also use that heat to boil water, spin a steam turbine, and produce electricity. Storing heat to make electricity has its drawbacks. The process recovers only about 40% of the total energy that’s been put into it, mainly because of losses in converting heat to steam and then to power, Gimon said. That’s not great, compared with the typical low-to-mid-90% “round-trip efficiency” rate for lithium-ion batteries. “But when I started modeling it, I realized TES [thermal energy storage] is cost-effective,” he said. Data centers that want to run independently of the grid and on clean energy will need to store enormous amounts of power for when solar and wind aren’t available. As long as the solar and wind power is cheap enough, and the value of the electricity being generated from the steam turbines is high enough, the efficiency losses are tolerable. In fact, thermal batteries would be cheaper than conventional lithium-ion storage over longer durations, Gimon said. Gimon also looked at how fossil-fueled boilers could run on fuel stored on-site, to give the thermal storage and gas turbines emergency backup power, much like data centers rely on emergency backup diesel generators today. This graphic shows how all the pieces fit together. All told, Gimon estimated that these “hybrid thermal power brick” systems can deliver reliable, round-the-clock power at a cost of about $120 per megawatt-hour — a figure that includes the cost of developing the renewables that deliver their primary power. Depending on where a data center is located, that can be competitive with building a dedicated gas-fired power plant. References range from about $72 per MWh for a data center in West Texas to the $140 to $165 per MWh that investment bank Jeffries estimated Meta is paying for an off-grid gas power plant in Ohio. But for large data center developers, “the issue right now isn’t so much cost, but speed to power,” Gimon said. Data center developers have proposed hundreds of gigawatts of gas-fired power plants across the country, but those plans are constrained by the gas-turbine supply chain, workforce availability, and pipeline capacity. By comparison, thermal energy storage systems are relatively new technologies whose producers are eager to scale up, he said. And while demand for steam turbines is beginning to tick up, those manufacturers are not nearly as backlogged, he said. Arpit Dwivedi, founder and CEO of thermal energy storage startup Cache Energy, agreed that the industry could scale up quickly. His company’s technology uses standard steel components and stores heat in limestone-derived pellets coated in a proprietary binder. Those components are “simple and abundant,” which makes it easier to “build things faster,” he said. The startup has enough manufacturing capacity today to build about a gigawatt-hour of its systems per year, “and we haven’t made a big deal about it,” Dwivedi said. He estimated the company could scale up to 10 GWh per year in 12 months and 100 GWh per year in 24 months without much trouble. Cache Energy has already deployed its technology to store on-site wind power for industrial heating and space heating, Dwivedi said. The company has been talking with data center developers about using its heat batteries for electricity generation, though he declined to share more information. For data center developers to adopt thermal energy storage at scale, “we need one or two real projects that show it really works” in that setting, he said. Hybrid thermal systems also open opportunities for solar and wind developers. Gimon estimated that a renewables-only project could boost its value threefold by adding a thermal battery and steam turbine that can deliver reliable “clean, firm” power. Landing an off-grid data center client could help them avoid the risk of yearslong wait times to connect to the grid, and would give them enough time to secure federal tax credits before they expire. Data center developers could also look to hybrid thermal systems to streamline their path to securing a grid interconnection, he said. artigo.texto: BYD Launches Second-Generation Seagull EV With Flash Charging The redesigned electric hatchback adds a fifth seat and optional Flash Charging, and it will take over from the larger Dolphin in BYD's lineup. Updated on Nov. 20, 2026 in Electric Vehicles Live Poll Would you consider buying an electric car as your next vehicle? BYD has released a second-generation Seagull electric car that adds a fifth seat and offers Flash Charging on certain versions, which can raise the battery from 10% to 70% in five minutes. BYD plans to use the new Seagull to replace the larger Dolphin hatchback in its lineup. Why it matters The Seagull led BYD's fully electric lineup in sales through September, with more than 245,000 units sold across the family. Its move to a larger body and faster charging positions it as a central model in the automaker's electric strategy. The new Seagull is 13.8 feet long and offers an 85-kilowatt motor with 114 horsepower or a 95-kilowatt motor with 127 horsepower, with CLTC-rated ranges of 199 to 261 miles depending on battery size. Flash Charging restores 20% to 97% in 12 minutes at minus-30 degrees Celsius, though the two lowest-priced variants do not include it as standard. The players BYD BYD is a Chinese automaker and battery manufacturer that has become one of the largest electric vehicle sellers in the world. The details The second-generation Seagull sends power to the rear wheels and uses a multilink independent rear suspension. It features a 15.6-inch infotainment screen, added physical buttons, a redesigned center console with storage, and the DiLink 150 smart cockpit on every version. The optional DiPilot 300 system adds roof-mounted lidar, city navigation assistance and smart parking. Timeline - September: Seagull leads BYD's fully electric lineup in sales. - November 20, 2026: Launch details of the new Seagull are reported. Roadmap The Seagull's launch extends BYD's Flash Charging battery technology into an entry-level body, showing how the company is moving fast-charging capability down its price range. The shift replaces the larger Dolphin hatchback, signaling a broader reshuffling of BYD's electric lineup as competition in affordable EVs intensifies. Buyers of the two lowest-priced Seagull variants will need to pay extra to get Flash Charging, since it is not standard on those trims. Prospective owners in China can currently get a starting price of $9,500 under the super trade-in promotion, while regular prices range from 65,900 to 99,900 yuan. The takeaway Fast charging is moving into mainstream, lower-priced electric cars, so buyers comparing EVs should check whether the charging feature is standard or an add-on on the trim they want. artigo.texto: Emerging Alternatives to UPS in Data Centers Data centers are exploring BESS, rack batteries, buffer modules, and microgrids as UPS alternatives, with hybrid backup designs often the most practical path. For decades, uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems have been an essential component of most data centers. By providing short-term backup power and helping regulate voltage to servers and other IT equipment, UPS units have played a key role in maintaining uptime. But the power landscape is changing. A growing number of alternatives to traditional UPS devices are emerging, and many promise advantages such as longer runtimes, lower maintenance requirements, or better space efficiency. Here is a look at several emerging UPS alternatives, along with guidance on when it may make sense for data centers to move away from conventional UPS systems – or adopt a hybrid strategy that combines newer technologies with tried-and-true UPS infrastructure. Why Traditional UPS Strategies Are Under Pressure Before exploring specific alternatives, it is worth considering why UPS systems may no longer be the ideal answer for every data center’s power protection and backup needs. One major factor is the rise in data center power consumption. The more power a facility draws during normal operations, the more UPS capacity it needs to support critical loads during an outage. Because UPS systems can be expensive to deploy and often require battery replacements every 3 to 5 years, operators experiencing rapid power growth may be motivated to evaluate alternatives. The increasing use of on-site power generation is another driver. As more data centers add generation assets to supplement or reduce reliance on the grid, the preferred response to a power disruption may be an immediate transfer to on-site generation rather than depending solely on a centralized UPS to bridge the gap. Some new power protection architectures are designed specifically to support that model. Alternatives to Traditional UPS Systems Data center operators that decide conventional UPS systems are no longer the best fit have several options to consider. Battery Energy Storage Systems Extend Backup Duration Battery energy storage systems (BESS) use high-capacity batteries to store large amounts of electricity. Today, they are most commonly deployed to capture energy from renewable sources such as solar or wind for later use. But they can also play a role in data center backup power strategies. BESS and UPS systems both rely on stored battery power, but BESS systems are typically designed on a much larger scale. That distinction matters because a BESS deployment can provide backup power for much longer periods than a traditional UPS. While many UPS systems are designed to bridge only 10 to 15 minutes, BESS can support loads for hours, depending on system size and configuration. The tradeoff is cost. BESS generally requires a higher upfront investment and more complex integration. However, for data centers that experience longer outages, want to store renewable energy, or are building more flexible on-site energy strategies, BESS can be an attractive alternative or complement to UPS infrastructure. Rack-Level Batteries Save Space and Localize Protection Most data center UPS systems are centralized, supporting dozens or even hundreds of servers from a single installation. That model is relatively straightforward, but it also consumes valuable floor space that could otherwise be used to increase density and capacity. Rack-level batteries address that challenge by placing backup power directly inside the rack. In effect, they provide localized power protection without requiring the same dedicated floor footprint as a large, centralized UPS. They can also help reduce the heat concentration associated with larger battery rooms or UPS installations. Rack-level batteries share some of the same limitations as traditional UPS systems, including periodic replacement and lifecycle management. Still, they offer important space-saving advantages at a time when many operators are under pressure to maximize capacity within existing facilities. Buffer Modules Bridge Short Power Interruptions As their name implies, buffer modules are designed to absorb brief power interruptions or voltage fluctuations. If a server suddenly loses its primary power source, a buffer module can deliver enough energy to keep the equipment running while power is transferred to another source. Historically, buffer modules could bridge only milliseconds of downtime. Newer systems, however, can provide coverage for up to 20 seconds – long enough in some cases to support the startup of a diesel generator or another on-site generation source. That capacity is what makes buffer modules a possible alternative to traditional UPS deployments in certain environments. If the goal is to maintain server operation only long enough for on-site generation to come online, buffer modules may offer a lower-cost, low-maintenance option than a full UPS system. On-Site Microgrids Reshape Backup Power Planning Most data centers still rely primarily on the utility grid, using on-site generators only for backup or supplemental power. But some facilities are investing in on-site microgrids – collections of generation and energy assets capable of serving a substantial share of the facility’s power needs on an ongoing basis. In the right configuration, the microgrid can reduce dependence on traditional UPS architecture by improving resiliency and enabling faster transfer to local power sources. If sufficient generation capacity is available and the system is designed with appropriate redundancy, the facility may rely less on large, centralized UPS systems for extended backup coverage. That said, microgrids do not automatically eliminate the need for power conditioning or ride-through protection. artigo.texto: Swedish battery storage company Polarium declared bankrupt Swedish battery storage company Polarium was declared bankrupt by the Stockholm District Court on Friday, the company said in a statement. Polarium Energy Solutions AB, which develops lithium-ion energy storage systems for telecom, real estate, industrial and residential customers, filed for bankruptcy earlier in the day after concluding there was “no basis for continuing to operate the business in its current form.” Mikael Kubu of Ackordscentralen has been appointed bankruptcy trustee and now takes over responsibility for the company, including whether to keep it running and whether to start a sale process. The company blamed sharply falling battery prices driven by growing competition from Chinese suppliers, reduced demand from the telecom industry and delays in some distributed battery energy storage (BESS) development projects. China has expanded battery manufacturing far faster than demand has grown, the company said, and that overcapacity, combined with a shift to cheaper battery chemistry, has pushed down prices across the value chain and sharply cut gross margins. At the same time, telecom operators and tower companies have scaled back investment after several years of steady growth, just as Polarium had invested heavily to meet rising demand. “Like the auto industry, several European battery and energy storage companies have been hit hard by the dramatic increase in competition from Chinese players, and a number of European manufacturers have been forced to file for bankruptcy or restructure financially,” said Harald Mix, Polarium’s chairman. Polarium said it has made extensive cost cuts and reorganized in recent years, more than halving its operating expenses since 2024, but demand has remained too low relative to costs. The board had been weighing options for some time. It tried without success to find a buyer for all or part of the business and evaluated a court-supervised reorganization, but concluded that the funding need was too large for that to succeed, leaving bankruptcy as the only alternative. Mix said he and the other major shareholders had contributed substantial capital since he became chairman just over two years ago, including more than $34 million (SEK 350 million) from his private investment company. “That gave us time to make important changes and to honor our commitments to customers. But despite extensive measures, we have not managed to build a business that can hold up over the long term in an extremely competitive market,” he said. Mix said he would open talks with the trustee on whether the most viable parts of the business can be carried forward, so that expertise, customer relationships and some jobs can be saved. He is prepared to look into whether his private investment company could finance such an acquisition, and if so, he intends to find a solution in which most of the ownership goes to employees and the other shareholders. “Our hope is that the trustee will choose to keep the business running for now, with continued support for customers, while options for the future are examined without delay,” Mix said. Chief executive Pontus Winberg said the company is doing everything it can to keep the business running after the bankruptcy, but that further cost cuts are necessary and employees will have to leave. Polarium is the second Swedish battery company tied to Mix to go bankrupt in less than two years. Founded in 2015, it was the first company launched by Vargas, the investment firm Mix co-founded with Carl-Erik Lagercrantz. Vargas went on to co-found Northvolt, once Europe’s leading contender to build battery cells for electric vehicles, which filed for bankruptcy in March 2025.

artigo.texto: VNET Group Q3 2026: Wholesale Data Center Capacity Surges 44% on AI Demand As seen on the 24/7 Wall St. homepage on November 23, 2026. AI demand is showing up in the capacity numbers: wholesale data center capacity in service jumped 44% year over year to 1,127MW, plus a fresh 60MW order from a major cloud provider. The loss per ADS beat expectations, full-year revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance was reaffirmed, and the board authorized a $50 million ADS buyback against a $611 million market cap. Continue ReadingShow less VNET Group posted a GAAP loss per ADS of $0.04 for the third quarter of 2026, beating expectations. Part of that came from a fair-value gain on financial instruments that meaningfully narrowed the net loss attributable to VNET to $12.44 million, compared with $45.97 million in the same period a year earlier. VNET reported $443.66 million in total net revenues, missing expectations, though the figure still represented 15.4% growth year over year. Wholesale IDC was the strongest segment, with revenues up 27.6% year over year and reaching 41.1% of total net revenues, while retail IDC grew a more modest 5.1%. Wholesale data center capacity in service jumped 44% year over year to 1,127MW, and the quarter ended with a fresh 60MW order from a leading cloud service provider, a concrete signal that AI-driven demand is translating into contracted business. Another 548MW of wholesale capacity was under construction at quarter end. Sponsored Despite the revenue miss, management reaffirmed its full-year 2026 guidance, targeting revenues of $1.72 billion to $1.77 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $531.47 million to $561.41 million. The board also authorized a $50 million ADS repurchase program, a notable capital return commitment against a $611 million market cap. Risks worth watching include gross margin compression from heavier depreciation as the rapid capacity build comes online, a wholesale utilization rate that slipped to 70.7% from 74.3% a year earlier as new capacity ramps up, and a significant debt load. Regulatory scrutiny around Chinese firms accessing Nvidia computing power abroad adds an additional layer of uncertainty the guidance does not fully address. Sources Mentioned: VNET

artigo.texto: SpaceX wants to build a data center in the Arizona desert that would draw 6,000 megawatts of power at full build-out. That is nearly two-thirds of the all-time peak demand that Arizona Public Service, which serves about 1.5 million homes and businesses, hit across its entire system this summer, according to KJZZ. The Cochise County campus is the larger half of a plan SpaceX announced on Nov. 12 to spend more than $74 billion on two AI supercomputing sites: roughly $50 billion in southeastern Arizona and more than $24 billion at Starbase, Texas, Reuters reported. The company is pitching both as projects that pay for themselves, with on-site power in Texas, dry cooling in Arizona, and promises of lower bills and taxes for neighbors. Residents, local officials, and now Arizona’s attorney general want proof first. Who covers the cost of the power plants, water, and grid upgrades behind AI, the company or the people who live next door, is quickly becoming the question that decides whether these campuses get built. The stakes for SpaceX are large. Its AI segment produced more than half of its third-quarter revenue, ahead of rockets and Starlink, according to Reuters, and Fortune has reported on how renting out computing capacity to Anthropic and Google has become central to the company’s valuation. The political ground is shifting under the industry, too: voters sided against data center development in 37 of 38 local ballot contests with complete counts this month, as Fortune reported after the midterms. In Texas, a land swap puts the project past a moratorium The Texas campus is a gas-fired power plant and “super-compute facility” on 444.45 acres near the Port of Brownsville, The Texas Tribune reported. Brownsville de-annexed the land earlier this year at SpaceX’s request, after the company offered $220 million for city water and wastewater projects. The neighboring city of Starbase, which incorporated around SpaceX’s launch site in 2025, then annexed it. That sequence leaves the project outside the reach of Brownsville’s 90-day data center moratorium, which took effect in early November. The city says its decision was based on the “information and circumstances presented at the time.” Because the plant would generate its own electricity, SpaceX says the facility won’t draw from the public grid. It will still burn a lot of gas. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality issued an air permit on Nov. 16 that allows 35 natural gas turbines producing 750 megawatts and up to 248 tons of nitrogen oxides a year, Newsweek reported, citing Politico. The South Texas Environmental Justice Network has announced a protest, arguing the facilities would pollute the air, use up water, and raise residents’ energy bills. Other residents see opportunity. “There’s a lot of people that need jobs in our community and SpaceX has contributed to those jobs,” Janie Melendez, a Brownsville school teacher who previously served on the Texas Republican Party’s executive committee, told the Tribune. Melendez has felt SpaceX’s pull in another way. “Since SpaceX moved in, my home has tripled in value,” she said. Rising values are a win for owners, but they tend to lift property tax bills and rents, which can squeeze newer residents and renters. The tax question is now live. On Nov. 17, Cameron County commissioners voted 3-2 against moving ahead with talks on a 10-year, 100% property tax abatement for the project. Starbase’s own city commission is scheduled to consider a tax abatement on Dec. 9. And in January, SpaceX will face a new governor, Gina Hinojosa, who has vowed to freeze data center approvals until lawmakers pass new protections. In Arizona, a 6-gigawatt campus tests a rural grid The Arizona campus would sit on 747 acres near the Willcox Playa, about 80 miles east of Tucson, according to the Arizona Daily Star. It would take power from the grid through the Sulphur Springs Valley Electric Cooperative and the Arizona Electric Power Cooperative, and SpaceX says the nearby Apache Generating Station, which burns coal and natural gas, would grow from about 1 gigawatt to more than 6 gigawatts. The permit application lists $3.6 billion in planned grid upgrades. SpaceX’s pitch to the county is aggressive. At a community meeting, Riley Trettle, who heads SpaceX’s energy and supercomputer department, said the project would reduce residents’ electricity bills, lower property taxes by 20%, and create about 1,000 permanent jobs, according to the Star. The application projects a one-time $250 million sales tax benefit for the county and $35 million to $103 million in sales tax revenue, and the company expects about 5,500 construction jobs. Water is the sharper worry. The campus would be dry-cooled and would not pump groundwater for industrial use, though an existing well could supply up to 10 acre-feet a year for drinking water and maintenance. Residents point to an aquifer already drawn down by large dairy farms, and experts told the Star that the water used to generate the campus’s power could raise annual data center water use by 60% to 90%. The permit doesn’t estimate that figure. On Nov. 19, Attorney General Kris Mayes asked the Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission to postpone its Dec. 9 vote until state and federal agencies can review the project. Her letter questions how SpaceX would cover power needs beyond what the regional cooperative can generate, and raises concerns about water, fire safety, traffic, wildlife, and nearby Fort Huachuca. “The people of Cochise County deserve answers before county officials approve a project of this magnitude,” Mayes said in a statement. She plans her own town hall at Cochise Elementary School on Dec. 3. Is growth paying for growth? Arizona’s larger utilities are already wrestling with the same cost split. artigo.texto: Protesters demand Anne Arundel County close data center loophole in Severn expansion fight Protesters are demanding the Anne Arundel County Council close a loophole in a data center moratorium that allows the expansion of existing facilities. A crowd of protesters demonstrated Saturday on Telegraph Road in Hanover in opposition to an expansion of a data center in Severn. "Why didn't they close that loophole when they had an opportunity?" said Micheala Burgnon, with Indivisible Odenton. The County Council voted to extend a moratorium on building new data centers until 2028, but the moratorium does not apply to expanding existing facilities, including a 110,000-square-foot data center in Severn, where the owner wants add another 89,000 square feet to it. "The expansion would more or less drop a data center the same size as the existing one right next to the existing one," said Erin Sherman, with Indivisible Odenton. The plan also calls for demolishing existing paved areas on the west side of the building and installing 13 backup generators. The owners have not said what type of fuel they want to use, which, coupled with a lack of information in general about the facility, is troubling to residents. "I think of data centers as kind of a necessary evil. My problem is with a lack of transparency surrounding them as well as the unknown environmental aspects," said Kiri Shipp, a resident "We don't know enough about this data center and what's happening right in our back yard," said Starr Hood, a resident. Protest organizers with Indivisible Odenton started a petition drive to get the Anne Arundel County Council to close the loophole. Organizers canvassed neighborhoods collecting signatures. "(We're) asking them to stop the expansion. We've got over 1,000 signatures on that petition so far," Burgnon said. The petition will be delivered to the next meeting of the County Council on Dec. 7.

artigo.texto: Stafford County residents raise concerns over massive data center project during town hall STAFFORD COUNTY, Va. (7News) — For the second time in recent days, Stafford County residents voiced concerns over a massive data center project expected to come to a vote in less than a month. The Stafford County Board of Supervisors is considering a proposal that would build 37 data centers on 9 million square feet of land along Kings Highway near I-95. More than 100 residents signed up to speak about this project during the public comment period for Thursday's planning commission meeting. SEE ALSO | Tracking potential high impact Thanksgiving Day nor'easter On Sunday, dozens of residents sounded off during a town hall meeting hosted by Board of Supervisors Chairman Deuntay Diggs. "Obviously, I'm against the data centers. I want Stafford to just be a sleepy bedroom community. What is wrong with that? Why do we have to be all this stuff? And remember, every time you put a data center on a piece of property, that's a place you can't have your magical stuff for people to do in Stafford County because now there's no land available," one resident said. Another resident added, "We just know this is too big of a project to do all at one time without knowing what the impact's going to be 15 years down the road." At both meetings, community members raised concerns about electricity use and costs, property values and health. During Sunday's town hall, residents lined up behind microphones to directly address Diggs. "I do think it's going to impact my hearing, my ability to enjoy my property peacefully, which I have a right to," one resident said. Another resident echoed this sentiment: "There is nothing to stop this grotesque health problem, this hazard. I want to know how you guys react to, 'Is it the money we need, or is it the people we're going to protect?'" Members on the board of supervisors have expressed the need for these facilities because of the tax revenue they could bring. Diggs and other officials have estimated this project could generate millions of dollars each year. "Overall, the project is going to bring in about $193 million. When you look at the general government, this is just an approximate number, we're at about $220 million to run just the general government itself," Diggs said. "We could fund our first responders, increases for salaries for our educators. It helps with a multitude of issues, in terms of our water throughout the county." 7News On Your Side asked Diggs why the board is considering this project despite the opposition heard at both of these recent meetings. "Well, the issue is we need revenue here in Stafford, and we've raised taxes for five consecutive years on our constituents. When I look at our last election, it was about affordability. We're looking at how do we fill that gap, not just with data centers, but overall economic development," Diggs said. "We're listening to our constituents, and we're put in a predicament right now where constituents are saying, 'Do not raise our taxes,' but then they're also not wanting data centers. We're trying to figure out what other economic development can fill the revenue gap." The Stafford County Board of Supervisors is expected to vote on this project on Dec. 15.

artigo.texto: Abeeólica vai ao STF contra leilão de baterias Associação de energia eólica questiona constitucionalidade de deixar conta com geradores e pede cautelar para suspender disputa Depois de acionar a Justiça Federal para suspender o leilão baterias, a Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias) entrou com uma nova ação no Supremo Tribunal Federal para contestar o rateio dos custos de contratação do certame, marcado para 2 e 4 de dezembro. A ADI (Ação Direta de Inconstitucionalidade) protocolada no STF na 5ª feira (19.nov.2026) questiona a constitucionalidade de um trecho da Lei 15.269 de 2025, conhecida como Reforma do Setor Elétrico, que determina que os custos de contratação de reserva de capacidade por meio de sistemas de armazenamento em baterias sejam rateados exclusivamente entre os geradores de energia. Leia a íntegra da ação (PDF – 1,2 kB).0 Diferentemente do pleito feito na Justiça Federal, a Abeeólica não pede ao Supremo o adiamento ou cancelamento do certame, mas a suspensão imediata do trecho questionado. Na prática, a associação cobra que a regra que atribui o custo aos geradores não seja aplicada nos leilões de reserva de capacidade. A entidade solicita ainda que o pedido liminar seja apreciado pelos ministros com urgência, antes da realização dos leilões, seja por decisão monocrática ou pelo plenário, sem audiência prévia dos órgãos envolvidos. Embora os 2 pedidos tenham finalidades distintas, os argumentos usados pela Abeeólica são os mesmos. A associação defende que a implementação das sistemas de baterias busca garantir segurança e a estabilidade de todo o sistema elétrico nacional, beneficiando diretamente todos os consumidores. Por isso, sustenta que atribuir a conta apenas aos geradores fere os princípios de isonomia, livre concorrência e segurança jurídica. A entidade afirma que há tratamento discriminatório e quebra da neutralidade tecnológica nas contratações. No modelo tradicional de leilões de reserva de capacidade do setor elétrico, o encargo é cobrado de todos os consumidores finais. Para a Abeeólica, o certame deveria seguir a mesma regra das demais disputas, já que as baterias oferecem a mesma finalidade sistêmica. Segundo a associação, teria “isolado” a tecnologia de baterias para ser custeada apenas pelos geradores, sem justificativa técnica ou jurídica plausível. PROCESSO QUESTIONA ANEEL O outro processo instaurado pela associação, que corre na Justiça Federal desde 2ª feira (16.nov), pede pedindo que a disputa não seja realizada antes da definição das regras sobre quem arcará com os custos de contratação dos sistemas e como se dará o rateio das despesas. Leia a íntegra da ação (PDF – 19 MB). Além de classificar como inconstitucional o mesmo trecho da lei que atribui exclusivamente aos geradores o custeio da contratação de baterias, o processo também questiona as regras propostas pela Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) para dividir as despesas entre os diferentes geradores. A Ação Civil Pública contesta os critérios de rateio definidos pela agência, que propôs fatias de 25% a 100% de participação entre os diferentes geradores, dependendo da flexibilidade da fonte de geração. Nesse modelo, usinas eólicas, solares e nucleares pagariam mais, enquanto térmicas arcariam com gastos intermediários e as hidrelétricas ficariam com os menores custos. Segundo a associação, o formato faria algumas geradoras pagarem até 4 vezes mais que outras, sem critérios jurídicos claros. As regras sobre o rateio foram colocadas em consulta pública pela Aneel, mas ainda não foram aprovadas definitivamente pela agência. Como ainda não há regulamentação definida, a avaliação é que seria impossível para agentes de geração calcular os riscos e impactos econômicos antes de dar lances no leilão. Na ação, a associação cita estimativas do TCU (Tribunal de Contas da União) de que os contratos provenientes do leilão podem somar de R$ 108 a R$ 153 bilhões. CONGRESSO ATUA PARA MUDAR REGRAS Em paralelo ao debate regulatório, o Congresso discute uma mudança na lei para retirar dos geradores a obrigação exclusiva de custear as baterias. Em 13 de outubro, a Câmara aprovou o regime de urgência do PL 3.716 de 2026, apresentado pelo deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP). A proposta, que está sob relatoria do deputado Danilo Forte (PP-CE), revoga o trecho da lei de 2025 e estabelece a aplicação da regra geral de divisão dos custos. O texto pode ser votado pelos deputados nas próximas semanas. Conforme já antecipado pela Aneel, caso o texto seja aprovado antes da realização do leilão, o edital precisaria ser alterado, pois as despesas passariam a ser divididas entre os usuários finais do SIN (Sistema Interligado Nacional), incluindo consumidores. PARA QUE SERVEM AS BATERIAS Os sistemas de armazenamento permitem guardar a energia produzida nos momentos de maior oferta e devolvê-la à rede quando o consumo aumenta. Na geração solar, por exemplo, as baterias podem ser carregadas durante o dia, quando há maior produção, e despachadas no início da noite, período em que a oferta solar cai e a demanda é mais elevada. O mecanismo ajuda a reduzir o desperdício de energia e fornece flexibilidade ao sistema. As baterias podem ser acionadas rapidamente para equilibrar geração e consumo, embora não substituam os investimentos necessários na expansão das redes de transmissão e distribuição.

artigo.texto: In Boost form, the revised 2027 Seal U DM-i can charge from 30% to 80% in 15 minutes. The same charge takes 20 minutes in Comfort and Design, using DC charging at up to 55 kW. BYD says that is three times the charging power of previous versions, which were limited to 18 kW. All three trims also support AC charging at up to 11 kW. The change comes with a switch to a 1.5-litre turbo petrol engine rated at 130 CV throughout the range. In the front-wheel-drive versions, it replaces the previous naturally aspirated engine. BYD Iberia managing director Alberto de Aza said the company had acted on customer feedback about areas needing improvement. Spanish automotive coverage published on 19 and 20 November 2026 reported that the updated model was already available in the Peninsula and Balearic Islands. The Boost pairs the petrol engine with a 204 CV electric motor, for a total of 238 CV, 9% more than before. The electric motor in the previous configuration was rated at 218 CV. Its 18.3 kWh Blade Battery is rated for 80 km of electric driving and a combined range of 980 km. Acceleration from 0 to 100 km/h takes 8.1 seconds. Comfort also produces 238 CV, but keeps the 26.6 kWh battery. BYD quotes 130 km of electric range and 1,030 km combined, the highest combined figure in the range. It takes 8.4 seconds to go from 0 to 100 km/h. Design adds a second 204 CV electric motor at the rear axle, giving it all-wheel drive and a combined maximum of 374 CV. It reaches 100 km/h from rest in 5.1 seconds. A presentation by BYD dealer Autos Carretero in Albacete on 20 November quoted a 5.2-second time. Its 26.6 kWh battery brings the quoted electric range to 114 km, a 62.8% increase. Combined range is 914 km. Chassis revisions include a four-link independent rear suspension and double-pinion steering. BYD says the changes improve cornering stability and motorway comfort. The steering is intended to feel more precise. Two extra front parking sensors have been added. The car also has a tyre-pressure monitoring system and an assistance function for a high-speed puncture. The boot now holds 530 litres in Boost and Comfort, or 510 litres in Design, after changes to the side panels and a slightly lower floor. Google Built-in comes as standard. The central display measures 12.8 inches in Boost and 15.6 inches in the other trims. This in-car technology is separate from Spain's radio infrastructure plans, including the DAB+ coverage framework for RTVE. In Spain, Boost starts at €30,790. Comfort costs €34,490, while the all-wheel-drive Design is priced at €36,990. These figures apply in mainland Spain and the Balearic Islands and include BYD promotional campaigns, Plan Auto+ aid and a financing discount. Reported pre-discount prices are €39,300 for Boost and €43,500 for Comfort. The fully electric Seal U starts at €32,541 for Comfort and €35,736 for Design. Those prices also include a Certificado de Ahorro Energético.

O movimento também ampliou os prazos e os riscos enfrentados pelas construtoras. Como resultado, os custos de construção subiram 13% em relação ao ano anterior, mais que o dobro da taxa global, segundo um novo relatório da Turner & Townsend, empresa internacional de gerenciamento de projetos. A alta registrada neste ano foi aproximadamente três vezes a média dos últimos dez anos. O estudo analisou mais de 500 projetos em andamento ou concluídos recentemente, distribuídos por 62 mercados globais, e incluiu uma pesquisa com 400 especialistas do setor de data centers em todo o mundo. Leia também: Por que empresas de inteligência artificial estão investindo bilhões em data centers? Embora tenha ocorrido alguma estabilização da inflação dos custos neste ano, ela não foi suficiente para compensar o forte crescimento da demanda e a velocidade exigida na construção e na entrega dos empreendimentos. “Cronogramas mais agressivos levam, especialmente, empreiteiras e subcontratadas a incorporar maiores margens para riscos em seus preços”, afirmou Paul Barry, responsável pela área de data centers da Turner & Townsend na América do Norte. “Sejam adicionais pela aceleração, mais horas extras e incentivos para atrair trabalhadores, ou mesmo taxas mais altas por assumir o risco de entregar em um ritmo mais rápido do que o habitual”, explicou. Todos esses fatores, somados ao salto da demanda e à pressão sobre a cadeia de suprimentos, se traduzem em custos maiores, acrescentou. Leia também: AIE aponta que consumo de energia em data centers pode duplicar até 2030 Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC Os investimentos de capital em data centers no mundo devem passar de cerca de US$ 800 bilhões (R$ 4,72 trilhões) neste ano para US$ 1,8 trilhão (R$ 10,62 trilhões) por ano em 2050, segundo relatório recente da PwC. A expectativa é que os Estados Unidos concentrem quase metade dos investimentos globais em infraestrutura de IA, incluindo data centers e chips. A eletricidade é essencial para essas instalações, e 56% dos participantes da pesquisa global da Turner & Townsend apontaram a disponibilidade de energia como um grande obstáculo à entrega dos projetos. Pouco mais da metade afirmou que as conexões às redes elétricas normalmente levam de um a dois anos; quase um terço relatou prazos superiores a dois anos. Os custos de energia variam conforme a região: de US$ 15,01 (R$ 88,56) por watt no Vale do Silício a US$ 10,51 (R$ 62,01) por watt em Dallas, considerando um projeto típico de 60 megawatts. Leia também: Energia vira gargalo para data centers e limita avanço da IA Assim como em outros segmentos da construção nos Estados Unidos, a falta de trabalhadores continua sendo um obstáculo significativo. Pouco mais de um quarto dos entrevistados afirmou que a capacidade das empreiteiras de administrar o volume de obras pendentes era suficiente. Para o próximo ano, Barry espera alguma moderação, com aumentos de custos na faixa de 6% a 10%. Muitos dos grandes projetos já começaram ou estão começando agora, de modo que os riscos de custos foram incorporados aos contratos. “Se essa demanda continuar, haverá um fluxo contínuo de novos projetos e assim por diante, mas acredito que tivemos um grande salto em 2026, especialmente de novos projetos de grande porte que foram contratados”, afirmou Barry. 🔷 Canal 562 ClaroTV+ | Canal 562 Sky | Canal 592 Vivo | Canal 187 Oi | Operadoras regionais 🔷 TV SINAL ABERTO: parabólicas canal 562 🔷 ONLINE: www.timesbrasil.com.br | YouTube 🔷 FAST Channels: Samsung TV Plus, LG Channels, TCL Channels, Pluto TV, Roku, Zapping | Novos Streamings Este conteúdo foi fornecido pela CNBC Internacional e a responsabilidade exclusiva pela tradução para o português é do Times Brasil.

artigo.texto: COP31 in Türkiye saw the launch of a Global Energy Storage Alliance (GESA), with 27 co-initiating organisations at the outset. The alliance was founded by the China Energy Storage Alliance, the China Renewable Energy Engineering Institute, and China Southern Power Grid Energy Storage. Co-initiators include CATL (HKG:3750), BYD Energy Storage, and other industry players. GESA brings together battery manufacturers, power utilities, state-owned enterprises, and research institutions to collaborate on six key areas. These include facilitating international dialogue, building a global storage project and standards database, advancing research and technology, improving market mechanisms, strengthening supply chains and trade, and mobilising investment, particularly in developing economies. GESA describes itself as open, technologically neutral, and market-oriented. The alliance is dominated by organisations and companies from China, though it also includes ACWA Power (TADAWUL:2082) from Saudi Arabia, among other international co-initiators. With China continuing to lead the battery and energy storage industries, GESA provides another potential path to strengthen that position. However, its influence will depend on securing broader international participation. For China, the alliance provides a way to develop international standards for energy storage products that will inevitably be exported globally. As the battery energy storage industry expands, GESA’s focus on international standards, capacity building, and climate action, alongside its goal of increasing investment in developing economies, aligns with COP’s drive for an equitable and just transition. Following its COP31 launch, GESA has invited international industry players to join the platform to help align technical standards and mobilise storage investment in emerging markets. artigo.texto: Under the new rules, installations and shipping companies must generally surrender emissions allowances by 30 September each year. The decree entered into force on 22 November, the day after its publication in the BOE. Real Decreto-ley 41/2026, dated 20 November and published in BOE No. 290 on 21 November, amends Law 1/2005, Spain’s emissions-trading statute, and transposes Directives (EU) 2023/958 and 2023/959. For shipping companies, the surrender requirement will be phased in until it covers 100% of verified emissions from 2026 onwards. Maritime coverage also depends on the voyage: 100% of emissions are covered on voyages between ports under EU member-state jurisdiction, while 50% are covered on voyages from a port outside the EU to a port under a member state’s jurisdiction. The BOE text refers to emissions verified and recorded for 2024, including allowance deliveries entered in the Union Registry. The law also lets certain shipping companies seek reimbursement from commercial operators for allowance costs. That does not remove the shipping companies’ own obligations. Until 31 December 2030, ships with ice class IA or IA Super, or an equivalent class under HELCOM Recommendation 25/7, may surrender 5% fewer allowances. The Ministry of Transport and Sustainable Mobility is responsible for the maritime system, including its monitoring and verification requirements. Repeated non-compliance can lead to orders expelling or immobilising vessels. A separate emissions-trading system covers fuels consumed in buildings, road transport and other sectors. The regulated entities are companies that release those fuels for consumption, not the final consumers. They need authorisation and must submit annual verified emissions reports by 30 April. From 2028 to 2030, they must also report the average share of allowance costs passed on to consumers. Hospitals that meet the specified conditions may qualify for financial compensation. The BOE text says the decree transposes Directives (UE) 2023/958 and 2023/959, which amend the EU emissions-trading framework established by Directive 2003/87/CE. The changes extend the system to maritime transport and establish a separate fuel scheme under the EU’s «Objetivo 55» package. Spain says transposition is needed to access the Social Climate Fund, established by Regulation (EU) 2023/955. The fund supports vulnerable households and microenterprises, as well as vulnerable transport users. It is financed mainly through a share of EU revenue from emissions-allowance auctions. To receive funding, member states must submit national Social Climate Plans that meet the regulation’s requirements. A proposed Spanish Plan Social para el Clima envisages more than €9 billion for measures and investment aimed at reducing vulnerable groups’ dependence on fossil fuels. The proposal went through public consultation and information proceedings in May and June 2026. More than half of its proposed resources are earmarked for housing, including over €4.7 billion for work in that area. The plan remains a proposal. A separate account of campaign proposals in Zaragoza appears in earlier campaign coverage. For aviation, the decree updates free allowance rules and creates a reserve for sustainable aviation fuels and other eligible non-fossil fuels covering 2024 to 2030. It also sets out rules for returning allowances received incorrectly and meeting obligations under the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). Operators must report annually on aviation’s non-CO2 climate effects. Industrial installations face revised free-allocation rules. Certain sites subject to energy-audit requirements may receive reduced allocations if they fail to follow recommendations. Installations whose emissions exceed the 80th percentile of relevant benchmarks must submit climate-neutrality plans. Verification of targets and milestones is a condition of receiving the free allocation available under EU rules. A new chapter also makes the Ministry for Ecological Transition and the Demographic Challenge the national authority for the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (MAFC), working with customs authorities and the European Commission. Other provisions extend beyond emissions trading. The decree changes rules for data centres, including a compensation system for deviations from additionality and hourly-correlation requirements. It establishes offences for breaches involving those requirements or energy and water efficiency, as well as certain sustainability disclosures. Operators hosting public-sector information systems classified as category ALTA face digital-sovereignty duties and may be subject to corrective orders and penalties. Their responsibility is limited to matters within their direct or contractual control. For electric-vehicle charging stations, the power threshold relevant to certain permits and public-utility declarations falls from 3,000 kW to 250 kW. Some electricity-supply infrastructure can avoid administrative authorisations if it does not require environmental assessment or seek public-utility status, and if the required project documents are filed in advance. A separate amendment provides an exemption route for qualifying charging-station infrastructure of up to 3,000 kW. The decree also recognises electricity consumed from nearby storage installations associated with consumption as renewable self-consumption. The government cited the overdue transposition deadline and infringement proceedings against Spain to justify using an emergency decree. Its final provision sets 22 November 2026 as the date the decree enters into force.

artigo.texto: SK Broadband plans to reach KRW 5 trillion in annual sales by 2030, and it wants to get there after cutting its data center and submarine cable businesses loose. Korean outlet 헤럴드경제 and The Information both reported the target as the company laid out its post-spinoff strategy. The plan turns a telecom operator that has leaned on infrastructure assets into a company built around three businesses: fixed-line, media and enterprise. The SK Broadband data center spinoff creates a new company called SK Horizon, which takes over the data center and submarine cable operations. SK Broadband keeps its name and, by its own estimate, keeps more than KRW 4 trillion in annual sales and roughly KRW 1.2 trillion in EBITDA. This analysis walks through what the numbers imply, what the financing tells us, and which details remain unconfirmed as of November 23, 2026. Korean carriers are in a busy stretch. Our recent look at KT’s five-year 5G standalone run and the December plans of SK Telecom and LG Uplus showed how much strategic movement is happening in the sector. The SK Broadband move adds a different angle, because it concerns balance sheet structure rather than radio technology. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. SK Broadband’s KRW 5 Trillion Sales Target for 2030 The headline number is simple. SK Broadband wants annual sales to reach KRW 5 trillion by 2030. The reports describe it as a goal tied directly to the restructuring, not as a forecast that already includes every deal in the pipeline. Context matters here. The company says the entity left behind after the spinoff will post more than KRW 4 trillion in annual sales. The 2030 goal therefore asks for growth on top of a base that has already lost its data center and submarine cable revenue. That is a harder claim than a target that counts infrastructure income. The reports do not say which year the KRW 4 trillion base refers to, and they do not break the target into segments. Readers should treat the 2030 figure as management ambition. It is a useful marker for how the company wants investors to measure it, but it is not guidance audited by anyone outside the firm. The tone of the announcement is also worth reading. SK Broadband framed the separation as an opportunity to focus more tightly on its core. In the company’s own words, the spinoff gave it an opportunity to focus even more on its three core businesses. That framing signals that management sees the old mixed structure as a distraction rather than a strength. What the SK Broadband Data Center Spinoff Splits Apart A spinoff separates one business into two legal entities. Here, SK Broadband remains the surviving company and keeps its name. The newly established company, SK Horizon, receives the data center and submarine cable operations. Reports from 헤럴드경제 and The Information describe the split in those terms. The structure shapes what each company can do next. A pure data center operator can raise money against long-lived assets, sign multi-year capacity contracts and build sites in phases. A broadband and media operator needs different capital, different talent and a different investor story. Putting both under one roof forces investors to price a blend. Separation also sharpens accountability. Once SK Horizon reports on its own, its utilization, build cost and customer mix become visible in ways they were not inside a larger carrier. SK Broadband, by contrast, gets judged on subscriber economics, content costs and enterprise contracts. Neither company can hide weak results inside the other’s strong ones. The sources do not describe the legal mechanics, the effective date or any change in employee numbers. Those details stay out of this article until the companies publish them. SK Horizon: The New Home for Data Centers and Submarine Cables SK Horizon is the vehicle for the infrastructure half of the old business. The fact sheet from the announcement ties it to two asset classes, data centers and submarine cables. It also ties it to an expansion plan and to a large outside equity commitment, covered in the sections below. What SK Horizon takes on SK Horizon takes responsibility for the spun-off data center and submarine cable operations. It plans to grow its infrastructure to 318 MW, a figure that includes eight operating data centers plus new facilities in Ulsan and Guro. That is the full list of operational facts the announcement confirms. What stays at SK Broadband SK Broadband keeps its fixed-line, media and enterprise businesses. Those three areas now carry the whole story for the surviving company. The enterprise line is the one most likely to feel the spinoff in practice, since business customers who once bought connectivity and data center services from one provider may now deal with two companies. Whether the two entities keep a commercial relationship is unreported. The announcement does not say if SK Broadband will resell SK Horizon capacity or bundle the services. Buyers of both should watch for that detail. The Numbers Behind the SK Broadband 2030 Sales Target Four figures define the plan. SK Broadband says it will hold more than KRW 4 trillion in annual sales and about KRW 1.2 trillion in EBITDA after the spinoff. It aims for KRW 5 trillion in sales by 2030. SK Telecom says KKR-managed funds and the IMM Investment-Stonebridge consortium will invest a combined KRW 3.08 trillion in SK Horizon. Some simple arithmetic helps frame them. A jump from just over KRW 4 trillion to KRW 5 trillion represents growth of roughly 25 percent at most from the base the company cites. That is our calculation from the reported figures, not a number the company published. Spread over several years, it implies a modest annual pace rather than a sprint. artigo.texto: A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox. The demand for large-scale data centers in the U.S. this year, driven by the need for computing power for artificial intelligence, grew well beyond the supply of powered land and the labor to build these structures. It also pushed timelines and risk for contractors. All that resulted in costs rising 13% year-over-year to more than twice the global rate, according to a new report from Turner & Townsend, a global project management company. The gain this year was about three times the last ten-year average. The report looked at over 500 live or recently completed projects in 62 global markets. It also included a survey of 400 experts in the global data center industry. While there was some stabilization in cost inflation this year, it was not enough to offset the huge growth in not just demand but speed of construction and delivery. "More aggressive schedules tie to contractors in particular and subcontractors baking in more risk allowances in their pricing," said Paul Barry, North America data center lead for Turner & Townsend. "So whether that's acceleration allowances, whether that's more overtime and labor attraction allowances, even just higher fees for taking on the risk of delivering at a faster pace than what they would traditionally take on." All of those things, combined with the spike in demand and the strain on the supply chain, translate into higher costs, he added. Capital expenditure on global data centers is projected to rise from about $800 billion this year to $1.8 trillion per year in 2050, according to a recent report from PwC. The U.S. is expected to capture almost half of all global investment in AI infrastructure, which includes both data centers and chips. Power is, of course, key to all data centers, and 56% of those surveyed by Turner & Townsend globally said it was a major obstacle to delivery. Just over half said utility connections typically take between one and two years, and almost a third reported timeframes of over two years. Costs for power vary regionally — from $15.01 per watt in Silicon Valley to $10.51 per watt in Dallas, based on a typical 60-megawatt design. As with every type of construction in the U.S., labor continues to be a significant headwind. Just over one quarter of respondents said their contractor capacity, that is, the ability to manage construction backlogs, was sufficient. Going forward, Barry said he expects costs to moderate somewhat, with cost increases in the 6% to 10% range in the next year. A lot of the major projects have already started or are starting now, so cost risk has been baked into those contracts. "If this demand continues, then there'll be more continued flow of project starts and so on, but I think we've hit a big surge in 2026, especially of new big major projects that have been procured," said Barry.
