artigo.texto: BOSTON — Opponents of data center development have launched a campaign to put new restrictions before Massachusetts voters in 2028, as a $16 billion project proposed in Sutton sharpens the debate. The Committee to Restrict Data Centers, which filed initial paperwork with state regulators in September, announced the campaign recently and launched sign4restrictingdatacenters.org, where residents can pledge support for a ballot petition and request a signature form by mail. The Kraft Group is pursuing a data center campus in Sutton that, if completed, would rank as the fourth-largest data center in the country. The proposal has drawn opposition from residents of the central Massachusetts town, adding to the unfolding national debate over AI development, electricity consumption, water use and potential effects on utility bills. The website urges visitors to help restrict data centers, citing concerns about increasing electric bills, water consumption and noise from equipment that can “sound like jet engines.” It also calls for local voter approval of proposed facilities. At the bottom of the site, organizers included a declaration: “No Ai was used on this site.” The committee’s proposal, designated Petition 26-08 by the attorney general’s office, would establish requirements for new data centers and expansions of existing facilities, including a two-thirds vote of approval by residents in the host community. Under the petition, a data center could not receive a municipal permit unless its electricity supplier agreed not to shift costs onto other customers and committed to providing enough electricity from 100% renewable resources to meet the facility’s needs without reducing renewable energy available to others. Operators would also have to guarantee recovery of infrastructure costs if a facility closes, reduces capacity or violates its contract. The proposal also requires water suppliers to certify that existing systems can accommodate a facility without materially affecting service to existing customers in the host or neighboring communities. Operators would need drought-related water reduction plans. Municipalities would have to publicly disclose permitting documents online, and voters would decide whether to approve a proposed facility at an election at least 180 days after the community announces its permitting decision and releases the relevant documents. The state auditor could audit data centers and their electricity and water suppliers, with municipalities authorized to require facilities to cease operating until certain violations are corrected. The committee is chaired by Jim Fleming, a political consultant who operates a signature-gathering company and said he has connections to communities that have raised concerns about data center projects, including Westfield and Holyoke. Sen. John Velis, a Westfield Democrat, is also promoting the campaign. “The completion and proposed construction of data centers around the state has caused local community groups to organize to either stop or delay new centers,” Velis said in the committee’s press release, citing concerns about electricity costs, environmental uncertainty, water usage and noise. Fleming submitted the proposal shortly before this year’s August filing deadline, and Attorney General Andrea Campbell’s office certified it in September. The committee is not planning to collect signatures for the first available deadline this month, Fleming said. Organizers have until Nov. 18 to submit 74,574 signatures, representing 3% of the votes cast in the 2022 gubernatorial election, to qualify for the next stage of the process. Because the proposal is intended for the 2028 ballot, they can pursue the initial signature threshold next fall, when the requirement will be based on votes cast in this month’s gubernatorial election. That approach gives organizers more time to build public support and leaves them an opportunity to submit alternative versions of the proposal by next August’s filing deadline. Fleming indicated the language already approved by the attorney general may not be the version ultimately advanced. Filing early also puts lawmakers on notice as they begin a legislative session in January. If enough signatures are collected next fall, the Legislature would have until early May 2028 to act on the proposal. If lawmakers do not pass it, supporters would need to gather a smaller round of signatures by early July to secure a spot on the November ballot. Fleming said the prospect of a ballot question is intended, in part, to prompt legislative action before voters are asked to decide the issue. “If the legislature passes a law like this that is good, and not just an executive order, then we will wrap this entire process. And this will hopefully encourage them to do this,” he said. The petition would go further than Gov. Maura Healey’s executive order, signed Sept. 8, which established requirements for state agencies reviewing large data center projects. The order generally applies to facilities exceeding 25 megawatts, while the petition sets a lower threshold of 5 megawatts of peak annual demand. Healey’s order directs state agencies, including the Department of Environmental Protection and the Energy Facilities Siting Board, to develop policies addressing electricity, water, environmental impacts and community benefits. It requires developers to procure incremental clean electricity, with an alternative compliance payment available, and directs agencies to develop ratepayer protections. Unlike the proposed ballot measure, the order does not require a communitywide vote. Instead, it calls for community benefit agreements and municipal guidance. It also applies only to facilities built or expanded after it took effect. Like any executive order, it can be amended or revoked by a future governor. The campaign is emerging amid broader political resistance to data centers. Voters favored restrictions in 40 of 41 local ballot contests held

artigo.texto: Ford Starts US Battery Production Using CATL Technology Ford has started producing lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells at its Michigan facility using technology licensed from China's Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL). The development marks a step in Ford's efforts to reduce electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing costs while building domestic battery production capacity, despite growing scrutiny of US companies' technological ties with China. The first cells, manufactured at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan, are being shipped to Louisville, Kentucky, for prototypes of Ford's upcoming Fathom electric pickup. Production began in October 2026, with the first shipments announced on November 18. Alan Clarke, Ford's Vice President of Advanced Development Projects, said the partnership provides access to technology that the automaker needs to accelerate its manufacturing capabilities. “If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible,” Clarke said during a tour of the facility. He added that working with CATL would allow Ford to acquire LFP technology and develop its own manufacturing capabilities. Ford Seeks to Reduce Battery Manufacturing Costs The $3 billion facility in Marshall, Michigan, is owned and operated by Ford, while CATL provides the licensed technology and manufacturing expertise. The arrangement allows the US automaker to produce battery cells locally without developing the entire manufacturing process independently. LFP batteries use lithium, iron and phosphate rather than nickel and cobalt, materials used in several other lithium-ion battery chemistries. According to Ford, eliminating nickel and cobalt helps reduce costs, while the chemistry's durability supports repeated charging cycles. The technology was developed in the United States but commercialized at scale primarily in China, where manufacturers such as CATL expanded production capacity and established expertise in battery manufacturing. Ford's decision to license the technology reflects the challenges facing automakers seeking to compete on EV prices while developing domestic battery supply chains. The Marshall facility is designed to produce 40 cells per minute, equivalent to approximately 20GWh of annual capacity. This is below the original capacity target of up to 40GWh, following adjustments to Ford's EV investment strategy and changing market demand. US-China Tensions Complicate Battery Strategy The arrangement has attracted scrutiny from US lawmakers and government officials concerned about the involvement of Chinese companies in strategic manufacturing sectors. In September 2026, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy sent a letter to Ford CEO Jim Farley expressing concern about the company's relationship with Chinese suppliers and the potential implications for the US automotive industry. The criticism comes as Washington increases scrutiny of Chinese involvement in domestic supply chains, particularly in sectors considered strategic to manufacturing and national security. Ford has maintained that licensing CATL technology enables it to manufacture batteries in the United States while retaining ownership and operational control of the facility. The automaker also plans to use the manufacturing experience acquired in Michigan to support its battery energy storage operations in Kentucky. Mexico's EV Industry Faces a Similar Supply Chain Challenge Ford's strategy has implications for Mexico, where automotive manufacturers are also adapting production operations to the transition toward electric mobility. Mexico Business News reported in August 2026, in Record Mexican EV Sales Contrast 57% Slump in Domestic Production, that electrified vehicle sales increased 46.5% year over year between January and July, reaching 112,313 units. However, domestic EV production declined 57% during the first half of the year, reflecting weaker demand in export markets, particularly the United States. The difference between domestic demand and manufacturing performance highlights the challenges facing Mexico as it seeks to capture a larger share of the EV supply chain. Investment in local production is continuing. In July, the Mexican government announced that Kia would invest US$649 million between 2026 and 2028 to establish production of its EV3 electric vehicle at its Pesqueria, Nuevo Leon, facility. The project also includes charging infrastructure and energy-related investments, according to the Mexican Presidency. Meanwhile, BMW is preparing its San Luis Potosí plant for electric vehicle production. In its October 28 report, BMW San Luis Potosi Taps AI to Modernize Supply Chain, Mexico Business News reported that the company is nearing completion of an on-site battery assembly facility, with production scheduled to begin alongside its next-generation electric model. Ford Prepares for 2027 Vehicle Launch Ford plans to increase production at the Michigan facility in 2027 as it continues certifying manufacturing processes. The battery cells will support development of the Fathom pickup, whose launch is expected in the fourth quarter of 2027. The facility will also provide manufacturing experience for Ford's energy storage operations, extending the use of battery technology beyond automotive applications.

Segundo ele, essa medida visa a ajudar o setor de inteligência artificial a concorrer com os competidores chineses. “Não vamos permitir que nossas empresas construam data centers fora do nosso país”, disse Trump durante uma coletiva de imprensa com jornalistas realizada na Casa Branca, em Washington, após voltar de sua visita à Ásia. Ele prometeu um imposto "altíssimo" às companhias que agirem dessa forma. 🤳 Notícias em primeira mão: baixe nosso aplicativo gratuito e leve o jornalismo do SBT News com você, onde estiver! Clique aqui Caso o governo americano lance mão dessa medida, o Brasil pode ser afetado negativamente, já que a maior parte dos data centers brasileiros é operada por companhias americanas. Trump tem defendido de forma contundente a construção de data centers dentro dos Estados Unidos - algo que é visto com maus olhos por uma fatia considerável dos eleitores. Em diversas comunidades pelo país, a instalação desse tipo de infraestrutura enfrenta resistências devido a preocupações em questões como demanda de energia elétrica, custos aos serviços públicos e outros impactos negativos. Em sua visita à Ásia, o líder americano se reuniu com o presidente chinês, Xi Jinping. Nesta quinta-feira, Trump afirmou em entrevista à emissora Fox News que os governos de Washington e Pequim concordam com a necessidade de regulamentar a inteligência artificial (IA) por motivos de segurança. As falas de Trump também ocorrem em meio a uma crise na principal desenvolvedora de chips utilizados para treinar modelos de inteligência artificial, a Nvidia. O CEO da empresa, Jensen Huang, deixou o cargo após a revelação de que ele havia tido um caso com uma mulher suspeita de ser uma espiã chinesa. A situação levou os Estados Unidos a restringirem ainda mais o acesso da China a esse tipo de tecnologia.

artigo.texto: Affordability and data centers were on the ballot this November. Voters made it clear that they are concerned about both issues: prices are too high and the neighborliness of data centers is in doubt. In a time of economic turbulence, cities and counties are struggling to pay for schools, roads and public safety without the tax revenue data centers generate. Where can part of the solution to affordability and concerns with data centers be found? Vacant lots. Vacant lots can host data centers that are well maintained, comply with local architectural requirements, have security and bring in much-needed cash for local projects. An eyesore and security problem can become a revenue generator and a secure property. However, some are determined to keep data centers from developing the local economy and unsightly properties at any cost. In early November, an activist helped block the development of a $5 billion data center that was set to break ground in the next year or so. The data center was supposed to be built on the site of Landover Mall, which closed in 2002. The vacant lot is now overgrown with grass and weeds, stretching across nearly 90 acres in Landover, Md. AMERICA'S REDDEST STATE CHASES BILLION-DOLLAR BOOM AS OTHERS SOUR ON MASSIVE EMERGING INDUSTRY Prince George's County, home to the former mall, is facing a $130 million budget deficit. It has lost a Six Flags amusement park, is losing the Washington Commanders to Washington, D.C., and has suffered thousands of federal job losses. Developers projected about $53.5 million a year in local tax revenue if the data center were to be built. The activist, Taylor Frazier McCollum, isn't moved by those numbers or how they help her neighbors. "Money is, you know, a made-up concept," she said. "We buy into it every day, and we choose that this has value and this doesn't have value and to me the environment has the highest and utmost value and I need to honor that in any way." The rejection of a project to help revitalize a site that sorely needs it and fill the county's coffers perfectly encapsulates the political debate around data centers. Too often, proposed data centers receive automatic opposition from activists and politicians. As a result, some of America's most vulnerable and desperate communities are losing millions of dollars in tax revenue that could fund schools, fix roads, pay emergency responders and more. Landover Mall is sadly not the only example. Local opposition blocked or delayed at least 75 data center projects across the country worth approximately $130 billion in the first quarter of 2026, which Data Center Watch describes as the largest single-quarter total on record. That's roughly as much as all of 2025, in just three months. HOW AMERICA CAN WIN THE AI RACE WITHOUT BURNING VOTERS In Virginia, Prince William County stands to miss out on as much as $400 million in projected annual tax revenue following the collapse of Digital Gateway, once billed as one of the largest data center complexes in the world. The county had approved the project, but courts invalidated its rezoning approvals. The remaining developer withdrew its legal challenge in July 2026, effectively ending the plans. On the other hand, communities that are looking to the future and allowing data centers are reaping the benefits. Virginia’s Loudoun County has embraced data centers, which have generated 38% of general fund revenue in the county’s FY2026 budget. That revenue has helped the county lower its real property tax rate every year for a decade, from $1.145 per $100 of assessed value in 2016 to $0.805 in 2026. That's real money back in homeowners' pockets. That is revenue its neighbor, Prince William County, is missing out on. HOMEOWNERS IN THE HEART OF AMERICA’S AI BOOM ARE GETTING AN UNEXPECTED PAYOFF In Henrico County, Virginia, data center tax revenue pays for an Affordable Housing Trust Fund that helps first-time homebuyers with down payments. A single mother working toward a nursing degree said her new mortgage costs less than her old rent. In Richland Parish, Louisiana, Meta's data center expansion helped the parish pay for $50,000 teacher bonuses. THE POWERFUL WAY AMERICAN COMMUNITIES CAN BENEFIT FROM THE NEW TECH BOOM REVEALED BY DATA CENTER CEO Data center developers have a responsibility to communities: listen to their concerns, be transparent and collaborative about their plans, design in ways their neighbors approve and work to mitigate or eliminate undesirable local impacts. They must also pay their own electric and water costs, establish noise limits and continually work with local community groups and elected officials to address concerns as they arise. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Data center development can be and often is a win-win for developers and the community. But even these efforts are not enough for some. Money may be a "made-up concept" to some, but the lower tax rates in Loudoun County, the down payment in Henrico and the teacher bonuses in Richland Parish are real. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Data centers can turn a decades-long vacant parking lot overgrown with weeds into an economic engine, helping to close a $130 million hole in the budget. Immovable opponents are ignoring the economic benefits data centers can bring and leaving funding for community projects on the table. History shows other counties will take advantage of this lack of foresight and benefit.

artigo.texto: Key Points - Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann recently suggested that SpaceX could acquire stalled data centers. - The key trigger for such an acquisition would be data centers that already have power. - As pushback against AI data centers grows, electricity becomes an increasingly important factor for investors to consider. Wall Street analysts can only make educated guesses, just like every other investor. But they do have an advantage since they are often industry experts. This is why Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann's suggestion that Space Exploration Technologies(NASDAQ:SPCX) could buy up stalled data centers is so interesting. The key theme, however, is that SpaceX will likely only be interested in data centers that already have dedicated power. Here's why this is so important and what it could mean for your stock selection process as you look at companies like Bloom Energy(NYSE:BE), NextEra Energy(NYSE:NEE), and Brookfield Renewable(NYSE:BEP). Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » SpaceX sees the problem very clearly SpaceX has a large AI data center in Memphis that it has dubbed Colossus. It is a huge asset, and it uses massive amounts of power. To ensure there is enough electricity to run the data center, SpaceX built its own dedicated natural-gas power plant. Local residents aren't happy about this, but it highlights that SpaceX is clearly aware of the power problem posed by AI data centers. Image source: Getty Images. As the backlash against AI data centers grows, access to electricity is becoming an increasingly important and contentious issue. Which is why Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann thinks SpaceX could end up buying data centers that have dedicated power agreements in place. However, you don't need to play this specific angle to benefit. Increasingly, AI companies are being forced to supply their own power. And there are a handful of companies that look set to benefit, including Bloom Energy, NextEra Energy, and Brookfield Renewable. Bloom Energy is a high risk/high reward option Bloom Energy makes hydrogen fuel cells. Notably, each fuel cell it sells comes along with a long-term service contract, creating an annuity-like income stream. The company's products are factory-built and can be easily deployed wherever they are needed, providing off-grid power. The company has been losing money for years but is likely to be profitable in 2026. That could be an important inflection point for the business. But investors are well aware of the opportunity, pushing the stock higher by more than 1,200% over the past three years. With a lofty price-to-earnings ratio of roughly 100x, it is very clearly a well-loved stock. And yet, the opportunity to power AI data centers remains substantial, and perhaps only getting larger. If you are an aggressive growth investor, you should at least consider Bloom Energy, even if you only end up adding it to your wish list. NextEra Energy covers two bases NextEra Energy is one of the world's largest utilities. In fact, it is looking to get even bigger, with its proposed acquisition of Dominion Energy(NYSE:D). Notably, Dominion's regulated electricity operations include one of the world's most important data center markets. The pairing will also vault NextEra into the number two spot with regard to U.S. nuclear power generation. Basically, NextEra looks like it is doubling down on electricity demand and AI at the same time. But there's an interesting twist here. NextEra is well positioned to benefit from data centers that get attached to the grid. However, it is also one of the world's largest producers of solar and wind power, a business that falls outside of the regulated framework. So it can also sell power directly to AI customers under long-term contracts. For more conservative investors, NextEra could be an attractive way to play AI's power demand, both from within and outside the regulated framework. You'll also get to collect NextEra's well-above-market 2.9% dividend yield. Brookfield Renewable is focused on clean energy For investors looking to maximize the income they generate, Brookfield Renewable and its 5.2% may be even more attractive. The partnership is focused on clean energy, but has a surprisingly diversified portfolio. For starters, it operates hydroelectric, solar, and wind power facilities. It has increasingly been investing in battery storage. And it owns half of Westinghouse, which is one of the world's largest service providers to the nuclear power industry. On top of that, it is also geographically diversified, with assets located in North America, South America, Europe, and Asia. It is a one-stop shop for investors seeking a focused clean-energy investment and for customers seeking renewable energy. The key here, however, is that Brookfield Renewable largely sells power under long-term contracts outside of the regulated framework. It already has large deals with AI giants Microsoft(NASDAQ:MSFT) and Google. Add in the goal of at least 5% annual distribution growth, and income lovers would be remiss if they didn't at least examine Brookfield Renewable and the AI opportunity ahead of it. There's usually more than one angle to play If you think Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann is on to something, you could simply buy SpaceX. That's fine, but it isn't the only takeaway from his insight. The real story is that access to electricity is increasingly important. And you can also play that investment theme with companies like Bloom Energy, NextEra Energy, and Brookfield Renewable. Should you buy stock in Bloom Energy right now? artigo.texto: Under ETS2, fuel suppliers, not households, will carry the direct compliance duties. They must monitor and report emissions linked to the fuels they sell, then surrender the corresponding allowances no earlier than 1 January 2028. The carbon cost may pass along the supply chain and show up in fuel prices, but households will not have to register or surrender allowances themselves. The Council of Ministers approved the decree-law on 20 November 2026, completing Spain’s transposition of recent EU emissions-trading reforms. The measure incorporates Directives (EU) 2023/959 and 2023/958 and establishes the separate ETS2 regime for CO₂ from fuels used in buildings and road transport, alongside other smaller sectors outside the original EU carbon market. Monitoring obligations began in 2024. Spain’s earlier attempt to legislate the expansion through a bill submitted in 2024 failed; the decree-law now requires parliamentary validation. The government says the change could help Spain access more than €6.8 billion from the Social Climate Fund between 2026 and 2032. The funding requires 25% national co-financing and could support measures worth around €9 billion under Spain’s Social Climate Plan. The proposed measures include energy-efficiency renovations, rehabilitation of vulnerable urban areas, social housing, rural mobility and accessible public transport. Future ETS2 auction revenue may also help fund the energy and climate transition. The system extends the “quien contamina paga” principle to activities outside the existing emissions-trading regime. Its stated purpose is to encourage lower emissions and cleaner, more efficient options in buildings and mobility, while helping households and businesses adapt. The EU’s Social Climate Fund is intended to address the distributional effects of extending carbon pricing to these sectors. Separately, RUSSPAIN has reported on irrigators’ concerns in El Ejido. In its announcement, the Ministry for the Ecological Transition and the Demographic Challenge (MITECO) said the decree-law also transposes Directives (EU) 2023/959 and 2023/958. They form part of the EU’s «Objetivo 55» package, which sets a bloc-wide target of cutting net greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% by 2030 compared with 1990. Sara Aagesen, Third Deputy Prime Minister and minister for the ecological transition, said the transposition was needed to access EU funding and would help protect vulnerable people in housing and transport. The legislation also revises rules for industrial installations and electricity generation, changes the aviation regime and brings maritime transport fully into the European system. For industry and power generation, the framework sets a 62% emissions reduction by 2030 against 2005 levels. It also provides for clean technologies such as renewable hydrogen, which receives free allowances under the updated framework, and expands the Innovation Fund to support decarbonisation projects. The broader reforms form part of the EU’s Fit for 55 package, which aims to cut net emissions by at least 55% by 2030 from 1990 levels. The decree-law was approved shortly before Spain’s 29 November 2026 elections and must be validated by Congress or, under the reported institutional circumstances, by the Permanent Deputation. The European carbon-market framework also sets a €45 initial reference level for its price safeguard, with intervention contemplated if prices rise significantly above it.

artigo.texto: Rowan students will work at Vineland’s massive data center under a new program Engineering students will work in six-month stints at DataOne in Cumberland County as the Vineland data center finds its footing. Engineering students at Rowan University will work at DataOne, a massive data center complex in Vineland, as soon as next year under a new agreement, Rowan announced Tuesday. The announcement comes after DataOne was hit in September with a $1 million fine for violating clean-air laws. The center has faced criticism — and a now-dismissed lawsuit — from neighbors who say it has impacted their quality of life. DataOne’s CEO, Charles-Antoine Beyney, said the program is an effort to partner with one of the state’s largest universities, teach young people about data centers, and create a local artificial intelligence workforce. “They can realize that data centers, AI factories, when they are properly built, are definitely not the enemy of mankind,” Beyney said. “On the contrary, they are beautiful assets that generate tremendous amount of value for all the local communities.” The agreement took effect on Sept. 29. Beyney, a French entrepreneur who has developed data centers around the world for nearly two decades, founded DataOne, the European data center company building the 2.4 million-square-foot, 300-megawatt plant in Cumberland County. The Vineland facility’s internal technology, operated by Nebius Group, an Amsterdam-based AI infrastructure company, will fuel Microsoft’s AI tools. The project is expected to bring about 200 long-term jobs to the city. Leaders at DataOne approached Rowan about a partnership, and Rowan agreed, said Giuseppe Palmese, the dean of the Henry M. Rowan College of Engineering. Rowan has been expanding its engineering co-op programs, Palmese said, which give students the chance to work at local companies for six to eight months to gain mechanical and electrical skills. Students will have to apply and interview for the data center jobs, which will begin the summer before their senior year and carry into the fall semester. The first group of students — three or four workers — are expected to be onboarded by April, Beyney said, when most construction at Vineland’s DataOne facility, less than a half-hour drive from Rowan, will be done. Students will be paid for their work, Beyney said. No money is being exchanged between Rowan University itself and DataOne as part of the program, Palmese said. Because data centers fuel AI, Palmese said, they are likely here to stay. Thus, working at DataOne will give students the chance to get ahead in the field and experience a data center while it is still in development, he said. Palmese said some students have expressed interest in the program already, while others have criticized AI. “When we work in a place like a data center, there are issues there to deal with. You have the environmental aspects of it, noise pollution aspects of it, and what engineers do is solve those problems,” Palmese said. “So it’s an overall benefit to our students.” Rowan University likely will not be the only education partner for DataOne, Beyney said. He expressed interest in sending DataOne representatives to local high schools and colleges to teach about data centers and AI. “We could be sending some people to at least get the right information in front of the students, because they are being so disinformed and so fake-news-fed by so many different forms of medias,” Beyney said. “Sometimes it’s good to have the real truth.” A Pew Research poll from this summer shows that American opinions on data centers, including among young people, have grown more negative, at least when it comes to how the plants will affect the environment. Beyney said neighborhood complaints about noise are not his biggest concern right now, even as controversies surround AI plants across the country. “We are not building for the next six months. We are building for the next decade, or two decades. So I don’t care about the noise that can happen right now,” Beyney said, “but I do care how strong the value proposition of DataOne will be for the community.” “They will realize that everything we say was true,” Beyney said. “We were not liars. We were even under-promising and over-delivering.” Inquirer South Jersey

artigo.texto: Moment Energy has launched Nova, which integrates repurposed EV batteries from multiple vehicle platforms using an AI-powered BMS Individual battery packs can be replaced as they age, with the company targeting a system lifetime of over 20 years The system has achieved UL 1973 and UL 9540 certifications and has been tested to UL 9540A Moment Energy, a Canada-based battery energy storage system (BESS) provider that uses repurposed EV batteries, has introduced its new BESS, Nova. The 200 kW / 500 kWh BESS is designed for commercial and industrial (C&I) applications and is produced at the company’s Megafactory 1. The deliveries for this product are planned for Q1 2027. Moment Energy states that its Nova system is capable of integrating batteries sourced from multiple EV platforms and accommodating differences in battery condition and state of health. The system uses the company’s proprietary AI-powered battery management system (BMS). It continuously evaluates battery packs with different states of health and optimizes their operation to maintain system performance, efficiency, and reliability. The company emphasizes that the system comes with a swappable battery architecture that allows individual battery packs to be replaced as they age, without replacing the entire system. According to Moment Energy, this architecture extends the system lifetime by over 20 years under the company’s capacity augmentation service. Multiple Nova units can also be combined to create higher-capacity storage systems. Operating at 800 V DC, each unit measures 2.94 x 1.80 x 2.54 m and uses liquid cooling for thermal management. It is designed to operate between -25°C and 50°C and at altitudes of up to 2,000 m. It also carries a high seismic rating under IEEE 693. Safety is particularly important in this scenario, as the previous operating history and varying degrees of degradation may introduce additional considerations compared to newly built batteries. The company claims the Nova achieved UL 1973 and UL 9540 certifications and has been tested to UL 9540A, which evaluates fire propagation associated with thermal runaway in battery energy storage systems. Moment Energy describes it as the first BESS made using repurposed EV batteries to achieve both UL 1973 and UL 9540 certification. The system uses EV batteries sourced from vehicles already operating in North America, which are subsequently reengineered for stationary storage. The company has also highlighted the system's compliance with US Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements.

artigo.texto: Conheça Maxx Morando, baterista e marido de Miley Cyrus Músicos se uniram em matrimônio em uma cerimônia privada na cidade de Palm Springs, na Califórnia, no sábado (21); eles foram vistos juntos pela primeira vez em 2021 A cantora Miley Cyrus, 33, se casou com o músico Maxx Morando, 28, em uma cerimônia privada na cidade de Palm Springs, na Califórnia, no sábado (21). O artista é mais conhecido por tocar bateria e atualmente faz parte da banda de rock alternativo Liily, de Los Angeles. Segundo a revista americana People, boa parte da família de Cyrus marcou presença no casamento da cantora: sua mãe, Tish Cyrus; seu pai, Billy Ray Cyrus; e sua irmã, Noah Cyrus; além da namorada de Billy Ray, Elizabeth Hurley, e o filho dela, Damian Hurley. Neste domingo (22), ela também publicou registros da cerimônia em suas redes sociais. Conheça Maxx Morando, o marido de Miley Cyrus Nas redes sociais, o artista é mais reservado e, ao todo, realizou apenas 20 publicações em sua conta do Instagram. A última delas foi em setembro, em apoio ao lançamento de "Bass Persuades", o álbum mais recente de Miley. Para seus quase 70 mil seguidores, ele ainda compartilhou outras conquistas da amada. Segundo a People, ele trabalhou em duas faixas — "Handstand" e "Violet Chemistry" — do álbum de Cyrus, "Endless Summer Vacation". Morando também produziu várias canções e escreveu a faixa-título do nono álbum de Cyrus, "Something Beautiful". Para o último álbum de Miley Cyrus, Maxx Morando foi creditado como co-produtor, ao lado de Michael Pollack e Kid Harpoon. Antes de fazer parte do Liily, Maxx também tocou na banda The Regrettes de 2015 a 2018. Os dois mantêm um relacionamento discreto desde que foram vistos juntos pela primeira vez em novembro de 2021. Em uma entrevista concedida à Vogue britânica em junho de 2023, a vencedora do Grammy detalhou a história de como conheceu Morando. "Fomos colocados em um encontro às cegas", disse Cyrus. "Bem, foi às cegas para mim, mas não para ele", esclareceu ela à publicação. "Pensei: 'O pior que pode acontecer é eu ir embora'." Esta é a segunda vez que a cantora pop sobe ao altar; ela foi casada com o ator Liam Hemsworth entre 2018 e 2019, com o divórcio oficializado em 2020. artigo.texto: What if AI data centers could help make senior housing more affordable by turning wasted server heat into a useful community resource? Two seemingly unrelated trends are creating major infrastructure challenges in the United States. One is familiar to virtually every CIO; the other may be less so. Less familiar, America’s demand for senior living communities is rising faster than developers are building them. The oldest baby boomers turn 80 this year, and the shortfall of senior housing units is growing more severe. According to NIC MAP’s 2026 Senior Housing Market Outlook, the need for additional senior housing will reach approximately 576,000 units by 2030 and exceed one million units by 2035 if construction continues at its current pace. Much more familiar is the rapid expansion of AI data centers and their effects on surrounding communities. A 2026 report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects data centers could account for 11.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption by 2030, up from an estimated 4.7% in 2024. With new facilities being proposed across the country, growing electricity demand, water consumption, noise pollution and more have created widespread community concerns. What if these two challenges could help address each other? Data centers generate enormous amounts of heat that must be removed so servers can reliably operate at or near peak performance, but creative planning can turn this heat into a valuable resource for nearby residences, potentially reducing heating expenses and demand for additional energy. The underlying technology is already working in Europe, and a proposed development in Chicago offers a glimpse of how it could be adapted in the United States. I believe there’s an opportunity to take this idea further by exploring partnerships between data center developers and senior housing operators. In the right circumstances, these arrangements could reduce heating costs and create new revenue opportunities to help make senior housing more affordable for our most populous generation as they enter their golden years. Excess heat as a community resource Cooling is a fundamental requirement of data center operations, and historically, data centers have rejected heat into their surrounding environments, whether through air cooling, evaporative cooling or other methods. Liquid cooling is increasingly being incorporated into data center designs to accommodate the higher power requirements of AI infrastructure. In any of these scenarios, removing heat offers an opportunity to use it rather than simply discard it. In Groningen, the Netherlands, data center operator QTS has partnered with local energy provider WarmteStad to supply recovered heat to a district heating network. As CIO has reported, the system uses heat pumps powered by renewable energy to circulate hot water through an existing underground district heating network that supplies residual heat to 10,000 households, buildings and knowledge institutions. Both sides receive something useful. The community gets access to a heat source that would otherwise be discarded, and the data center benefits from the cooling provided through the energy exchange. This approach is not always appropriate. The engineering requires more than connecting two buildings. Data center cooling systems generally operate at temperatures below those required for conventional building heating. Heat pumps would likely need to raise the temperature, and a distribution network must transport the energy to where it can be used. Still, Groningen demonstrates how data center heat capture can become part of a community’s energy infrastructure, and the United States is beginning to explore similar opportunities. In Chicago’s Bronzeville neighborhood, for example, developers have proposed Metropolis Pointe, a mixed-use development combining a data center with residential, commercial and community facilities. Griffin Venture Group, the project’s developer, announced additional infrastructure milestones in August 2026, including plans for a 170,000-square-foot data center and a 42,000-square-foot central utility plant. The proposed utility system would integrate heating and cooling across the campus with the goal of reducing energy costs for residents. Although still in the proposal stage, Metropolis Pointe’s design reflects an important evolution in thinking as developers begin to consider how infrastructure can support the needs of neighboring communities and buildings. If this approach can work for conventional residential developments, it can likely be applied to improve the lives of our growing senior population. A new partnership model for senior housing Senior living communities may be particularly well suited for this. They operate 24/7 with substantial year-round energy requirements. Heating, hot water, kitchens, laundry facilities and common areas all contribute to operating expenses, and in colder climates, traditional HVAC or electric heating can be an especially high cost. As high energy costs persist in the United States and across the world, construction costs have also increased, financing remains costly and challenging, and many older Americans cannot absorb higher housing expenses on their fixed budgets. NIC MAP estimates that meeting future senior housing demand will require more than $1 trillion in cumulative investment through 2050. Hopefully efforts to close that gap will incorporate new approaches to development and financing, not just more of the same accepted inefficiencies. I envision at least two potential opportunities for data center developers to help. First, heat recovery can reduce operating expenses. A senior living community located near a suitable data center could potentially receive recovered heat through a shared thermal network, offsetting some of the energy otherwise purchased for heating and hot water. artigo.texto: A sodium-ion battery material developed in an IISER Bhopal-led study has retained about 70% of its original capacity after 24,000 charging cycles in laboratory tests, while taking roughly six minutes to charge fully. The result could be relevant to rooftop solar systems, backup power and larger renewable-energy storage projects if the material can be manufactured and tested at commercial scale. The study, titled “Spin-State Regulation Engineering of Pyrophosphate-Based Polyanionic Cathodes for Ultra-Long-Life Sodium-Ion Batteries”, was published in the peer-reviewed journal Advanced Materials, according to the Times of India. The research team was led by Prof Rohit Ranganathan Gaddam of the Department of Chemical Engineering at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Bhopal, with collaborators from IIT Gandhinagar, the University of New South Wales and the University of Southern Queensland in Australia. The researchers focused on the battery’s positive electrode, or cathode. The material uses an iron-based compound with small quantities of manganese and fluorine. Gaddam told the newspaper that this design helps the cathode withstand the repeated expansion and contraction that occurs during charging and discharging, a process that can gradually reduce battery capacity. In the reported laboratory tests, the cathode retained approximately 70% of its capacity after 24,000 cycles. The researchers also reported that it could be fully charged in about six minutes. Under faster charging of roughly three minutes, it retained nearly 81% of its capacity after 10,000 cycles. The material’s reported energy-storage capacity was 336 watt-hours per kilogram. The team also assembled a complete test battery using a hard-carbon negative electrode and reported stable performance in trials. However, the most prominent figures relate to the cathode material and laboratory testing, not to a commercially available battery pack. A market-ready product would require integration with other components, safety assessment, manufacturing trials, durability testing under real operating conditions and further scale-up work. The study’s reported cycle life is therefore not the same as a guaranteed 65-year service life for a household or vehicle battery. The newspaper said the laboratory result could theoretically correspond to more than 65 years of use under particular charging assumptions, but actual service life would depend on how the battery is manufactured and operated. Temperature, charging patterns, system design and other components would all influence real-world performance. Sodium-ion technology is being explored as an alternative to lithium-ion batteries, which currently power most phones, laptops and electric vehicles. Sodium is widely available in materials such as common salt and seawater, while lithium supply is concentrated in a limited number of countries and is largely imported by India. Sodium-ion batteries may be particularly suited to applications where low cost and the storage of larger quantities of electricity matter more than compact size and maximum energy density. For cities and urban households, the most immediate potential application is stationary storage. A durable battery could store electricity generated by rooftop solar panels during the day and provide power during outages or periods of low generation. At a larger scale, sodium-ion systems could support solar and wind projects by storing surplus electricity and releasing it when demand rises. Such systems could improve the usefulness of distributed renewable energy, although the study does not establish that these urban or grid applications are ready for deployment. Longer-lasting storage could also reduce the frequency with which batteries need to be replaced, lowering material use and potentially reducing lifetime costs. But those benefits will depend on the eventual price of manufacturing, the energy and materials required to produce the cells, recycling arrangements and the performance of complete battery systems rather than individual cathodes. The Bhopal-led research is thus a promising materials advance, not yet a commercial battery announcement. Its significance for India’s energy transition will depend on whether the reported performance can be reproduced in larger cells, maintained through manufacturing and validated in real-world storage systems. Until those steps are completed, the technology remains a strong laboratory result with potential relevance to cleaner and more resilient urban energy infrastructure.

artigo.texto: RI targets global carbon trade, from Japan's market to CORSIA November 21, 2026 18:01 GMT+700 Director of Forest Utilization Business Development at the Ministry of Forestry Ilham presents on the international carbon market at the panel session “High-Integrity Forest Carbon: Indonesia’s Pathway under Article 6” at the Indonesia Pavilion, 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31), Antalya, Türkiye, Friday (Nov 20, 2026). /ANTARA/HO-Kementerian Kehutanan. Jakarta (ANTARA) - Indonesia is seeking to tap the international compliance carbon market under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement to maximize the carbon potential of its forestry sector and nature-based solutions (NbS). Director General of Sustainable Forest Management at the Ministry of Forestry Laksmi Wijayanti said opportunities were expanding, driven by demand from Singapore, Japan, and the international aviation scheme ICAO-CORSIA. In a statement issued in Jakarta on Saturday, she said the international carbon market requires high-quality credits with guaranteed integrity, including measures to prevent double counting and ensure transparency in carbon accounting. “The forest carbon transaction pathway through Article 6 requires clear governance, credible accounting, environmental and social safeguards, transparent record-keeping, and commercially viable schemes for investors and buyers,” she said. Speaking at the opening of a panel session titled “High-Integrity Forest Carbon: Indonesia’s Pathway under Article 6” at the Indonesia Pavilion during COP31 in Antalya on Friday (November 13, 2026), she said Indonesia's forest carbon potential stood at 13.4 gigatons of CO2, based on 2025 BloombergNEF data. Director of Forest Utilization Business Development at the Ministry of Forestry Ilham presented strategies for optimizing forest utilization businesses through carbon credit sales under the market-based mechanisms (Articles 6.2 and 6.4) and the non-market mechanism (Article 6.8) of the Paris Agreement. According to Ilham, demand for NbS carbon credits under the Article 6.2 mechanism was substantial and urgent, particularly from Singapore, Japan through the Joint Crediting Mechanism (JCM), and the ICAO-CORSIA scheme. “Currently, Singapore allows the use of international carbon credits to offset a maximum of 5 percent of companies’ taxable emissions,” he said. Meanwhile, Japan, through the JCM, has set a cumulative international mitigation target of around 100 million tons of CO2 by 2030 across all partner countries. Indonesia is actively exploring JCM cooperation with Japan, with peatlands and mangroves serving as important areas for opening access to the Japanese market. These ecosystems distinguish Indonesia from Japan's other partner countries. Another opportunity, he said, comes from ICAO-CORSIA, which is estimated to require 200 million to 250 million eligible carbon units by January 2028. The government has prepared a regulatory framework for carbon trading through Presidential Regulation No. 110 of 2025 and Forestry Ministerial Regulation No. 6 of 2026. The framework includes provisions on authorizing international transfers of mitigation outcomes (ITMOs) and technical arrangements for carbon trading in the forestry sector. “Indonesia has prepared regulations to support carbon trading under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, including provisions on authorizing the transfer of mitigation outcomes and preventing double counting,” Ilham said. Verra's Regional Representative for Asia Pacific, Win Sim Tan, said the use of existing methodologies could accelerate carbon project development, as the government would not need to develop new methodologies from scratch. She cited several Verra methodologies already accepted by Singapore, including those covering REDD+, afforestation, and forest protection. Meanwhile, International Emissions Trading Association (IETA) International Policy Director Andrea Bonzanni said Indonesia also needed to engage actively in technical discussions on the Article 6.4 mechanism during the ongoing UNFCCC negotiations at COP31. He noted that issues concerning permanence, standard methodologies, and tools had yet to adequately accommodate the forestry sector in the draft CMA discussions on Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Bonzanni also reminded the government of the need to balance international carbon credit transfers with the achievement of Indonesia's national climate targets, known as nationally determined contributions (NDCs). On the market demand side, Emergent CEO Eron Bloomgarden said forested countries needed certainty about long-term demand to ensure a reliable supply of carbon credits, while buyers also needed certainty about supply. artigo.texto: O mercado brasileiro de data centers projeta dobrar sua capacidade até 2030, com investimentos estimados em US$ 17,4 bilhões. Atualmente, o país possui 706 MW de capacidade instalada e deve adicionar 134 MW até o fim de 2026, movimentando cerca de US$ 8 bilhões em investimentos anuais. O Brasil concentra 49% da capacidade de data centers da América Latina, segundo a Moody’s Ratings. As informações são da Gazeta do Povo. A Gartner estima que os investimentos globais em infraestrutura de data centers devem alcançar US$ 2,52 trilhões em 2026, crescimento de 44% em relação ao ano anterior. O Brasil figura entre os pioneiros na adoção de Inteligência Artificial Generativa, ao lado de Índia, China, México e Arábia Saudita, conforme levantamento da consultoria EY. O país possui aproximadamente 200 unidades comerciais de data centers, de acordo com a Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC). Luis Tossi, vice-presidente da ABDC, destaca que o Brasil reúne atributos raros: disponibilidade de energia em grande escala, matriz elétrica majoritariamente limpa e renovável, território amplo, conectividade internacional e estabilidade geopolítica. O Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), sancionado em setembro, suspende tributos federais sobre componentes eletrônicos e produtos de tecnologia da informação, reduzindo desvantagens competitivas do país. Estudo da FGV Projetos calcula que um data center de 100 megawatts adiciona R$ 1,5 bilhão ao PIB brasileiro e R$ 590 milhões em renda do trabalho. Cada obra gera em média 12.560 empregos diretos e indiretos durante a construção, que dura de 18 a 36 meses. Após a entrada em operação, o empreendimento mantém cerca de 15% desses postos de forma permanente. Guilherme Neves, professor de cibersegurança do Ibmec-RJ, ressalta que cerca de 60% das cargas digitais brasileiras são processadas fora do território nacional. Processar dados localmente reduz latência, protege informações sensíveis e estimula um ecossistema de inovação em nuvem, inteligência artificial e startups. O professor alerta que infraestrutura sem política industrial transforma o país em armazém de dados, citando a Irlanda, que destina 23% de sua eletricidade a data centers. A capacidade instalada de data centers no Brasil pode atingir entre 26 GW e 45 GW até 2050, dependendo da expansão de energia renovável, segundo a Schneider Electric. O consumo de eletricidade do setor pode alcançar de 160 a 280 terawatts-hora até 2040, equivalente a cerca de 10% da demanda total projetada. Tossi explica que é necessário entregar grandes blocos de potência com segurança, redundância e previsibilidade. Os pedidos de parecer de acesso à rede elétrica somavam 38 GW até julho de 2026. Neves aponta que um data center entra em operação em 12 a 18 meses, enquanto uma linha de transmissão leva até sete anos entre leilão e conclusão. O custo de desenvolvimento de projetos construídos do zero subiu 21% por megawatt desde o fim de 2024. A região Nordeste oferece vento, sol e energia limpa, mas enfrenta desafios de segurança hídrica.

artigo.texto: Minneapolis Data Center Moratorium Ends With No New Rules After Veto Override Fails The Minneapolis City Council fell short Nov. 20 in its 7-5 vote to override Mayor Jacob Frey’s veto of a data center ordinance, leaving the city with no new rules as its six-month moratorium ends Nov. 21. The ordinance would have limited data centers to existing downtown buildings, capped their size, required energy and water disclosure and created overlay districts requiring council approval for each site. Frey said those changes amounted to a de facto ban and would create inconsistent rules. Council members including Jamal Osman warned data centers can now move in with almost no limits. Advocates cited energy and water use. Data centers now fall back under existing zoning rules. Minneapolis is set to lose its temporary limits on new data centers this weekend with no new rules in place, after the City Council failed Nov. 20 to override Mayor Jacob Frey’s veto of a data center ordinance. The override vote failed 7-5. The council needed nine votes to overturn the mayor’s action. The city’s six-month moratorium on data centers ends Nov. 21, and the city council says it can’t enact another one. After the vote, council members debated whether to try to pass new rules before the deadline. “Right now as we stand, there is no regulation on data centers,” Council Vice President Jamal Osman said during the meeting, according to CBS Minnesota. Ward 9 Council Member Jason Chavez warned that without action, “It is going to be open season everywhere else.” If no new rules pass before the moratorium expires, data centers fall back under the city’s existing zoning code, which allows them with a permit in 10 of the city’s 15 zoning districts. The council approved the ordinance 7-6 on Nov. 12, after a proposal to ban new data centers outright failed 6-7. The ordinance would have allowed data centers in existing buildings in two downtown zones while creating an overlay district and capping their size, and it required disclosure of energy and water use. The overlay district meant the council would have to approve each new data center. Frey vetoed the ordinance Nov. 19. In his veto letter, he said the staff recommendation the council started with is “one of the strictest data center regulatory frameworks in the country,” and that the council’s late amendments “result in a de facto ban.” He objected most to requiring a separate overlay district for each site, writing that it “would create inconsistent rules for everyone, including residents, and would lead to arbitrary rule making.” He also argued that downtown needs commercial development to ease the city’s “property tax crunch.” In a statement to the MSR, Frey said: “I look forward to quickly developing a thoughtful policy that supports economic development and our property tax base while addressing community concerns around noise and energy use.” In an email to media Nov. 20, Frey’s press secretary, Jennifer Lor, said the staff framework, which the council’s Committee of the Whole approved Nov. 10, would have restricted new data centers to existing downtown buildings, required them to share buildings with other uses, limited server space, encouraged renewable energy and required disclosure of energy, water and generator use. The overlay district, she said, came from an amendment by Council Member Robin Wonsley that failed in committee and was added before the final vote. Lor disputed suggestions that the staff approach would shut residents out. Data centers would still need a conditional use permit, which triggers a public hearing, she wrote. “Primary zoning is not the equivalent of ‘as of right’ development.” Minneapolis Downtown Council CEO Adam Duininck, who urged Frey to veto the ordinance, told the MSR the main concern for developers is predictability. “Capital flows toward certainty,” Duininck said. “When approval ultimately depends on a discretionary vote of a city council, uncertainty increases substantially.” Ward 8 Council Member Soren Stevenson, who voted for the ordinance, said in a Facebook post Nov. 19 that the council had turned to regulation only after a full ban failed. “When the ban didn’t pass, we voted for a regulatory framework that offers protections and ensures that community members will at least have a say in data center proposals,” Stevenson wrote. He called the veto “one of the most dangerous I have seen yet.” Osman, who represents Ward 6, also criticized the veto in a Facebook post that day. “That means data centers can move in with almost no rules. No size limit. No clean energy. They don’t have to tell us how much water and power they use. And neighbors don’t get a say,” Osman wrote. “This is exactly what I wanted to avoid.” Advocates, including Twin Cities Democratic Socialists of America, the Climate Justice Committee and Sunrise Movement Twin Cities, rallied outside City Hall on Nov. 10 for a ban or, at minimum, strict regulations, citing data centers’ energy and water use and arguing that downtown buildings could be used for housing or grocery stores instead. “Instead of building more affordable housing, we are saying our greatest imagination of how to build new buildings should go towards a data center,” Wonsley, who represents Ward 2, said at the rally. “That’s shameful.” If a ban failed, Wonsley said, the council should at minimum pass the strongest possible regulations. “We want to make the terrain as difficult as possible so that they know you don’t have a home here in Minneapolis,” she said. Kai Uehara, an organizer with Twin Cities DSA’s Stop Data Centers campaign, called the outcome disappointing but said the fight in Minneapolis isn’t over. “We were hoping that we’d be able to come to some common sense regulations, and that we’d be able to get enough city council members to understand that we’re not trying to do a full ban on data centers,” Uehara told the MSR. “We’re trying to make sure that our elected officials are being accoun

artigo.texto: O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou nesta sexta-feira (20) que pretende impedir empresas americanas de construir data centers fora do país. Durante coletiva de imprensa na Casa Branca, Trump declarou que companhias que instalarem centros de dados no exterior poderão enfrentar impostos elevados. A proposta foi apresentada durante declarações sobre inteligência artificial, mas o presidente não detalhou as alíquotas nem os mecanismos para aplicar as restrições. Dados da CNN. O Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) do Chile recuou 1,8% no terceiro trimestre, em comparação ao período anterior, registrando a maior queda desde 2020. O resultado reflete dificuldades na mineração, desemprego elevado e eventos climáticos severos. A presidente do Banco Central chileno, Rosanna Costa, alertou que a recuperação econômica pode demorar mais que o esperado, diante da baixa confiança empresarial e da ausência de sinais claros de retomada dos investimentos. A Anthropic adotou um modelo incomum em sua oferta pública inicial de ações (IPO), realizada na quinta-feira (19). Assim como a SpaceX, a empresa impôs restrições aos bancos responsáveis pela operação. Entre as exigências estavam limites ao número de profissionais envolvidos, maior controle sobre informações financeiras e cláusulas que restringiam a atuação de banqueiros junto a empresas concorrentes. A Petrobras deve anunciar nesta segunda-feira (23) um novo plano de investimentos para o período de 2027 a 2031. Analistas estimam gastos entre US$ 115 bilhões e US$ 120 bilhões, acima dos US$ 109 bilhões previstos anteriormente. A estatal pretende acelerar projetos de exploração e produção de petróleo, ampliar a fabricação de diesel e investir em biocombustíveis. A meta é reduzir a dependência brasileira de diesel importado. O secretário do Tesouro dos Estados Unidos, Scott Bessent, afirmou neste domingo (22) que o governo Trump busca esclarecimentos sobre as vendas de chips da Nvidia à China. A investigação ocorre após a saída de Jensen Huang da liderança da empresa, em meio a suspeitas de envolvimento com uma suposta espiã chinesa. O presidente Donald Trump sancionou uma lei que oficializa o fim da produção de moedas de um centavo de dólar nos Estados Unidos. A medida busca reduzir gastos, já que cada unidade custava quase quatro centavos para ser fabricada. A fabricação havia sido interrompida em novembro de 2025, mas as moedas existentes continuarão em circulação. A nova legislação também estabelece regras de arredondamento para pagamentos em dinheiro.

artigo.texto: Telebras estima iniciar operação de data center de IA em 1 ano Anatel formalizou a destinação de R$ 375 milhões em recursos remanescentes do leilão do 5G para o empreendimento O presidente da Telebras, Hermano Albuquerque, disse ao Poder360, em entrevista gravada na 5ª feira (19.nov.2026), que a estatal pretende iniciar a operação de um novo data center voltado para o uso de IA (inteligência artificial) no fim do ano que vem. O prazo considera o uso de uma estrutura de contêineres para dar celeridade ao início do funcionamento. Posteriormente, novas infraestruturas serão montadas para acomodar o crescimento do empreendimento. O data center foi orçado em R$ 375 milhões. O montante será pago pela EAF (Entidade Administradora da Faixa de 3,5 GHz), entidade que administra os recursos adquiridos no leilão do 5G. O aval da Anatel (Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações) foi oficializado na 4ª feira (18.nov). Eis a íntegra do acórdão (PDF – 133 kB). Mesmo com os recursos liberados, a Telebras ainda precisa definir uma estratégia para manter a operação do data center. Hermano disse que a estatal ainda não realizou um levantamento completo para a manutenção do empreendimento, mas que a empresa desenha um plano para que o data center já inicie o funcionamento com receita operacional “basicamente já pagando os custos operacionais”. Ao Poder360, Hermano disse que a Telebras ainda não definiu onde será construído o data center. Declarou que a decisão será tomada “em breve” e citou Brasília (DF) como uma das possibilidades. Atualmente, a estatal de capital misto possui 5 data centers próprios, sendo o maior deles em Brasília. Os outros empreendimentos ficam no Rio de Janeiro (RJ), Campo Grande (MS), Salvador (BA) e Florianópolis (SC). Assista à entrevista com o presidente da Telebras (15min34s):

artigo.texto: Com o objetivo de suprir 75% da demanda de eletricidade com energia renovável. A fábrica da LEGO no Vietnã colocou recentemente em operação energia renovável proveniente de seu sistema de armazenamento de baterias. Este é um marco significativo no plano para atingir o uso de 100% de energia renovável na fábrica do Grupo LEGO no Vietnã. O sistema foi desenvolvido por meio de uma colaboração entre a LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam e a Vietnam- Singapore Industrial Park Joint Venture Company Limited (VSIP), como parte de uma solução de energia renovável em larga escala, projetada especificamente para o setor de manufatura industrial no Vietnã. Segundo a empresa, este é o primeiro sistema de armazenamento de energia baseado em baterias desta escala no Vietname, contribuindo para expandir a aplicação de soluções de energia renovável na produção industrial. A entrada em funcionamento do sistema de armazenamento de baterias é o próximo passo na implementação do Acordo de Compra Direta de Energia (DPPA, na sigla em inglês) entre o Grupo LEGO e a VSIP, assinado em setembro de 2025. De acordo com o acordo, a LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam opera o sistema de energia solar no telhado da fábrica e também utiliza energia renovável fornecida por meio do sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) operado pela VSIP. Especificamente, a eletricidade produzida pelo sistema de energia solar no telhado será integrada ao sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias da VSIP e transmitida diretamente para a fábrica por meio de uma linha de transmissão dedicada. Quando a quantidade de eletricidade produzida exceder a demanda, o excedente será armazenado no sistema de baterias e fornecido de volta quando necessário. Essa solução ajuda a regular o fornecimento de eletricidade de acordo com a demanda real, aumenta o potencial de aproveitamento de energias renováveis e mantém um fornecimento estável de eletricidade para dar suporte às atividades de produção. Em conjunto com os 12.400 painéis solares instalados nos telhados dos edifícios da fábrica, espera-se que o sistema de armazenamento de energia atenda a aproximadamente 75% das necessidades totais de eletricidade da LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam durante os primeiros cinco anos de operação. Notavelmente, espera-se que essa solução integrada ajude a evitar a emissão de aproximadamente 20.000 toneladas de CO₂e por ano. A redução de emissões é calculada com base no fator de emissão da rede elétrica do Vietnã, de 0,561 toneladas de CO₂e/MWh, incluindo a eletricidade produzida pelo sistema de energia solar fotovoltaica já existente no telhado da usina. Para os 25% restantes de suas necessidades de eletricidade, a LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam está explorando novos contratos de compra de energia (PPAs) para expandir gradualmente a proporção de energia renovável utilizada. Embora ainda não seja possível atender a todas as necessidades por meio desses contratos, a fábrica planeja utilizar certificados de energia renovável (RECs) para a eletricidade restante. O Sr. Jesper Hassellund Mikkelsen, Vice-Presidente Sênior de Manufatura para a Ásia do Grupo LEGO e Gerente Geral da LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam, avaliou que a implementação do sistema é de grande importância para a estratégia de desenvolvimento sustentável do grupo. “Este é um passo muito significativo para os objetivos de desenvolvimento sustentável do Grupo no Vietnã e globalmente. Ao combinar tecnologia avançada com estreita colaboração com parceiros, estamos concretizando nossas metas de energia renovável. Este marco também demonstra o valor prático que a indústria manufatureira pode criar quando as empresas trabalham juntas”, disse Jesper Hassellund Mikkelsen. Por parte dos parceiros de desenvolvimento de infraestrutura industrial, o Sr. Nguyen Phu Thinh, Diretor Geral da VSIP, afirmou que a implantação em larga escala de soluções de energia renovável na fábrica da LEGO demonstra o potencial para alcançar os objetivos de desenvolvimento sustentável por meio da cooperação entre empresas. Segundo o Sr. Nguyen Phu Thinh, o acordo de compra direta de energia entre o Grupo LEGO e a VSIP representa um marco significativo para ambas as partes e demonstra o potencial de cooperação entre desenvolvedores de infraestrutura industrial e empresas de manufatura na construção de modelos operacionais sustentáveis. “O Contrato de Compra Direta de Energia (DPPA, na sigla em inglês) entre o Grupo LEGO e a VSIP não é apenas um marco importante para ambas as partes, mas também uma forte demonstração do potencial de cooperação entre desenvolvedores de infraestrutura industrial e empresas de manufatura para criar um novo modelo operacional de produção sustentável”, enfatizou o Sr. Nguyen Phu Thinh. Promover modelos de produção sustentáveis no Vietnã A fábrica da LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam, inaugurada oficialmente em abril de 2025, foi construída para atender às necessidades de crescimento de longo prazo do Grupo LEGO na região, promovendo também a conquista dos objetivos de desenvolvimento sustentável. Localizada na cidade de Ho Chi Minh, a fábrica ocupa 44 hectares de terreno, o equivalente a aproximadamente 62 campos de futebol . A construção compreende cinco edifícios com uma área total de cerca de 150.000 m², incluindo escritórios, uma central de energia, uma área de moldagem e embalagem de plástico, um armazém automatizado e outras instalações de apoio. Segundo informações divulgadas pela empresa, a fábrica emprega atualmente 1.350 pessoas e está equipada com maquinário de produção moderno, atendendo aos rigorosos padrões de qualidade e precisão dos produtos LEGO. Além de expandir o uso de energia renovável, a LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam também está implementando diversas soluções para reduzir seu impacto ambiental durante o processo de produção. artigo.texto: Keeping mobility affordable while advancing Europe's climate objectives was the focus of a policy debate organised by FIA Region I in Brussels. IRU joined policymakers, consumer organisations and industry representatives to discuss how the EU's new emissions trading system (ETS2) can support a fair transition for road users and transport businesses. The event, “ETS2 and affordable mobility: Is Europe ready for a fair transition?”, explored the implications of ETS2 for mobility costs across Europe, drawing on new research commissioned by the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) Region I. Under the study’s central scenario, ETS2 could increase petrol prices by EUR 0.207 per litre and diesel prices by EUR 0.242 per litre, excluding VAT. It also highlights the uneven impact of higher fuel costs, particularly on vulnerable and car-dependent households with limited access to affordable transport alternatives. IRU Senior Adviser Passenger Transport Suzanne Hoadley brought the road transport operator perspective to the debate. Supporting a fair and affordable transition EU countries are preparing for ETS2 implementation in 2028 and weighing measures to address its impact on consumers and businesses. “Ensuring that ETS2 revenues generated from road transport are reinvested in the sector's decarbonisation is a key policy priority,” said Suzanne Hoadley. “It would help operators make the transition while maintaining affordable and accessible services.” The EU Social Climate Fund and national Social Climate Plans offer further opportunities to support vulnerable mobility users, particularly in areas where affordable alternatives remain limited. The debate highlighted the importance of bringing consumer and operator perspectives together as Europe prepares for ETS2.

artigo.texto: O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump Repórter Publicado em 20 de novembro de 2026 às 15h56. Donald Trump ameaçou proibir empresas americanas de construírem data centers no exterior, prometendo penalidades severas. A medida visa conter o avanço tecnológico da China e impacta o modelo global de expansão de gigantes de tecnologia. O Brasil também enfrenta restrições adicionais sobre exportação de chips de IA para data centers. O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou nesta sexta-feira, 20, que não permitirá que companhias americanas construam data centersfora do território norte-americano e prometeu aplicar "penalidades tremendas" a quem tentar expandir essa infraestrutura no exterior. A declaração foi feita durante uma coletiva de imprensa na Casa Branca, após seu retorno de uma viagem à Ásia. Trump justificou a medida como uma forma de conter o avanço tecnológico de Pequim. "Não vamos permitir que data centers vão para outros países porque a China vai tomar todos eles, e não vamos permitir que isso aconteça, e vamos aplicar penalidades tremendas às empresas que tentarem fazer isso", disse o presidente, comparando a disputa atual pelo setor de data centers à corrida global por semicondutores. Durante a coletiva, o republicano citou um alvo imediato e afirmou que seu governo agirá para bloquear o projeto de uma empresa americana na Finlândia — uma referência ao plano do Google de investir cerca de US$ 15 bilhões em data centers e infraestrutura de inteligência artificial no país europeu entre 2027 e 2028. A ameaça de proibição ou de taxação pesada atinge diretamente o modelo global de expansão das gigantes de tecnologia americanas, como Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta e Oracle, que operam redes de computação em nuvem em diversos continentes. O endurecimento do discurso também ocorre em meio a um entrave doméstico: a forte resistência de comunidades locais nos próprios Estados Unidos contra a instalação de novos data centers. Essa oposição já levou ao cancelamento de cerca de US$ 260 bilhões em projetos planejados no país apenas em 2026. Na coletiva, Trump pediu às comunidades americanas que não barrem os empreendimentos, sugerindo que negociem contrapartidas financeiras com as empresas de tecnologia. Embora a Finlândia tenha sido o exemplo citado nominalmente por Trump nesta sexta-feira, a nova ofensiva de Washington sobre a infraestrutura de inteligência artificial endurece ainda mais o cenário para o Brasil, que já vinha sendo alvo direto das restrições tecnológicas americanas. Na última segunda-feira (16), o Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos incluiu o Brasil — ao lado de Singapura, Malásia, Tailândia e Indonésia — em uma lista de países submetidos a novas barreiras comerciais. A regra passou a exigir uma licença prévia do governo americano para a exportação de chips avançados de inteligência artificial destinados a data centers instalados nesses territórios. O governo Trump justificou a inclusão do Brasil na lista de restrições pelo risco de acesso remoto da China à capacidade de processamento americana. A preocupação de Washington recai sobre a presença e a expansão de gigantes chinesas de tecnologia no mercado brasileiro — como ByteDance, Alibaba Cloud, Tencent Cloud e Huawei Cloud —, que operam ou constroem estruturas de nuvem e dados no país. Com a nova ameaça de barrar até mesmo investimentos diretos de empresas americanas no exterior, o ambiente para a atração de grandes projetos de infraestrutura digital no Brasil tende a enfrentar uma pressão geopolítica ainda maior.

artigo.texto: Jordan, Uzbekistan Discuss Investment in 450MW Mujib Energy Storage Project 22/11/2026 | 12:44:38 Amman, Nov. 22 (Petra) -- Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources Dr. Saleh Kharabsheh on Sunday discussed potential Uzbek investment and technical cooperation in Jordan's planned 450-megawatt pumped-storage hydropower project at Mujib Dam. During a meeting with a specialized delegation from Uzbekistan, Kharabsheh outlined the project's investment framework, which provides for seven hours of energy storage and aims to improve the flexibility of Jordan's electricity grid and its ability to accommodate renewable energy. The minister said the project was presented as an investment opportunity at the 2026 Jordan-EU Investment Conference and remains open to competitive bidding. It will be developed under a Build-Own-Operate-Transfer (BOOT) arrangement within a public-private partnership (PPP) framework, allowing private investors to finance, construct and operate the facility before transferring ownership. Kharabsheh explained that the system would use electricity to pump water from a lower reservoir to an upper reservoir during the day, then release the water through turbines at night to generate electricity. He emphasized the importance of international technical expertise in developing the project, while highlighting Jordan's capabilities in construction, engineering industries and skilled technical personnel. The Uzbek delegation presented its country's experience in hydropower, including four operating plants, additional projects under development and domestic capabilities in manufacturing hydropower turbines. Delegation members expressed interest in exploring opportunities to cooperate on and participate in the Mujib project. The talks also addressed technical and investment requirements, tendering and company prequalification procedures, grid connections, electricity tariffs and operational arrangements. Both sides agreed on the importance of continued coordination and technical exchanges to advance bilateral cooperation and investment in the energy sector. //Petra// RZ
