artigo.texto: Trump diz que não vai permitir construção de data centers fora dos EUA Presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, ameaçou taxar empresas norte-americanas que construírem data centers no exterior O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou, nesta sexta-feira (20/11), que não vai permitir que empresas norte-americanas construam data centers em outros países. “Não vamos permitir que isso aconteça. Sabe, eles permitiram que isso acontecesse com os chips e tudo mais, e foi muito destrutivo para o nosso país”, disse ele. De acordo com Trump, as restrições são necessárias para manter a imagem competitiva e impedir que a infraestrutura de inteligência artificial (IA) saia do território americano. Ele também afirmou que o país vai “lutar com todas as forças pelos centros de dados” e aplicar uma “enorme multa” às empresas que contruírem no exterior. A declaração ocorreu em Washington após viagem de Trump à China para a cúpula da Cooperação Econômica Ásia-Pacífico (APEC). No país, o republicano se reuniu com os presidentes da Rússia e da China, Vladimir Putin e Xi Jinping. Pela primeira vez na história, os três líderes se reuniram para negociações. Restrições Na última segunda-feira (16/11), o governo americano anunciou uma norma que estabelece restrições para exportar, reexportar ou transferir chips de IA para data centers instalados fora dos EUA. Entre no canal de WhatsApp do Metrópoles Brasil, Indonésia, Malásia, Singapura e Tailândia estão entre os países que passarão a exigir licença para exportação ou transferência desses chips. Isso não significa que o Brasil não possa mais comprar chips dos EUA, só que agora será necessária uma autorização do governo norte-americano. A medida visa impedir que empresas da China utilize estruturas de data centers em outros países para se aproveitar da “capacidade de processamento de chips de IA” dos EUA. Por isso, a norma estabelece que centros de dados que fornecem grandes volumes de capacidade computacional às empresas chinesas precisarão de autorização do país. “A norma foi elaborada para garantir que as restrições ao acesso a tecnologias americanas sensíveis não sejam contornadas por meio de acordos de computação remota que envolvam centros de dados (data centers) instalados em países terceiros”, diz o texto.

artigo.texto: Brasil pode virar polo global de data centers, projeta The Economist Energia renovável e cabos submarinos favorecem país, mas gargalos na rede elétrica e disputa entre EUA e China podem frear expansão, aponta revista Com quase metade da capacidade de processamento instalada na América Latina, o Brasil tem condições de se tornar um polo global de data centers, avalia a revista britânica The Economist. A publicação aponta três vantagens para o país atrair investimentos no setor: a demanda de um mercado cada vez mais conectado, a oferta de eletricidade de fontes renováveis e a infraestrutura de cabos submarinos que liga o Nordeste a outros continentes. A expansão, porém, depende da capacidade de conectar novos empreendimentos à rede elétrica e pode esbarrar na disputa entre Estados Unidos e China pelo acesso aos chips mais avançados. A revista cita como exemplo a expansão da empresa Ascenty em Vinhedo, no interior de São Paulo. O complexo de 61 megawatts (MW), o maior da América Latina, já tem um novo prédio em construção e pode ganhar outros dois. Os projetos representam uma aposta de 1,2 bilhão de dólares da empresa. Parte da demanda vem dos próprios usuários latino-americanos. Segundo a Economist, a maior parte dos dados da região ainda é armazenada e processada nos Estados Unidos. O potencial brasileiro também passa por atender usuários de outros mercados. A Economist cita o projeto da ByteDance, dona do TikTok, para instalar um complexo de data centers no Nordeste, com investimento que pode chegar a 39 bilhões de dólares. A conexão por cabos submarinos com a Europa e a África seria um dos atrativos para a empresa chinesa. Já para o treinamento de modelos de inteligência artificial, em que a proximidade com o usuário final pesa menos, o Brasil disputa investimentos com destinos como o Canadá, os países nórdicos e o Oriente Médio. A oferta de eletricidade renovável é uma vantagem brasileira, mas os locais mais bem conectados à internet nem sempre coincidem com aqueles onde há energia disponível para grandes projetos. A revista aponta a demora na conexão à rede elétrica e a complexidade do licenciamento como obstáculos. Também registra protestos pontuais contra novos empreendimentos na América Latina, um sinal de que a reação das comunidades pode ganhar peso à medida que os projetos avançam. A disputa tecnológica entre Washington e Pequim acrescenta um risco. O Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos anunciou em 16 de novembro que data centers brasileiros precisariam de licença para importar os semicondutores mais avançados. A medida reflete, na leitura da revista, o receio americano de que empresas chinesas usem infraestrutura instalada no Brasil para treinar remotamente modelos de inteligência artificial com chips sujeitos a controles de exportação.

artigo.texto: Moradores de Atibaia se mobilizam contra chegada de data center na cidade Moradores questionam falta de transparência e temem possíveis impactos ambientais de instalação de data center no interior de SP São Paulo — Com pouco mais de 160 mil habitantes, Atibaia, no interior de São Paulo, entrou na mira de grandes empresas de tecnologia. O município deve ser a futura sede de um data center de R$ 3 bilhões, em uma região de divisa entre área rural e área urbana da cidade. Temendo possíveis consequências ambientais, os moradores da cidade passaram a se mobilizar contra o projeto, redigindo uma petição que solicita à prefeitura a proibição de data centers de hiperescala no município. O requerimento do movimento popular Fora Data Center pede o envio à Câmara de Vereadores de um projeto de lei complementar para alterar o código de obras e o plano diretor municipal. Um abaixo-assinado do coletivo reuniu, até meados de novembro de 2026, mais de 4 mil assinaturas. O grupo de moradores reclama de não ter sido avisado sobre o projeto e nem convocado para audiências públicas acerca do tema. Entre no canal de WhatsApp do Metrópoles SP Concessionária apresentou estudo de impacto Em uma audiência pública, em 17 de junho deste ano, a Isa Energia, a concessionária que atende a região, apresentou um estudo de impacto de vizinhança do projeto de implantação dos ramais de seccionamento para interligação da Linha de Transmissão (LT) 440 kv Bom Jardim – Água Azul à Subestação (SE) de Transmissão 440/500 kv – Fernão Dias. Segundo o movimento Fora Data Center, na audiência, o projeto foi apresentado como solução para a necessidade de melhorar a infraestrutura e garantir maior capacidade de transmissão de energia para a demanda local, sem aprofundar detalhes. Um comunicado no site da própria Isa, no entanto, revelava que o projeto teria como objetivo viabilizar o funcionamento de data centers na região, como o Data Center Alfa, já com previsão de conexão à Subestação Atibaia 2. A conexão foi autorizada pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) em outubro de 2025. O documento, ao qual o Metrópoles teve acesso, permite a expansão em 15 quilômetros da linha de transmissão e a implantação de dois novos módulos de entrada de linha em 138 kV, com a premissa de atender o Data Center Alfa. A Prefeitura de Atibaia, por sua vez, afirmou à reportagem que não identificou nos registros da Secretaria do Meio Ambiente, pedido de licenciamento ambiental vinculado ao projeto. “Caso seja formalizada proposta de implantação de data center, serão exigidos todos os estudos, licenças e autorizações legalmente aplicáveis, observadas as competências do município, da Companhia Ambiental do Estado de São Paulo (Cetesb) e dos demais órgãos responsáveis”, disse a gestão municipal. Apesar da negativa da prefeitura em relação à existência de um projeto, a empresa DataSpots já apresenta o Data Center Alfa em seu portfólio como aprovado e estruturado. A autorização do ONS também foi notícia em portais e veículos de comunicação, apontando o projeto como algo já encaminhado. Uma das publicações, no portal Datlaz, ligado a uma plataforma de inteligência geoespacial, afirma que a DataSpots prevê R$ 39 bilhões em investimentos no país, sendo Atibaia uma das cidades escolhidas. Para a comunidade, o fato de a empresa dar como certa a construção do empreendimento contrasta com a falta de posicionamento claro da prefeitura e a ausência de audiências públicas para debater os impactos do futuro data center. Moradores temem riscos ambientais O projeto da DataSpots, empresa do Grupo ON, foi anunciado como um empreendimento de alto potencial energético, com previsão de início operacional entre 2029/2030. O Data Center Alfa terá uma infraestrutura de transmissão de energia elétrica que opera na tensão de 138.000 volts — o que permite demandar e injetar potências elevadas, de dezenas a centenas de megawatts, como 50 MW ou 100 MW. O terreno inicialmente previsto para a instalação do complexo possui uma área equivalente a 50 campos de futebol, localizado no Bairro do Tanque, divisa entre área rural e área urbana. O movimento Fora Data Center alerta para o risco da retirada de vegetação nativa da Mata Atlântica e de contaminação irreversível do lençol freático, em razão dos reservatórios de óleo diesel no subsolo, utilizados por data centers de hiperescala para alimentar centenas de geradores de emergência (UPS). Os moradores do Bairro do Tanque também temem um estresse hídrico, que pode gerar falta de água, já que o bairro é atendido parcialmente pelo sistema de abastecimento de água encanada e não dispõe de atendimento por rede coletora e tratamento de esgoto. “A gente mora em um bairro que não tem saneamento, não tem água encanada, não tem esgoto. Então, todo mundo que mora no bairro onde vai ser colocado esse data center, depende de poço para ter água. A maioria usa um poço caipira e já está ficando sem água na época de seca”, conta Gabriel Tonobohn, morador do bairro há 3 anos e meio. Gabriel também conta que a região não tem barreiras sonoras, podendo ser altamente impactada com os ruídos gerados pelo empreendimento. “Qualquer barulho que acontece na rua, a gente ouve, mesmo que esteja longe. A gente ouve quando a subestação de energia soa um alarme, não conseguimos dormir. Então, se você tiver um ruído de um data center ali, certamente todo mundo vai ouvir, todo mundo vai ficar incomodado com isso”, destaca. Além disso, há uma preocupação relacionada às zonas de calor — uma área ao redor da infraestrutura onde a temperatura do solo e do ar se eleva significativamente — geradas por data centers. Em um contexto predominantemente rural, poucas casas têm condições arquitetônicas para amenizar o impacto do aumento da temperatura. “As pessoas moram aqui há mais de 20 anos e são familiares. artigo.texto: Several Indiana Cities Sour On Local Tax Breaks For Data Centers By Carson Gerber FPI News SOUTH BEND – Randy Figg has a major regret during his nearly five years serving on the St. Joseph County Council: voting to approve one of the most lucrative local tax abatement packages in the state for the more than $11 billion Amazon Web Services data center campus near New Carlisle. He said when the project was first brought to the council in 2024, economic development officials indicated AWS would walk away if it didn’t get the tax breaks that will save the company billions of dollars over more than 30 years. In retrospect, Figg said, that likely wasn’t the case. In just the first half of this year, those abatements cost the county $38 million in property tax revenue. “Can you imagine if St. Joe County had that money?” Figg said. “I’m done with taxpayers supporting these businesses.” That sentiment is growing among state and local officials as data centers continue to draw fierce opposition from residents who blame the developments for rising utility bills and are demanding the nation’s tech giants pay their fair share. Once considered a necessary tool to attract business investments, more Indiana cities and counties are questioning the use of local tax abatements for data centers that are searching for communities open to development. Out of 92 counties, 36 have moratoriums or bans on the projects. Gov. Mike Braun on Monday said even though he supports data center developments, they shouldn’t receive local tax abatements. Qualifying projects already don’t have to pay state sales taxes and can get lucrative incentive packages from the Indiana Economic Development Corp. “These are the richest companies in the world,” Braun said during the Indianapolis Business Journal’s Future of Energy Summit. “They should be enhancing the community.” Justin Ross, a public finance economist at Indiana University, said many city and county officials didn’t understand their bargaining power when data centers first started building in the state. Now, with fewer counties allowing the developments and surging demand for AI, local officials are realizing they have the upper hand in negotiating economic development deals, he said. “They’re saying, ‘Not only can we not give them a tax exemption or abatement. We can actually ask for more and get it,’” Ross said. Saying ‘No’ That’s the approach Kokomo is taking. In October, the city announced Digital Realty was pursuing a 476-acre data center campus in an industrial-focused region of the city. The caveat: the project would not receive any local tax abatements, an unusual move for an Indiana city or county considering a major project. Mayor Tyler Moore said they “rolled the dice” and put the no-tax-abatement stipulation in place because residents don’t want their tax dollars subsidizing data centers. Also, the developments don’t create enough permanent jobs to justify one, he said. Digital Realty said in a statement it accepted those terms and decided to build in Kokomo because of the city’s “skilled workforce and history of successfully delivering large-scale projects.” “We value open dialogue with residents and local leaders, and that feedback is helping guide how we invest in and grow with the community,” the company said in an email. The city anticipates the project will generate between $44 million and $55 million in annual property tax revenue once complete in 2033. Moore said a portion of those dollars would go to every school district in the county and likely allow the city to do away with its recently implemented trash fees. Moore said he “wholeheartedly” believes local tax abatements for data centers are on the way out as officials realize companies will build without getting one. “I think a lot of them are seeing the public outcry,” he said. Earlier this month, an Indianapolis City-County Council committee recommended that the full council reject about $113 million in tax breaks for DC Blox, a data center developer approved to construct two buildings on Indianapolis’ east side. The recommendation represented a stark break with a decision in September by another city development commission that approved a $240 million tax break for Sabey Data Centers located on Indy’s southwest side. Local officials across the state are questioning the use of tax abatements as they anticipate significant revenue losses from last year’s Senate Bill 1, which will cost cities and counties more than $1.4 billion in local property tax revenue by the end of 2028, according to the Indiana Legislative Services Agency. Figg said that’s a major reason he regrets voting to approve the abatements for the AWS campus in St. Joseph County, where the legislation is projected to cut $100 million from local coffers. The county estimates it will collect $1.4 million a year in taxes on the tech equipment in each data center building, but the abatement is about $7.2 million per building and lasts for over 30 years. AWS plans to build around 32 buildings in total. The county is also receiving around $1.15 million a year in property taxes on each building. Once the 50% property tax abatement expires in 2036, officials expect to receive $2.3 million from each building. Jeff Rea, president and CEO of the South Bend Regional Chamber, said in an op-ed piece that the county “played the long game” with the tax abatements in order to land the long-term economic benefits the project will bring, like over 1,000 permanent new jobs. But Figg said even though the county is getting additional tax money now, it also needs the revenue currently lost to the tax breaks to help offset losses from the Senate Bill 1. “We’ve got to come up with new revenue, and so you can’t be giving abatements away,” he said. ‘A True Commitment To Our Community’ As Indiana communities pull back on local abatements, some companies are taking matters into their own hands. artigo.texto: Indiana Township officials are preparing new regulations in case any data center developers come knocking. A public hearing to discuss a proposed zoning ordinance amendment setting various conditions on such developments is set for 6 p.m. Dec. 9 at Town Hall, 3710 Saxonburg Blvd. The 18-page draft is available for review at the township office and online at indianatownship.com. Supervisors may vote on the ordinance after the public hearing. “We want to have the public hearing and solicit input from the community,” Mayor Darrin Krally said. “I can’t say with certainty that it meets every single need as is today, but that’s why we have the process.” Several township officials said there have been no requests to build a data center as of mid-November, and it is important to get rules in the books before any plan submissions. “I have been fighting to keep data centers out of Indiana Township since summer 2025, when I first sent a model ordinance to our township manager (Dan Anderson),” Supervisor Jonathan Newmann said. “I would ban data centers outright, but state law currently prevents (us) from doing so. The next best thing is to pass the proposed ordinance the board is considering in December. Currently, our zoning code has no specific protections against data centers, and we saw in Springdale the disastrous consequences of not having a law in place when the developers come to town. “We need to get this ordinance on the books and keep pressure on Gov. (Josh) Shapiro to redeem his past failures on data centers by giving local municipalities like Indiana Township the power to completely ban them from our community.” Springdale’s problem Springdale residents spoke out against a proposed data center several times within the past year. Developer Allegheny DC Property Co. LLC revealed initial plans to build a hyperscale AI data center at the former site of the Cheswick Generating Station in August 2025. In December, borough council approved the conditional-use application for the project. The Allegheny County’s Economic Development (ACED) Planning Division has been reviewing the application because Springdale does not have ordinances in place establishing its jurisdiction over subdivision and land use decisions. County officials recently found nearly 100 problems with the application. However, many may easily be fixed, and two issues will have to be thoroughly addressed. The first involves noise pollution, and the second deals with soil contamination. It is unclear when or how those problems may be corrected. The ACED has until Jan. 26 to approve, approve with conditions or deny the developer’s Preliminary Land Development Plan. Indiana Township’s ordinance Indiana Township’s proposed zoning ordinance amendment would define data centers as a conditional use in the light industrial zoning district. Regulations include a minimum lot size of 15 acres and a maximum data center building height of 35 feet, plus up to an additional 10 feet for roof-mounted equipment such as cooling and ventilation systems, according to the ordinance. Data centers and data center accessory uses must be set back at least 200 feet from the lot line of any property line of a school, residence, child or adult daycare, hospital, nursing home, community center and similar developments. Other rules include a minimum setback of 150 feet from all other adjoining proper lines and road rights-of-way, and a landscape buffer must be at least 50 feet in width. Applicants also must conduct a sound study and vibration study by certified professionals, submit a water feasibility study and an energy usage plan. The energy use plan must show an annual electricity demand, energy supply sources that will be used, proposed sources of back-up power and energy storage capacity if applicable. The ordinance also would require applicants to monitor and report energy efficiency and emissions data to the township on a regular basis. An emergency response plan would be needed with detailed procedures for fire suppression, containment, ventilation and evacuation, as well as evaluation of the access roads and hydrant locations within the site to ensure suitable access for emergency equipment. Data centers also must provide at least one parking space for every employee, based upon the maximum number of employees on-site during the largest shift. The proposed ordinance was recommended for approval by the township’s planning commission in August. Krally believes the proposed regulations are strong and necessary. He also said a data center would be a benefit to the township and create jobs. “In general, data centers are definitely needed,” Krally said. “You and I are speaking on an iPhone. We use iPads. We use laptops. Everybody has their technology that they love. It definitely serves a need from a community standpoint — if you have tracks of land that are zoned accordingly and it can work with little or no disruption and whosever building it is responsible, coming in and helping the community (and) being a community partner. “A ban is ridiculous. We can’t have it anyways, but to me just banning is ignorant. You don’t say, ‘We’re never going to do it,’ without a conversation.” The mayor said he looks forward to the public hearing and finding ways to keep the community safe while helping America stay at the forefront of the technology race.

This week’s episode also includes a recap on the Socktober benefit for Rock House Kids and the upcoming Holiday Home Walk in Rockton. Neal’s segment is the third in the episode, beginning around the 19:30 mark. Neal and Summers conversation came after the more than five-hour public hearing where residents gave feedback on potential data center regulations, with the vast majority saying tougher restrictions are needed. “I’m glad that people showed up to voice their concerns because that’s what this moment is about,” Neal said. She also emphasized that although Microsoft is considering the development, the tech giant still has not put forward an official proposal for consideration. “There is nothing signed. There’s no shovels in the ground, anything like that,” she said. “Right now we’re just working on protecting us as residents.”

artigo.texto: Em um ano, data centers dos EUA geraram 25 milhões de toneladas de CO2 O gás liberado na geração de eletricidade para abastecer 403 centros de dados retém calor na atmosfera e favorece o aquecimento global A geração de eletricidade para abastecer 403 centros de dados de grande porte nos Estados Unidos esteve associada à emissão de 25,7 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono (CO2) entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025. A estimativa é de um estudo liderado pela Universidade Harvard e publicado em 16 de novembro na revista Nature Sustainability. O volume é de duas a três vezes maior que uma estimativa anterior para 2018. Conhecidas como centros de dados de hiperescala, as instalações analisadas abrigam servidores que sustentam serviços como o armazenamento de arquivos na nuvem e o treinamento de sistemas de inteligência artificial (IA). Os números englobam o consumo de eletricidade das instalações para o conjunto de serviços que elas oferecem. Consumo se aproxima de estados americanos No cenário central do estudo, os centros de dados consumiram cerca de 82 terawatts-hora em 12 meses, o equivalente a 1,8% de toda a eletricidade usada nos Estados Unidos no período. Entre no canal de WhatsApp do Metrópoles A estimativa variou de 68 a 99 terawatts-hora conforme o nível de atividade dos servidores. No limite superior, o consumo se aproxima do que estados como Indiana, Michigan e Tennessee usam, cada um, em um ano. A demanda também se concentrou em poucas regiões. Virgínia, Oregon, Ohio e Iowa responderam, juntos, por mais da metade da eletricidade consumida pelas instalações analisadas. De onde vem a eletricidade dos data centers ? - Gás natural: Foi a principal fonte, responsável por cerca de 38% da eletricidade usada pelos centros de dados. - Carvão: Respondeu por aproximadamente 15% do consumo. Somadas, as fontes fósseis forneceram cerca de 54% da eletricidade usada pelas instalações. - Redes elétricas regionais: Cerca de um quarto do consumo ocorreu em regiões onde a geração de eletricidade emitia mais CO2 por unidade de energia do que a média americana. Conforme o nível de atividade das instalações, as emissões associadas ao consumo de eletricidade ficaram entre 21 milhões e 31 milhões de toneladas de CO2 no período analisado. O estudo identificou diferenças entre as regiões porque a quantidade de CO2 liberada para gerar eletricidade varia conforme as fontes usadas em cada rede.

artigo.texto: - The EU and UK have concluded negotiations to link their emissions trading systems, with implementation targeted for 2028. - Cross-border CO2 storage could reduce offshore transport and storage costs for EU industrial emitters by as much as 28%. - The CCSA estimates the opportunity could generate $5.26 billion (£4 billion) in annual UK export revenues and attract $9.21 billion (£7 billion) in investment by 2040. The European Union and the United Kingdom have concluded negotiations to link their Emissions Trading Systems (ETS), marking a significant step towards an integrated European carbon market. The EU-UK ETS linkage could strengthen the Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) industry, expand cross-border CO2 storage and lower costs for industrial emitters. The agreement, announced at the EU-UK Summit in Brussels on Friday, is part of a broader effort to rebuild economic ties following Brexit. The arrangement will allow mutual recognition of EU and UK emissions allowances and provide exemptions from their respective Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms (CBAM) for goods traded between the two markets. Both sides aim to bring the agreement into effect in 2028, subject to the necessary legal procedures. The Carbon Capture and Storage Association (CCSA) welcomed the announcement, highlighting its potential to improve access to storage facilities across Europe and encourage investment in infrastructure. Billions In Investment Potential A connected storage market spanning the EU’s 27 member states, the European Economic Area and the UK could deliver substantial savings. The CCSA estimates that European industrial emitters could save an average of $12.07 (€11) per tonne, while companies in EU member states could achieve reductions of up to 28%, equivalent to approximately $17.55 (€16) per tonne in offshore transport and storage costs. The association also estimates that cross-border CO2 transport and storage could generate $5.26 billion (£4 billion) in annual export revenues for the UK and attract $9.21 billion (£7 billion) in investment by 2040. Olivia Powis, CEO of the CCSA, said: “We warmly welcome the agreement to link the EU and UK Emissions Trading Systems. This is a really positive step towards creating an integrated European CCUS market”. She added: “Our analysis shows the significant shared economic opportunity for the UK and Europe.” The International Emissions Trading Association (IETA) said linking the two carbon markets could improve liquidity, reduce transaction costs and make it easier for regulated companies to manage carbon-price risks. Research by Frontier Economics estimates that lower transaction costs alone could generate $845 million (€770 million) in shared benefits over the five years to 2030, highlighting the potential economic gains beyond the development of CO2 storage infrastructure. Dirk Forrister, President and CEO of IETA, said: “No single market can deliver net zero alone. Linking the EU and UK carbon markets deepens liquidity, strengthens the price signal and shows what cooperation can achieve – a blueprint for greater ambition worldwide. Linkages like this are vital and prove that markets work, and carbon markets matter.” Implementation Remains The Next Challenge The CCSA is calling for clear implementation deadlines and regulatory provisions to enable cross-border CO2 transportation and storage. It also wants EU policymakers to recognise storage facilities in third countries under the EU ETS by 2029. The wider EU-UK reset also covers food trade and youth mobility, reflecting efforts to deepen cooperation beyond carbon markets. artigo.texto: Governo Trump anunciou novas restrições ao acesso remoto a chips e servidores avançados utilizados em inteligência artificial TECNOLOGIA Trump quer taxar empresas que construírem data centers fora dos EUA Por Redação O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou, nessa sexta-feira (20), que empresas norte-americanas de tecnologia poderão enfrentar uma tributação elevada caso construam centros de dados de inteligência artificial (IA) fora do país. A declaração foi feita durante entrevista à imprensa na Casa Branca, sem detalhamento sobre valores, critérios ou prazos para a eventual cobrança. Trump defendeu a expansão da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial em território norte-americano e incentivou as comunidades a negociar contrapartidas financeiras com as empresas responsáveis pelos empreendimentos. Segundo o presidente, a população deve buscar benefícios econômicos com a instalação dos centros de processamento de dados, em vez de impedir sua construção. A declaração ocorre em meio ao debate sobre o impacto dos data centers no consumo de energia elétrica dos Estados Unidos. Na quinta-feira (19), o Senado aprovou uma proposta bipartidária para acelerar o licenciamento de usinas, linhas de transmissão e outras estruturas energéticas, com o objetivo de ampliar a oferta de eletricidade e atender à crescente demanda do setor tecnológico. O avanço dos projetos, entretanto, enfrenta resistência em diferentes regiões do país. Moradores e autoridades locais demonstram preocupação com o aumento das tarifas de energia, os impactos ambientais e a utilização de recursos públicos para viabilizar os empreendimentos. Diante desse cenário, empresas como Google e Meta têm anunciado medidas para ampliar a transparência, reduzir impactos ambientais e oferecer benefícios econômicos às comunidades que recebem suas instalações. A possível tributação também se soma às restrições comerciais adotadas pelo governo norte-americano para controlar o acesso internacional a tecnologias avançadas. Nesta semana, a administração Trump anunciou novas regras sobre o acesso remoto a chips e servidores de alto desempenho utilizados no treinamento de modelos de inteligência artificial. As medidas buscam limitar o uso dessas tecnologias por empresas chinesas e afetam o fornecimento de semicondutores para centros de dados instalados em diferentes países, incluindo o Brasil. Até o momento, Trump não apresentou uma proposta formal para a tributação das empresas que instalarem data centers no exterior.

artigo.texto: Google to use geothermal energy from Oregon volcano to power data centers Quaise Energy has signed a purchase agreement with Google to develop superhot geothermal energy near Bend, with electricity expected to begin flowing as early as 2030. The agreement marks big step for Project Obsidian, which Quaise is developing on Bureau of Land Management land south of Newberry National Volcanic Monument, 20 miles south of Bend. The project aims to tap deep underground heat to generate electricity for Google’s data center operations in The Dalles. The agreement also provides a major customer for the project’s initial phase, which Quaise has been developing around a planned 50-megawatt power plant. The companies did not disclose the financial terms of the agreement. Harry Kelso, a spokesperson for Quaise, said a power plant will bring economic benefit to Central Oregon. “To date, we’ve injected more than $6 million into Deschutes County businesses as part of Project Obsidian, and we expect that local impact to continue as the project advances,” Kelso said. The project is expected to support 200 to 400 construction jobs and create more than 50 permanent positions in engineering and operations, according to Quaise. Earlier this year, Quaise drilled its first well at the site, a confirmation well expected to reach a depth of about 15,000 feet. The company is using conventional drilling methods for initial development, with plans to introduce its experimental drilling technology in a later phase. The technology uses concentrated electromagnetic energy to break through hard rock and is designed to reach extreme underground temperatures that could make geothermal power more viable. Quaise estimates superhot systems could produce up to 10 times more electricity per well than traditional geothermal systems. Google has operated in The Dalles since 2006 and now has three data centers in the area. The company said its Oregon data centers use 83% carbon-free energy and that the new agreement will expand its investment in clean energy. Google also said it has invested more than $7 billion in Oregon over the past 20 years. Data centers have come under fire in recent months amid public backlash against their massive energy and water needs. Around 75% of Americans now say they oppose data center construction near them. Deschutes County Commissioner-elect Jamie Collins, a climate scientist and former environmental emergency response official, said in a statement on Tuesday that “transparent and deep engagement with our community” is needed. Collins is calling on Obsidian for public outreach and engagement with tribal nations and community organizations. He also wants to learn if some of the energy will be available for residents and businesses in Central Oregon. I’m excited that Central Oregon could become a net exporter of clean energy, but right now our county doesn’t have enough energy of any kind — or enough of the basic infrastructure like power lines — to meet our own needs over the next five years,” Collins said. Project Obsidian is separate from the geothermal development being pursued by Mazama Energy in another part of the Newberry area. Both companies are pursuing enhanced geothermal systems, which use engineered underground reservoirs to extract heat from rock rather than relying on naturally occurring underground hot-water reservoirs. Quaise announced a $180 million Series B financing round in August, including a $35 million investment from drilling contractor Nabors Industries. The company ultimately hopes to expand Project Obsidian beyond its initial 50-megawatt capacity, potentially reaching 250 megawatts or more if the geothermal resource supports further development.

artigo.texto: International battery, solar and wind energy company Neoen has selected a site for its proposed 400-megawatt lithium-iron-phosphate battery project a few kilometres south of Port Elgin. Neighbouring Arran-Elderslie’s council turned down the company’s site near Tara last year in response to community concerns, including that the site then under consideration tends to flood. The new site for what’s formally called a battery energy storage system, or BESS, is in Saugeen Shores. It is east of Highway 21, at 752 Concession Road 2. It was selected in close consultation with the Saugeen Ojibway Nation’s Environment Office. “Neoen Battery” would store enough electricity to power 385,000 households during peak demand, the company says. The batteries would store energy drawn from Ontario’s power grid during lower periods of demand, typically at night. It would occupy 12 hectares. Ontario’s Independent Electricity System Operator forecasts electricity demand to rise 65 per cent by 2050 due to economic development, population growth and electrification. The rise of interest in data centres and electric vehicle adoption add forecasting uncertainty, it noted. Neoen proposes this project in light of that demand. It has committed to never propose a data centre in Saugeen Shores. A Nov. 4 Saugeen Ojibway Nation letter signed by the chiefs to Luke Charbonneau, the mayor of Saugeen Shores, says “we trust we will have your council’s support for this project.” “This project represents a strong investment in clean energy within our territory and an opportunity for economic reconciliation, skills training and shared benefits,” the letter said. SON “expects” Saugeen Shores’ support, as it’s a matter of asserting “SON’s territorial rights,” information on SON’s Environment Office Facebook page says. Saugeen Shores is next to the reserve of the Chippewas of Saugeen First Nation, one half of SON. The other half is the Chippewas of Nawash Unceded First Nation. The reserves are a fraction of SON’s traditional territory — more than two million acres. There’s a Saugeen Shores public meeting about rezoning land for the proposed battery storage site on Monday, Nov. 23 at 6:30 p.m. in the council chambers. People may come in person or see the meeting online. The agenda will be posted. A needed Bruce County Official Plan amendment will be dealt with at a later date. Organic cash crop farmer Linda Baumberger’s farms in fields across Highway 21, about 350 metres from proposed battery storage site. She intends to oppose the project on what she called “prime” farmland, which she herself used to farm, she said by phone Thursday. “All of us landowners around here that are farmers are scared to death, because if this thing burns, like from thermal runaway, or has any sort of leaking or any sort of contamination . . .” Once contaminated, the land can’t be farmed again, she said. Lithium-iron-phosphate batteries, rather than generic lithium-ion, are proposed, minutes of a Nov. 10 Neoen battery community liaison committee meeting in Port Elgin said. This battery chemistry is considered “less susceptible to fire but is not risk-free.” The committee will discuss the batteries more at another meeting, the minutes say. Baumberger said taking farmland out of production runs counter to a rising need for food sovereignty amid growing food insecurity. “Less than five per cent of land in Ontario can be farmed.” And she’s worried about setting a precedent, she said. SON is considering entering into a business partnership with Neoen, which has a 20-year contract with Ontario’s Independent Electricity System Operation, with a few years extension possible, SON’s Environment Office Facebook page says. Information on Neoen’s website says Neoen and SON have signed a memorandum of understanding to co-develop and co-own “Neoen Battery,” each owning 50 per cent. It shows the batteries are projected to start operating in the fourth quarter of 2028. It promises a $450,000 annual “Community Benefits Fund,” direct investment in Saugeen Shores Fire Department, up to $130,000 in annual municipal tax revenue, about 200 construction jobs at construction, supplier opportunities and investments in local art, heritage and biodiversity initiatives. SON says it has been working with Neoen for a few months to find the most suitable site that meets its requirements “for environmental stewardship and the protection of the territory.” The site selected by both has had an archeological assessment and been subject to environmental surveys. A “key mandate” is evaluating environmental impacts and ensuring proper mitigation. The site would ultimately be returned to a farm field. The community liaison committee minutes say the proposed permanent project footprint is approximately 29 acres (12 ha), which leaves 27 ha (67 acres). But “the current land arrangement involves an option covering a larger parcel.” The landowner is expected to continue farming the remainder once the final footprint is established. A Bruce County planning summary says it has received a severance application for a lease for the 12 hectares. Neoen also needs a Bruce County Official Plan and zoning amendments. Neoen submitted planning applications to the town and to Bruce County on July 31, SON’s letter said. SON anticipates their decisions in early 2027. Siga A Crítica de Campo Grande no Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. Veja o resumo da notícia - Trump afirma que empresas de tecnologia podem sofrer imposto enorme ao construir data centers de IA fora do país. - O presidente defende que comunidades americanas negociem contrapartidas com os desenvolvedores dos centros de dados. - A expansão dos data centers eleva a demanda por energia e gera debate sobre preços, meio ambiente e infraestrutura. - O Senado aprovou legislação bipartidária para acelerar licenciamentos de usinas de energia e linhas de transmissão. - O texto prevê que os data centers arquem com os custos da energia que consomem. - Novas regras ampliam as restrições à exportação de chips avançados de IA, inclusive para o Brasil. O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou nesta sexta-feira (20) que empresas americanas de tecnologia poderão sofrer um “imposto enorme” caso construam data centers de inteligência artificial fora do país. Ele não apresentou detalhes sobre a possível medida e disse que ainda não havia comunicado seus próprios funcionários sobre a proposta. Trump também defendeu que comunidades americanas recebam benefícios das empresas que instalarem centros de processamento de dados em seus territórios. Segundo ele, os moradores devem negociar contrapartidas com os desenvolvedores. A declaração ocorre em meio ao aumento da demanda por energia provocado pela expansão dos data centers utilizados para inteligência artificial. Nos Estados Unidos, o crescimento dessas estruturas também tem provocado discussões sobre preços da eletricidade, impactos ambientais e infraestrutura. Senado aprova medidas para acelerar obras de energia Na quinta-feira (19), o Senado americano, controlado pelos republicanos, aprovou uma legislação bipartidária destinada a acelerar processos de licenciamento para usinas de energia, linhas de transmissão e outras estruturas do setor. A medida busca ampliar a oferta de energia para atender à demanda crescente e reduzir os custos da eletricidade. O texto também prevê que os data centers arquem com os custos da energia que consomem. O setor de tecnologia, entretanto, enfrenta resistência crescente de comunidades que recebem ou estudam receber grandes instalações. Empresas como Google e Meta afirmam estar ampliando o diálogo com moradores e adotando medidas para reduzir impactos ambientais e econômicos. EUA ampliam restrições a chips de IA A discussão sobre os data centers ocorre paralelamente a novas medidas do governo Trump para restringir o acesso a chips e servidores avançados produzidos nos Estados Unidos. As regras anunciadas nesta semana atualizam restrições à exportação de semicondutores avançados utilizados em data centers de inteligência artificial instalados fora do país. A medida deve dificultar o acesso de empresas chinesas a componentes usados para treinar modelos avançados de IA. As novas restrições também atingem o envio desses equipamentos para outros países, entre eles o Brasil.

artigo.texto: PETALING JAYA: BM Greentech Bhd is expected to see stronger earnings in the second half of the financial year ending March 31, 2027 (2H27), underpinned by an improved contribution from its bioenergy segment and a ramp-up in battery energy storage system (Bess) deliveries. The group’s earnings for the 1H27 largely came in within market expectations and the estimates of RHB Research and Phillip Capital Research, with core net profit rising 2% year-on-year to RM24mil. In a note, RHB Research said prospects for bio-energy, the group’s key earnings contributor, remain positive. Potential engineering, procurement, construction, and commissioning (EPCC) opportunities from the Sustainable Energy Development Authority’s 130MW Feed-in Tariff 2.0 programme supports its outlook, given the group’s estimated 60% to 70% market share among domestic boiler EPCC players. “Given a construction period of up to 30 months, we expect the programme to support earnings growth over the next two to three years,” the research house said, adding that the addressable market could reach RM1bil to RM2bil. “Looking ahead, we think that its bio-energy business remains a multiyear growth catalyst,” it said. RHB Research maintained its “buy” call on BM Greentech, with an unchanged target price (TP) of RM2.05. The brokerage continued to view the stock’s valuation as attractive at 13 times financial year 2027 (FY27) forecast price-to-earnings, one standard deviation below its five-year mean. Meanwhile, Phillip Capital Research saw the group’s earnings momentum picking up in 2H27 as Bess deliveries ramp up. In its second quarter, the company’s revenue and core net profit grew by 8% and 17% respectively, from the preceding quarter to RM177mil and RM13mil, mainly supported by stronger bioenergy deliveries and a 7.4-percentage-point increase in the water treatment segment’s pre-tax profit margin to 10.7%. Solar pre-tax profit, however, remained marginal at RM0.3mil due to a lower-margin utility-scale project mix and slower progress in the commercial and industrial segment. Phillip Capital Research expects the solar segment to benefit from increased Bess deliveries, with management guiding that Bess could account for about a third of solar revenue in FY27, rising to about 50% by FY28. The research house reiterated its “buy” recommendation with an unchanged sum-of-parts derived TP of RM2.20.

artigo.texto: 247 – O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou nesta sexta-feira (20/11) que o país não vai permitir que empresas norte-americanas construam centros de dados em outros territórios e ameaçou aplicar pesadas sanções financeiras contra as companhias que ignorarem a restrição. A declaração foi feita em Washington, na Casa Branca, após uma viagem oficial à China para a cúpula da Cooperação Econômica Ásia-Pacífico (APEC), onde o republicano se reuniu com os presidentes da Rússia e da China, Vladimir Putin e Xi Jinping. Segundo o chefe do Executivo norte-americano, a retenção da infraestrutura tecnológica no território nacional é fundamental para preservar a competitividade econômica e evitar que a capacidade de processamento associada à inteligência artificial deixe o país. Durante a coletiva de imprensa, o republicano utilizou o termo superinteligência e avaliou que a nação deve lucrar com a tecnologia. As restrições visam impedir que Pequim utilize estruturas remotas em países terceiros para burlar os controles americanos sobre semicondutores e tecnologias sensíveis. Governo endurece regras para chips e mira o mercado asiático A ofensiva contra a descentralização da infraestrutura ocorre após a administração americana endurecer, na última segunda-feira (16/11), as normas para exportação, reexportação e transferência de chips avançados de inteligência artificial. Com as novas regras, nações como Brasil, Indonésia, Malásia, Singapura e Tailândia passaram a exigir licença específica do governo dos EUA para receber esses componentes. A medida busca evitar que centros de dados instalados fora das fronteiras americanas forneçam grande volume de capacidade computacional a empresas chinesas. Em paralelo às restrições para estruturas externas, o governo dos EUA abriu espaço para a comercialização de semicondutores mais antigos com o mercado chinês. Para o presidente americano, a venda de componentes tecnologicamente inferiores não representa risco e funciona como uma forma de evitar que a China desenvolva toda a sua própria cadeia de fabricação de chips de forma independente. O principal foco de restrição de Washington continua sendo o acesso a semicondutores de alta tecnologia, como os fabricados pela Nvidia, que têm sido alvo de fiscalização rigorosa após relatórios apontarem o uso de chips restritos por universidades chinesas listadas em sanções. Impactos em planos internacionais e defesa de investimentos locais A postura nacionalista de retenção de servidores computacionais afeta diretamente iniciativas de outros governos, como o plano da gestão do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) de transformar o Brasil em um polo regional de centros de dados utilizando fontes de energia limpa. A política defendida pela Casa Branca exige que os complexos de servidores fiquem dentro do território norte-americano, com preferência para estados populosos ou com forte presença energética, a exemplo de Texas, Califórnia e Virgínia, para gerar empregos, riquezas e baratear a conta de luz das comunidades vizinhas por meio da autogeração de eletricidade. “Não vamos permitir que nossas empresas construam data centers fora do nosso país”, declarou Trump na Casa Branca. O mandatário também afirmou que eixos de negociação conjunta sobre inteligência artificial foram estabelecidos com o líder chinês Xi Jinping durante a viagem asiática. A entrevista coletiva na sala de imprensa ocorreu com a presença do vice-presidente JD Vance, do secretário de Estado Marco Rubio e do secretário do Tesouro Scott Bessent, momento em que o republicano voltou a criticar a atuação do Federal Reserve e abordou temas diplomáticos adicionais, como o conflito na Ucrânia e as negociações nucleares com o Irã.

artigo.texto: O oceano virou ar-condicionado de data center na China. Segundo o Catraca Livre, um data center chinês afundado a cerca de 10 quilômetros do litoral de Xangai entrou em operação em maio de 2026. Segundo o governo municipal de Xangai, é o primeiro centro de dados submarino abastecido diretamente por energia eólica no mar. A estrutura fica na região de Lingang e nasceu para a demanda crescente por processamento de informações, que inclui aplicações de inteligência artificial. O projeto mira dois custos operacionais centrais dessas instalações, a eletricidade que alimenta os computadores e a energia necessária para impedir que os servidores superaqueçam. O investimento no empreendimento foi divulgado em cerca de US$ 226 milhões pela reportagem do site Catraca Livre, veículo brasileiro que noticiou a entrada em operação da instalação submarina. O número circula como medida do porte do projeto e, por enquanto, não substitui um balanço detalhado do que já foi efetivamente gasto. A matemática que motivou a obra é simples e antiga. Quanto mais servidores ligados, mais eletricidade consumida e mais calor produzido, o que exige ainda mais energia para baixar a temperatura das máquinas. A aposta chinesa é atacar os dois lados dessa conta ao mesmo tempo, gerando energia limpa no próprio mar e usando a água do oceano para tirar calor dos equipamentos. Debaixo d’água, os equipamentos operam em módulos lacrados, feitos para aguentar as condições do ambiente submarino. Cabos instalados no leito do mar levam eletricidade aos computadores e garantem a conexão dos sistemas submersos com as redes em terra. As águas do litoral chinês funcionam como regulador constante de temperatura dos servidores dedicados à inteligência artificial, segundo a reportagem do Catraca Livre. Ao submergir as instalações, o sistema abre mão da climatização artificial tradicional e reduz de forma drástica o consumo de insumos essenciais. A diferença central para um prédio convencional está na refrigeração. Informações do governo de Xangai descrevem um circuito de troca de calor com tubos de cobre, que carrega o calor dos servidores para a água do mar sem que ela toque os componentes eletrônicos. Nos centros de dados comuns, a climatização que mantém milhares de servidores na temperatura certa devora parcela importante da eletricidade disponível. Os responsáveis pelo projeto chinês estimam economia de 22,8% no consumo de energia frente a instalações convencionais em terra. Os números de economia vêm dos próprios responsáveis, e não há auditoria independente publicada que os comprove. A eletricidade vem de turbinas eólicas instaladas no próprio mar, junto à área dos módulos. A ligação direta entre geração e consumo aproveita a energia perto de onde ela nasce e reduz a necessidade de transportar essa corrente pelas redes convencionais de transmissão até um prédio em terra firme. Essa alimentação direta é o traço que diferencia o empreendimento, na descrição do governo municipal de Xangai. O mar absorve o calor tirado dos servidores, e essa energia térmica precisa se dissipar na água ao redor.

artigo.texto: Aurora neighbors hope new data center moratorium passes city council Aurora residents who have been pushing for restrictions on new data centers are hopeful as a new moratorium is scheduled to be introduced to the city council. Michael and Linda Trimble know what it's like to live next to a data center. They used to live in Loudoun County, Virginia, which has the world's largest concentration of data centers. In fact, one was right across the street from their home, which they found problematic. "It was like they really did not think about the community where they were building the data centers," said Linda Trimble. "It was noisy. It was warmer. It took up a lot of space. They tried to put trees between to block off some of the noise, but it really didn't work," said Michael Trimble. They moved to Aurora to retire and get away from it, but a few months ago they learned that a new data center will be built nearby. "This is a big déjà vu for us," said Michael Trimble. "Here we are again, another data center." They learned the Trident data center will be built in their neighborhood in northeast Aurora. The couple is worried because Michael Trimble's health is now once again in jeopardy. He got pulmonary fibrosis after decades of working at Rocky Flats and says that a nearby data center can cause dangerous complications for him. "The particulate matter in the air is going to cause me problems, hospitalization and a higher mortality rate," he explained. The Trimbles' neighbor Shane O'Neil also has experience with data centers. "I was a data center manager, and those things generate a lot of noise," said O'Neil. He says he's worried about Michael Trimble and his other neighbors. "We have a huge, heavy, heavy presence of veterans in this community, and a little bit of noise like that, it's going to set them off," said O'Neil. That's why they are hoping Aurora City Council does something to protect them. The council has considered moratoriums recently and voted them down. The Trimbles and O'Neil say they felt betrayed by that decision. "Corruption. Pure. Plain and simple," O'Neil said. "It's all about money. It's about making people richer," said Michael Trimble. Now another moratorium is going to be introduced at Monday's city council meeting. This one would last until September 2027 and would prevent new data center construction west and south of the intersection of the proposed Aerotropolis Parkway and I-70. Council member Curtis Gardner, who has been against a moratorium, posted on Facebook that this time he is on board and thinks they have the votes to pass it. O'Neil and the Trimbles are hoping he is right "I hope the people on the city council have clear heads and realize that there are people here," said O'Neil. That city council meeting will be held on Nov. 23 at 6 p.m. at the Aurora Municipal Center.

artigo.texto: East Texas lawmaker co-authors bill ending data center sales tax exemption Senate Bill 293 would rescind the sales tax exemption passed over a decade ago. TYLER, Texas (KLTV) - State Sen.-elect Trent Ashby (R-Lufkin) co-authored a bill that would remove the sales tax exemption for qualifying data centers. Senate Bill 293 would rescind the sales tax exemption passed over a decade ago and would apply to data centers such as those with a footprint of at least 100,000 square feet. The bill’s filing comes amid concerns from Texans about the growth of data centers, as well as their use of water and electricity. “It just doesn’t make sense to continue to subsidize these data center companies that, frankly, are some of the most capitalized companies not just in the United States but in the world,” Ashby said. “When the law took effect in 2013, at that time the comptroller estimated that the cost of this bill would be about $15 million,” he continued. “The most recent estimate that we have for the comptroller is that in the upcoming biennium for our state, that this sales tax exemption will cost $3.3 billion.” Existing exemptions would expire when the bill takes effect. Economist Dr. Ray Perryman said he would rather see additional requirements for data centers to qualify for the sales tax exemption rather than removing it entirely. “Maybe requiring that you have your power worked out behind the grid, requiring that you have your water supplies worked out, those kinds of things,” Perryman said. “I’d prefer to see us do something like that that improves the overall structure but allows this development to happen.” Perryman mentioned changing the current law could impact rural Texans in particular. “It’s enough of an incentive that some of these data centers would go away and every time one goes away, you’re really talking about billions of dollars in spending, again quite often in a rural area that doesn’t have a lot of economic development,” added Perryman. In contrast, Ashby said he does not expect significant opposition from businesses. “I don’t think that we’re likely to see a large pushback from the data center community,” said Ashby. “These companies are so well capitalized and these data centers… are very profitable.” Enough lawmakers have signed onto the bill for it to pass the Texas Senate when they convene in January. O republicano comentava o desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial (IA). Segundo ele, os EUA devem concentrar os investimentos em infraestrutura tecnológica para fortalecer sua posição no setor. Trump quer concentrar investimentos em tecnologia Os data centers são estruturas responsáveis pelo armazenamento e processamento de grandes volumes de informações. Eles também fornecem a capacidade computacional necessária para o funcionamento de sistemas de IA. Leia também: “EUA exigirão licença para Brasil comprar chips de IA” A expansão dessas instalações ganhou importância com o avanço da IA e o aumento da demanda por processamento de dados. Grandes empresas de tecnologia investem na construção de novos centros para ampliar sua capacidade operacional e atender ao crescimento do setor. A proposta de Trump busca manter esses investimentos nos EUA. A declaração ocorre em meio a suspeitas de espionagem do governo chinês envolvendo a Nvidia, empresa norte-americana fabricante de chips. artigo.texto: For nearly 35 years, the railroad to Port MacKenzie has existed mostly as cleared ground. The idea dates to 1992, when the Cook Inlet port itself did not yet exist. Work came in fits and starts after that. A right-of-way was cleared, and much of the bed was built, but the rails themselves never went down, according to the Alaska Beacon. Now the 32-mile line has money. The railroad's board signed off on the $311 million project this past week, and a federal grant announced in October covers most of the bill. The railroad's chief executive, Bill O'Leary, told the Beacon that construction could begin next summer. In public, the line has been pitched as a freight corridor for minerals, natural gas pipeline materials and national security. Documents filed near its two ends tell a more complicated story. At the port, a coal power developer is pursuing plans for an "Advanced Manufacturing & Compute Campus." Near Houston, where the spur would meet the railroad's main line, the state's development authority has won approval for state land for what its application calls "a behind-the-meter data park." Read More on News Neither data center has been built, and no public record shows a committed tenant for either. But taken together, the records show a railroad being revived at the same moment, and in the same places, that Alaska is deciding whether to welcome a power-hungry industry. Why It Matters Across the U.S., the race to build data centers for artificial intelligence has collided with questions about where the power will come from and who pays for it. In Alaska, one answer on the table is coal. In March, the Interior Department announced that Terra Energy Center had reached a $1 billion agreement in principle with Hyundai Heavy Industries Power Systems. The deal covers boilers for a 1.25-gigawatt coal power plant in Alaska. The department called it "the first order of utility-scale coal power plant boilers in the United States since approximately 2006." A Korean private equity firm, KOREIT, pledged $500 million. The project also lands in the middle of a political transition. The incoming governor, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, has said he would seek a temporary ban on new data centers. What To Know The port end. In March, the Matanuska-Susitna Borough Assembly adopted a resolution backing a joint marketing effort with Terra Energy Center Corp. to court "large power consumers." The resolution lists its first priority as "Attraction of data center and advanced computing facilities." It promises "firm baseload power supply from TECC's planned generation facility" and says land near Port MacKenzie offers "exceptional access to tidewater." Neither the resolution nor the staff memo attached to it uses the word coal. The Interior Department's announcement does. The memo says Terra holds a land-use permit for about 1,058 acres near Lake Lorraine, in the port district. The permit lets Terra test the feasibility of "an Advanced Manufacturing and Computing Campus." A draft term sheet in a September 2025 Port Commission packet targets "approximately 30 MW initial load" for that campus. The developer would have to pour a slab by December 31, 2028, or the borough could take the land back. Mayor Edna DeVries vetoed the resolution in a message dated March 5, citing "the risk that Mat-Su Borough has placed themselves in." She noted that data centers "often require conditional use permits," a subject "the assembly has not discussed." The Assembly overrode her 6-1 on March 17, the Anchorage Daily News reported. The resolution says nothing in it obligates the borough to sell or lease land. Port backers are already planning around the tracks. The Alaska Beacon counted a coal-powered computing project among the developments lining up at the port ahead of the line. The mine. One industrial project already tied to the port is not a data center. In October 2025, the Department of War awarded $43.4 million under the Defense Production Act to Nova Minerals' subsidiary, Alaska Range Resources. The money is for military-grade antimony trisulfide. According to Nova, the plan pairs a mine with a refinery at Port MacKenzie. The mine and refinery are planned projects, not operating facilities. Critical minerals, a category that includes antimony, were among the reasons federal officials gave for funding the railroad. The grant announcement does not mention coal power or computing. The Houston end. In its application to the state Department of Natural Resources, the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority (AIDEA) describes plans for about 20,000 acres near Houston. They include "secure, scalable data centers," "a behind-the-meter data park" and a "data / energy campus." The application also mentions utility corridors for electricity, natural gas and fiber, and land "adjacent to the Alaska Railroad centerline." It does not mention the Port MacKenzie line. AIDEA's fact sheet puts the land about 2 miles north of Houston and says AIDEA would not pay for the land's value, only related costs such as surveying. In a July 30 letter to Mat-Su legislators, Executive Director Randy Ruaro wrote: "There is no committed data-center tenant." On November 10, the Department of Natural Resources approved a smaller transfer of about 6,800 acres. DNR cited 2,306 public comments and "substantial public concern" over the transfer, including "the prospect of scalable data center facilities," in its final decision. Days later, borough officials asked the state to reconsider. They wrote that "Point Mackenzie and portions of West Susitna offer more appropriate locations for these uses," the Anchorage Daily News reported. That would move the development to the port end of the line. What the grant announcement leaves out. The U.S. Department of Transportation's release on the $249 million grant does not mention data centers or coal. It describes moving "Alaska's vast mineral and energy resources." artigo.texto: The Data Center Backlash Has a Playbook Key Highlights - The 2026 midterm elections underscored the political influence of data center opposition, with voters approving 33 local measures restricting development or expressing opposition. - LocalQ Labs' research identifies election cycles, political geography, regulatory structures, and organized coalitions as emerging indicators of development risk. - Data center opposition increasingly combines local land-use concerns with broader environmental and political campaigns, complicating traditional outreach strategies. - Developers face growing pressure to integrate community intelligence into site selection and establish meaningful operating commitments, rather than treating public engagement as a permitting exercise. - Community benefit agreements, transparent communications, and resident participation are becoming central to the industry's long-term social license. The data center industry's next development constraint may have less to do with megawatts than with the politics of where those megawatts are deployed. The warning became difficult to ignore on November 3, when American voters approved 33 local ballot measures restricting data center development or expressing opposition to it, according to Ballotpedia's analysis of the 2026 midterm elections. The results included outright bans, partial prohibitions, temporary moratoriums, and new requirements for community oversight. Voters also rejected 13 measures that would have favored development or expressed support for it. For an industry accustomed to evaluating prospective sites through the availability of power, land, fiber, capital, and construction resources, the election results reinforced another increasingly consequential consideration: whether the communities hosting digital infrastructure are willing to accept its growing physical and economic footprint. As Data Center Frontier recently examined in its post-election assessment of the industry's political future, the national push to accelerate AI infrastructure construction is colliding with a more complicated political reality at the state and local levels. Opposition crosses party lines, while questions surrounding utility rates, water, environmental impacts, and local economic benefits have moved from planning commission meetings into broader electoral debate. That changing environment was the subject of a conversation recorded at the DCF Trends Summit 2026 in Reston, Virginia, where DCF contributing editor Doug Black sat down with Adam Waitkunas, president of Milldam Public Relations, and Julia Chuang, founder of LocalQ Labs and an associate professor of sociology at the University of Maryland. Their discussion explored a fundamental shift in the development equation: community opposition is becoming more organized and politically consequential, but also more observable through data. The challenge for developers is to understand that risk early enough to influence site selection and project design, while recognizing that public trust cannot be manufactured through conventional public relations alone. Community Intelligence Enters the Site-Selection Equation Chuang approaches data center development through the lens of sociology and the study of political and social movements. Her work at LocalQ Labs focuses on the relationship between organized opposition, local governance, and the conditions under which data center proposals encounter regulatory resistance. The company's platform tracks more than 1,300 U.S. facilities and projects, combining regulatory histories with information about local political conditions and opposition activity to identify patterns that may be difficult to recognize when examining individual sites. "I do think there are a lot of things you can see in the aggregate that you can't see when you go site by site," Chuang said. Among the relationships she identified are increased moratorium activity ahead of elections and greater exposure to permitting delays when projects enter rezoning or approval processes close to a local election. Chuang also described differences associated with state political control: in her analysis, states with Democratic trifectas tend to produce more regulatory activity without necessarily producing more outright bans, while some rural Republican jurisdictions have exhibited a stronger preference for prohibiting projects altogether. These are findings from Chuang's research rather than universal rules governing development outcomes, but they point toward an important change in how prospective sites might be evaluated. A project with available power and favorable industrial zoning may still face meaningful political exposure if an election is approaching, local officials are reconsidering development priorities, or opposition groups have successfully mobilized in neighboring jurisdictions. LocalQ Labs' published research similarly examines how restrictions emerge across communities, with local organizations learning from one another and adapting regulatory approaches to their own circumstances. Northern Virginia offers an instructive case. Despite the highly publicized controversy surrounding Prince William County's Digital Gateway development, Chuang cautioned against assuming that opposition necessarily increases as additional facilities enter an established market. In her analysis, Northern Virginia has maintained a comparatively low share of canceled or delayed facilities relative to its development activity, suggesting that some communities may become more accepting once facilities, infrastructure, tax contributions, and operating regulations are established. That interpretation does not diminish the region's continuing land-use disputes. Indeed, as DCF's recent examination of Virginia's changing data center policies detailed, the commonwealth is tightening the terms under which new development proceeds. artigo.texto: 247 – Moradores de Atibaia, no interior de São Paulo, estão se mobilizando contra a possível instalação de um data center avaliado em R$ 3 bilhões no município. O empreendimento, previsto para uma região próxima ao Bairro do Tanque, desperta preocupações relacionadas ao abastecimento de água, à preservação ambiental e aos impactos sobre a qualidade de vida da população. Organizados no movimento Fora Data Center, os habitantes cobram transparência das autoridades e defendem mudanças na legislação municipal para impedir a construção de grandes complexos de processamento de dados. Segundo reportagem do Metrópoles, o movimento reuniu mais de 4 mil assinaturas em um abaixo-assinado até meados de novembro. A mobilização ocorre em meio a questionamentos sobre a ausência de consultas públicas específicas para discutir o empreendimento, embora documentos relacionados à infraestrutura elétrica indiquem preparativos para atender à futura instalação. Com pouco mais de 160 mil habitantes, Atibaia passou a integrar os planos de expansão de empresas de infraestrutura digital. O projeto em discussão, denominado Data Center Alfa, é apresentado pela DataSpots, empresa do Grupo ON, com previsão de início das operações entre 2029 e 2030. A iniciativa prevê a construção de um complexo de grande porte em uma área de transição entre zonas urbanas e rurais. O terreno inicialmente considerado para a instalação possui extensão equivalente a aproximadamente 50 campos de futebol. Moradores cobram participação nas decisões sobre o empreendimento O movimento Fora Data Center elaborou uma petição destinada à Prefeitura de Atibaia solicitando medidas para impedir a implantação de data centers de hiperescala no município. O documento também reivindica o encaminhamento de um projeto de lei complementar à Câmara Municipal para modificar o Código de Obras e o Plano Diretor. Uma das principais reclamações dos moradores é a falta de informações detalhadas sobre o empreendimento e seus possíveis efeitos sobre a região. A comunidade afirma que não foi previamente informada sobre os planos de instalação do complexo nem convocada para participar de audiências públicas específicas sobre os impactos ambientais e sociais da atividade. A situação ganhou novos contornos após a divulgação de documentos e comunicados relacionados à ampliação da infraestrutura energética local. Documentos indicam planejamento de infraestrutura elétrica Em 17 de junho de 2026, a concessionária Isa Energia apresentou, durante audiência pública, um estudo de impacto de vizinhança referente à implantação de ramais destinados à conexão da linha de transmissão de 440 kV Bom Jardim–Água Azul à subestação de transmissão Fernão Dias, de 440/500 kV. De acordo com o movimento de moradores, a apresentação concentrou-se na necessidade de reforçar o sistema elétrico regional, sem detalhar suficientemente a relação da obra com os projetos de data centers. Entretanto, um comunicado divulgado pela própria concessionária indicava que a ampliação da rede também tinha como finalidade viabilizar empreendimentos de infraestrutura digital, incluindo o Data Center Alfa, com previsão de conexão à Subestação Atibaia 2. O Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) autorizou, em outubro de 2025, uma conexão destinada ao atendimento do projeto. Conforme documento obtido pelo Metrópoles, a autorização contempla a expansão de aproximadamente 15 quilômetros de linha de transmissão e a implantação de dois módulos de entrada de linha em 138 kV. A existência dessa autorização alimentou os questionamentos dos moradores sobre o estágio de desenvolvimento do empreendimento e o acesso da população às informações sobre sua implantação. Prefeitura afirma não ter recebido pedido de licenciamento Apesar dos documentos relacionados à infraestrutura elétrica, a Prefeitura de Atibaia informou que não encontrou, nos registros da Secretaria Municipal de Meio Ambiente, solicitação de licenciamento ambiental vinculada ao data center. Em manifestação encaminhada ao Metrópoles, a administração municipal afirmou que qualquer proposta formal deverá cumprir as exigências legais pertinentes. “Caso seja formalizada proposta de implantação de data center, serão exigidos todos os estudos, licenças e autorizações legalmente aplicáveis, observadas as competências do município, da Companhia Ambiental do Estado de São Paulo (Cetesb) e dos demais órgãos responsáveis”, declarou a prefeitura. A posição do governo municipal contrasta com as informações disponibilizadas pela DataSpots, que apresenta o Data Center Alfa em seu portfólio como um empreendimento aprovado e estruturado. Publicações especializadas também mencionaram o projeto entre os investimentos planejados pela empresa no Brasil. Segundo informações divulgadas pelo portal Datlaz, a DataSpots prevê investimentos de R$ 39 bilhões no país, incluindo a unidade projetada para Atibaia. Embora esses registros indiquem avanços no planejamento empresarial e energético, a autorização de conexão à rede elétrica não equivale, por si só, à concessão das licenças ambientais e urbanísticas necessárias para a construção. Consumo de água preocupa famílias que dependem de poços Entre os principais temores da população está a possibilidade de agravamento da escassez hídrica no Bairro do Tanque, onde parte dos moradores depende de poços para obter água. A região não dispõe de cobertura integral dos serviços de abastecimento e também enfrenta limitações na infraestrutura de coleta e tratamento de esgoto. O morador Gabriel Tonobohn, que vive no bairro há três anos e meio, relatou que a disponibilidade de água já representa uma dificuldade para diversas famílias, sobretudo durante os períodos de estiagem. “A gente mora em um bairro que não tem saneamento, não tem água encanada, não tem esgoto. artigo.texto: James City County supervisors this week postponed a decision on a battery energy storage facility proposed for the Grove community. The Board of Supervisors unanimously delayed action on issuing special use permits for the facility, deciding to wait until Jan. 12 to bring it up again. More than 40 community members attended Tuesday’s meeting. Pelican Energy Storage, a subsidiary of Nebraska energy company Tenaska, hopes to build the 650-megawatt facility along 220 acres on Pocahontas Trail. A substation and switchyard would also be constructed and include new high-voltage transmission lines to connect to an electrical grid. The facility would connect to Dominion Energy’s 500-kilovolt Surry-Skiffes Creek transmission line. It would use lithium ion batteries to receive electrical energy from the grid to charge while also storing energy, county planner Alison Jackura said. The county Planning Commission previously recommended approval of the project by a vote of 5-2 in October. The site, which is zoned general industry, is an abandoned industrial area that previously had contamination issues. It was owned by Dow Chemical Co. in 1958 as an acrylic fibers manufacturing site before being purchased by BASF Corp in 1978 and then by Mann Industries in 1989. It ceased operations in 1993. Keith Latham of Tenaska said the the facility would be a “really good source” in the community by helping during a energy plant outage or an extreme weather event. He touted additional benefits such as the creation of 150 construction jobs and over $1 billion in county revenue. AJ Alexander, a Newport News resident who lives 10 minutes away from the site, said the increase in tax revenue, jobs and clean energy from the facility would be significant for Grove. She asked supervisors to use the battery’s revenue to help reinvest in the community. Grove residents, however, have continued to voice their opposition to the project. George Buskey said he was worried about potential safety hazards such as fires, hazardous smoke and environmental contamination. He further said the community continues to be overlooked for commercial development and improvements to the area, such as grocery stores and community facilities. Supervisor Chair John McGlennon said citizens’ health and safety is paramount. He also noted that supervisors don’t have a clear understanding on how the project’s tax revenue would be dispersed. Supervisor Tracy Wainwright said that after receiving a lot of questions, it would be better to have answers before making a final decision. James W. Robinson, 757-799-0621, james.robinson@virginiamedia.com
