artigo.texto: If you've spent any time in Statesboro lately, you've probably heard somebody talking about the proposed data center on Burkhalter Road. Depending on who you ask, it's either the best thing that could happen to our community or the worst. One side sees jobs, investment, tax revenue, and a seat at the table in a rapidly changing economy. The other sees questions about water use, power consumption, noise, property values, and whether an industrial-scale operation belongs so close to residential neighborhoods. [wjcl.com], [griceconnect.com] Before I go any further, let me say something that may disappoint everyone. I don't have a horse in this race. I'm not a developer. I'm not a politician. I'm not a spokesperson for the project. I'm not carrying a protest sign against it. I'm just a citizen watching neighbors argue with neighbors about what kind of town Statesboro wants to become. And frankly, that's the part of this discussion that interests me most. Because long after the lawyers finish their work, long after the engineers submit their reports, and long after the council casts its votes, we'll still be neighbors. We'll still sit beside one another in church. We'll still meet in the grocery store. We'll still cheer for the Blue Devils and the Eagles. We'll still call Statesboro home. What strikes me is how quickly modern debates force us into opposing camps. You're either "for growth" or "against growth." You're either "pro-business" or "anti-business." You're either protecting the future or standing in its way. Life is rarely that simple. A person can welcome economic development and still have legitimate concerns. A person can oppose this project without opposing progress. A person can believe the developers are sincere and still ask hard questions. That's not obstruction. That's citizenship. And maybe that's what is getting lost. The real issue isn't whether a data center is good or bad. The real issue is whether we can have an honest conversation about it. Can residents ask questions without being dismissed as alarmists? Can supporters discuss potential benefits without being treated as villains? Can we disagree without assuming the worst about one another? I hope so. Because the future of Statesboro won't be determined solely by a data center. It will be determined by whether we can remain a community when difficult decisions come along. Every growing city eventually faces moments like this. A new industry. A new subdivision. A new highway. A new opportunity. A new risk. Reasonable people look at the same facts and come to different conclusions. That's nothing new. What would be new is forgetting how to listen. I've read enough history to know that today's controversy becomes tomorrow's memory. But the character we display during the controversy lasts much longer. So where do I stand on the Burkhalter Road data center? I stand with the people who are asking questions. I stand with the people who are trying to answer them. I stand with the belief that a community deserves both opportunity and accountability. And beyond that? I don't have a horse in this race. I just happen to live in the town where it's being run. Dr. Charles Cravey has a Bachelor of Science in sociology from Georgia Southern, a master's degree in sacred literature from Trinity Theological Seminary and a doctoral degree in theology from Trinity. In addition to being a retired pastor, Cravey is a writer, photographer, recording artist, songwriter, singer and producer.

artigo.texto: Indonesia backs safe harbour mechanism to boost forest carbon market November 22, 2026 16:56 GMT+700 Laksmi Wijayanti, Director General of Sustainable Forest Management at the Ministry of Forestry (2nd left), and Ilham, Director of Forest Utilization Business Development at the Ministry of Forestry (right), display a report during the launch of the document "Unlocking Demand in Voluntary Carbon Markets through Safe Harbour Mechanisms: A Recommendation to Governments" at the Indonesian Pavilion during the UNFCCC COP31 in Antalya, Turkiye, on Saturday (14/11/2026). ANTARA/HO-Ministry of Forestry Jakarta (ANTARA) - Indonesia welcomes the "safe harbour" mechanism to provide legal certainty for carbon credit buyers and investors, boost demand for high-quality credits, and advance its ambition to become a global forest carbon hub. Laksmi Wijayanti, Director General of Sustainable Forest Management of the Forestry Ministry, stated that the growth of the carbon market cannot rely solely on the availability of credits. "The market also requires buyer confidence, legal certainty, and guarantees that carbon credits genuinely reflect emissions reductions, ensuring they are not merely a form of 'greenwashing'," Wijayanti said in a statement in Jakarta on Sunday. According to her, companies currently face both legal and reputational risks when purchasing carbon credits or making public claims regarding their use. She noted that such uncertainty could discourage investment, including in projects that generate high-quality carbon credits. A safe harbour mechanism provides a legal protection framework for companies that use carbon credits in compliance with established requirements and standards, with the aim of encouraging their participation in voluntary carbon markets. The report was prepared by the International Emissions Trading Association (IETA), with support from the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets (CGCM), to help increase demand for carbon credits in international voluntary carbon markets. Indonesia is one of 14 countries that have joined the CGCM. Ilham, the Forestry Ministry's Director of Forest Utilization Business Development, said Indonesia was strengthening its carbon trading regulations through safe harbour approaches, internationally aligned contracts incorporating social safeguards, and dispute resolution mechanisms. "These improvements provide greater legal certainty for transactions while ensuring that carbon market development remains consistent with national green economic development policies and Indonesia's climate commitments," he said. He emphasized that the legal protection provided under a safe harbour mechanism did not amount to immunity, as its implementation remained subject to Indonesia's national laws and sovereignty. The implementation of this mechanism could also strengthen international market confidence, potentially supporting Indonesia's ambition to become an "International Forest Carbon Hub" and a benchmark for international voluntary carbon trading. Mark Kenber, executive director of the Voluntary Carbon Markets Integrity Initiative (VCMI), explained that a safe harbour mechanism was not a substitute for national regulations but rather complemented them. Companies would still be required to comply with the laws and regulations of the countries in which they operate. The safe harbour mechanism covers two key aspects: the quality of carbon credits and the accuracy of corporate claims. Carbon credits must comply with recognized standards and frameworks, including the Paris Agreement's Article 6.4 mechanism, the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM), the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA), and frameworks established by individual national governments. Meanwhile, claim accuracy concerns how companies communicate their use of carbon credits to the public. They must provide accurate information and avoid creating the impression that they have eliminated all their emissions when they have actually only offset them through the purchase of carbon credits. artigo.texto: Monday public hearing to allow comment on proposed data center ordinance MONDAY PUBLIC HEARING TO ALLOW COMMENT ON PROPOSED DATA CENTER ORDINANCE Planning Commission to consider recommending regulations that would require special use permits for all data centers and establish standards for location, utilities, noise and other impacts. The Dalton-Varnell-Whitfield County Planning Commission will hold a public hearing Monday, Nov. 23, to consider proposed amendments to the Unified Zoning Ordinance establishing regulations for data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities. Whitfield County posted an initial draft of the proposed ordinance on October 12 and invited public comment. The Dalton Daily Citizen has reviewed the revised ordinance scheduled for consideration Monday, including changes from the original draft. The following is a detailed examination of the proposed regulations, what they would require of data center developers and operators, and how the proposal has changed since it was first made available for public review. THE ORDINANCE AT A GLANCE Nine things to know about the proposed data center regulations - No automatic approvals. Every new data center would require a Special Use Permit from the applicable elected governing authority. - Industrial areas only. Small data centers could locate in M-1 or M-2 districts. Large, hyperscale and cryptocurrency mining facilities would be limited to M-2. - Distance requirements. Data centers would have to be separated from homes and other protected locations by 1,000 to 2,000 feet, depending on facility size, with additional property setbacks and landscaping requirements. - Water and electricity. The proposal would limit certain cooling systems, require detailed utility capacity reviews and address who pays for infrastructure improvements. - Noise and construction. Facilities would face noise, vibration, lighting and construction restrictions, including shutdown requirements for uncorrected noise violations. - Public notification. Developers of large, hyperscale and cryptocurrency mining facilities would have to hold community meetings and notify property owners within 2,500 feet. - Emergency planning and reporting. Facilities would need emergency response plans. Larger operations would also have to submit annual reports on water use, electricity demand, generator operations and complaints. - Cleanup guarantees. Developers would have to plan for eventual closure. Larger facilities would need financial guarantees of at least $1 million or 125% of estimated cleanup costs, whichever is greater. - Penalties for violations. Continuing violations could result in fines of up to $1,000 per day, with additional enforcement options. NOTE: These are proposed regulations, not adopted law. The Planning Commission’s Nov. 23 hearing is part of the review process. Elected governing bodies would have to adopt the ordinance before it takes effect. Every data center would require special approval Under the revised ordinance scheduled for consideration at the Nov. 23 Planning Commission meeting, all data centers would require a Special Use Permit and would be allowed only in designated industrial zoning districts. Data centers would not be permitted in residential, agricultural, commercial or other zoning districts. Under the original draft posted on the city website Oct. 12, small data centers would have been permitted by right in M-1 (Light Manufacturing) and M-2 (Heavy Manufacturing) districts, while large data centers would have been permitted by right in M-2 districts. Hyperscale data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities would have required Special Use Permits. The revised proposal eliminates those by-right allowances. Small data centers would still be eligible for consideration in M-1 and M-2 districts, while large and hyperscale facilities and cryptocurrency mining operations would be limited to M-2 districts. However, all would require Special Use approval. The ordinance would not permit data centers in other zoning districts, including residential, agricultural, commercial, Planned Unit Development (PUD), Urban Planned Unit Development (UPUD) and Mixed Use (MU) districts. A Special Use Permit would require review through the Planning Commission and approval by the applicable governing authority, rather than allowing a qualifying facility to proceed solely on the basis of its zoning classification. How data centers would be classified The proposed ordinance establishes three categories of data centers based on building size and electrical demand. Small data centers would have no more than 20,000 square feet of gross floor area and peak electrical demand of no more than 10 megawatts (MW). Both limits would have to be met for a facility to qualify as small. Large data centers would be those that meet neither the definition of a small data center nor that of a hyperscale data center. The revised draft replaces the original definition, which specified facilities with 20,000 to 100,000 square feet of floor area or electrical demand between 10 MW and 50 MW. Hyperscale data centers would be facilities exceeding 100,000 square feet of gross floor area or having peak electrical demand of at least 100 MW. Meeting either threshold would qualify a facility as hyperscale. The original draft established the hyperscale electrical threshold at 50 MW. The revised proposal doubles that threshold to 100 MW while retaining the floor-area threshold of more than 100,000 square feet. The ordinance also defines a data center campus, requiring the aggregate floor area and peak electrical demand of buildings and phases within a common campus to be considered when determining classification. The provisions are intended to prevent developers from avoiding applicable requirements by dividing projects into smaller buildings, parcels or phases. Understanding size and electrical demand Both building size and electrical demand are commonly used to classify data centers

artigo.texto: ONS permite data center em Atibaia apesar de risco na geração de energia Contrato de 2025 permitiu expansão de subestação local para atender projeto de data center. Decisão preocupa moradores de Atibaia São Paulo — A estrutura elétrica para um data center com investimento inicial previsto de R$ 3 bilhões foi autorizada pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) para a cidade de Atibaia, no interior de São Paulo. A permissão do ONS, porém, vai na contramão de um alerta feito pelo próprio órgão no Plano da Operação Elétrica de Médio Prazo (PAR/PEL), para o ciclo de 2027 a 2031. O documento aponta um risco de restrição na transferência de energia do sudeste/centro-oeste para a região sul, além de sobrecargas e possível colapso de tensão na rede paulista, devido à combinação entre o fluxo de energia que atravessa São Paulo e o crescimento acelerado da demanda local, sobretudo por data centers. Parte da energia gerada no sudeste e centro-oeste é enviada à região sul, por meio das redes de transmissão de São Paulo. Essa rota já exige muito das linhas e dos equipamentos que mantém a tensão estável, portanto, quando o consumo dentro de São Paulo também aumenta, a rede passa a carregar os dois fluxos ao mesmo tempo. Receba no seu email as notícias de Metrópoles SP Frequência de envio: Diário Ver todas Em razão disso, a tensão cai, linhas e transformadores ficam sobrecarregados e a margem de segurança diminui, o que limita o envio de mais energia ao sul e aumenta o risco de colapso de tensão. Entre no canal de WhatsApp do Metrópoles SP Os data centers entram nesse contexto como os principais causadores dessa sobrecarga. O texto aponta 212 projetos, solicitando cerca de 17,8 GW de acesso à rede. Esse consumo concentrado e contínuo é o que empurra a rede paulista além do limite, já que precisa atender a região sem deixar de enviar energia ao Sul. Prefeitura cita “consultas preliminares” O site da DataSpots, empresa responsável pelo projeto em Atibaia, informa que o empreendimento Data Center Alfa está “aprovado e estruturado”, com previsão de início operacional entre 2029 e 2030. A prefeitura do município, no entanto, confirma apenas o andamento de “consultas preliminares” para a implantação do empreendimento, ainda “sem processo formal de licenciamento ambiental ou urbanístico”. O complexo, que pode ser instalado no Bairro do Tanque, terá área equivalente a 50 campos de futebol. Moradores da cidade acusam as autoridades locais de omitirem a dimensão da estrutura e o impacto de seu consumo energético. Líder da Associação Salve Atibaia, Marcelo Laxe, diz que a estratégia busca “driblar” as análises de impactos ambientais de grandes infraestruturas. “A gente percebe que, nos últimos anos, boa parte das grandes obras no Brasil, em especial em Atibaia, têm sido fatiadas. Quando elas têm um determinado tamanho, uma determinada abrangência em termos de estrutura e de obras, elas têm que seguir um determinado regramento, que é mais restritivo. Então, as empresas dividem os projetos para ficar em uma camada mais baixa de regramento e vão instalando parte a parte […] Tudo isso para fugir dos regulamentos de grandes infraestruturas”, explicou. Subestação local foi ampliada para receber projeto O ONS deu permissão, em outubro de 2025, para a ampliação da capacidade do sistema local de fornecimento de energia elétrica, operado pela concessionária ISA Energia. O documento então aprovado garante o suprimento de energia em alta tensão para o futuro data center, permitindo a conexão física e operacional do empreendimento ao Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) no setor de 138 kV da Subestação Atibaia 2, Conectar-se a uma rede de energia em 138 kV permite demandar e injetar potências elevadas, de dezenas a centenas de megawatts, como 50 MW ou 100 MW. A permissão do ONS também prevê a expansão em 15 quilômetros da linha de transmissão e a implantação de dois novos módulos de entrada de linha em 138 kV, com a premissa de atender ao projeto de tecnologia. Em nota, a concessionária ISA Energia disse ao Metrópoles que a efetivação da conexão está condicionada à implementação de reforços e ampliações da infraestrutura elétrica previstos em parecer emitido pelo ONS. “Além disso, a companhia reforça seu compromisso com a segurança e a confiabilidade do sistema elétrico, e com a expansão da infraestrutura de transmissão necessária ao atendimento das novas demandas de energia”. O Metrópoles entrou em contato via e-mail, telefone e WhatsApp com a empresa DataSpots. Em mensagem, o CEO da empresa, Luiz Fernando Ortega, disse não ter interesse em falar sobre o projeto.

artigo.texto: A weekly roundup of public health news Data center boom could hurt progress fighting air pollution Fifteen years of progress combating climate change in the U.S. could be wiped out in three years as new gas-fired plants are built to power data centers, a new report from the Sierra Club warns. The U.S. has made substantial progress in reducing pollution from electricity generation in recent years, largely by closing coal-fired power plants and expanding renewable energy, according to the Nov. 16 report. Between 2015 and 2025, carbon dioxide emissions from power plants serving the electrical grid fell 22%, for example. That progress is now threatened as large data centers are being built to support artificial intelligence. While some facilities draw electricity from the existing grid, others are developing their own generating stations. More than 550 gas-fired power plants are planned or under construction nationwide, representing a nearly 40% increase in generating capacity, the report said. At least one-third of that new capacity is expected to serve data centers. Just a dozen data center projects with on-site gas plants could annually release nearly 180 million tons of carbon dioxide — a major driver of climate change — along with fine-particle air pollution linked to asthma, heart attacks and strokes. Many data centers operate under permits that limit public review and require little pollution reporting. A bill now making its way through Congress, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, would further weaken review requirements so data centers and their energy sources can be built faster, a move that has been condemned by health advocates. A new poll by the Environmental Protection Network found 88% of U.S. adults support equal pollution safeguards for AI data centers and believe their expansion should not cost Americans their health. High heat linked to premature births, dementia, traffic crashes As climate change increases temperatures across the U.S., new research shows heat is posing risks to health throughout the lifespan. The dangers of heat to human health come even before birth, a Nov. 18 study in JAMA Network Open finds. Exposure to high temperatures during pregnancy was linked with an increased risk of premature birth. Researchers examined more than 12 million births in Brazil between 2015 and 2019, finding high temperatures during the week before delivery were associated with a 14% higher risk of premature birth. Heat exposure earlier in pregnancy also was linked to premature delivery. Researchers suggested that high temperatures may trigger processes involved in labor or interfere with early fetal and placental development. High temperatures also can pose risks to health later in life, an October analysis in Alzheimer’s & Dementia shows. Researchers examined two decades of data on U.S. older adults, finding people who were exposed to more days of dangerously high heat had a 23% higher risk of developing dementia than those with little exposure. People who experienced an average of seven or more days annually in which the heat index reached at least 103 degrees faced the highest risk. The link between extreme heat and dementia was stronger among people in communities with greater socioeconomic disadvantage and less access to central air conditioning. Socioeconomic disadvantage also can play a role in whether people exposed to high heat die from cardiovascular disease, Nov. 18 research in PLOS Climate says. People with heart-related conditions face a greater risk of death when exposed to hotter summers and repeated heat waves, according to an analysis of nearly 64,000 people in the U.K. Risks were greater among people without college degrees and those living in poorer neighborhoods or areas with less green space. For every 1-degree Celsius increase in average summer temperature, the risk of death rose 15%. People exposed to four or more heat waves annually had a 24% higher risk of death than those experiencing two or fewer. Higher temperatures also can influence whether someone dies in a car crash, a new study in the Journal of Urban Health finds. Researchers examined 10 years of data from California, linking extreme heat with increases in the number of crashes and injuries. The most intense heat events were linked to about 180 additional crashes and 100 injuries annually statewide, they estimated. Policies could have long-term consequences for U.S. health Recent federal policy changes could cause lasting damage to the health of the nation, weakening public health agencies and worsening health disparities, a recent study warns. Cuts to healthcare, research, food assistance and public health programs under the Trump administration are impacting U.S. health, with further harms ahead, according to the study in The Lancet Regional Health–Americas. Vulnerable Americans are at highest risk. People with low incomes, rural residents, people of color, immigrants and people with disabilities are expected to face the greatest impacts, researchers said. The policy changes could lead to more illness and preventable deaths, long-term losses in public health capacity and damage to science. Among the most significant recent changes are cuts to Medicaid and new eligibility requirements that could leave millions of Americans without health insurance. The Congressional Budget Office has estimated that Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program changes could increase the number of uninsured people by 7.5 million by 2034. Medicaid enrollment had already fallen by 4.8 million people between April 2025 and April 2026, before most of the new requirements took effect. Meanwhile, the expiration of federal subsidies that allowed people to afford health insurance has increased costs and fueled declining enrollment. Rural communities face particular risks as Medicaid funding reductions threaten hospitals and healthcare providers already struggling with financial pressure

artigo.texto: Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) has invited bids for the supply of renewable energy from an Inter-State Transmission System (ISTS)-connected generating plant comprising a solar photovoltaic (PV) system and a co-located Battery Energy Storage System (BESS). The procurement will be conducted through competitive bidding, followed by an e-reverse auction. The last date for online bid submission is December 10, 2026, at 3 PM. DMRC will open the technical bids on December 11, 2026, at 3 PM. The date for opening financial bids and conducting the e-reverse auction will be announced after the technical evaluation. According to the Request for Selection (RfS) document dated November 19, 2026, the tender carries an earnest money deposit (EMD) of ₹23.9 crore. Selected bidders will have 15 months from the issuance of the Letter of Award (LOA) to complete the work. Bidding Schedule And Requirements DMRC has scheduled the pre-bid meeting for November 26, 2026, at 11 AM at Metro Bhawan, New Delhi. Prospective bidders can submit their queries and seek clarifications until November 27, 2026, at 5 PM. The tender document carries a non-refundable fee of ₹20,000, excluding applicable GST. Bidders must submit their technical and financial proposals through the Central Public Procurement (CPP) portal. The tender security can be submitted through bank guarantee, fixed deposit receipt or electronic payment modes, subject to the conditions specified in the tender document. The bid validity period is 120 days from the last date of submission. Solar And Storage-Based Renewable Power Procurement The tender covers renewable power procurement from an ISTS-connected solar PV generating plant integrated with a co-located BESS. The selection process will involve technical and financial bid evaluations, followed by an e-reverse auction. The procurement brings solar generation and battery storage together under a single renewable power supply arrangement. However, the available bid information sheet does not specify the proposed solar generation capacity, BESS capacity or the contracted power supply duration. The detailed scope of work, qualification requirements, bid evaluation framework and Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) provisions are referenced in the complete RfS documentation.

artigo.texto: Enquanto um estudo de Harvard mostra que os data centers de IA nos Estados Unidos poluem tanto quanto países inteiros, o Brasil tenta se vender como o destino oposto: R$ 560 bilhões em investimentos já mirados aqui, com a promessa de energia 100% limpa. O obstáculo está em Brasília. O programa que sustenta essa promessa, o Redata, foi sancionado em setembro e segue sem o decreto que permite às empresas usar o benefício. Por que o Brasil quer ser a exceção Nos EUA, 403 data centers mapeados por Harvard emitem 26 milhões de toneladas de CO2 por ano. 54% da energia que os abastece vem de carvão e gás. O governo americano chegou a adiar o fechamento de usinas de carvão para sustentar a demanda da IA. O Brasil tem a carta que falta aos americanos: a matriz elétrica era cerca de 90% renovável em 2024. O Redata usa essa vantagem como régua. O programa, sancionado em setembro, derruba a tarifa de importação de servidores de 38% para quase zero, mas só para quem operar com energia 100% renovável e sem consumo de água. Os projetos não faltam: o Rio AI City projeta R$ 360 bilhões em dez anos, e a ByteDance orçou R$ 200 bilhões para uma unidade no Porto de Pecém, no Ceará. Publicidade Um estudo já havia calculado que o Brasil pode atrair US$ 60 bilhões por ano em data centers até 2050. O que trava o negócio A exigência de água zero esbarra num problema que já apareceu em São Paulo: data centers de IA no estado consomem 16,1 bilhões de litros de água por ano. A meta do Redata é mais dura do que a prática atual do setor. No Senado, 22 emendas tentaram mudar o projeto. Ao menos duas discutiam quais fontes de energia entrariam na lista aceita, e uma delas, do senador Laércio Oliveira, queria incluir o gás natural. "Eu não vou comprar, é caro", disse Luciano Fialho, vice-presidente da Scala Data Centers, ao site Paraíba Business, nesta semana, sobre essa alternativa. Fialho atribui ao Congresso a perda de um investimento bilionário para a Índia. "Sabíamos que um dos destinos possíveis era o Brasil", disse, sobre o atraso na aprovação. Luis Tossi, vice-presidente da Associação Brasileira de Data Centers, disse ao mesmo veículo que "o país tem grande disponibilidade de energia renovável, mas isso não significa que toda essa energia seja acessível". O ponto em aberto O decreto que destrava o Redata é esperado para depois da volta do governo da COP31, por volta de 27 de novembro. Até lá, cada semana de atraso é uma semana em que outro país pode fechar o contrato que o Brasil diz que quer para si — a Índia já levou um negócio. A vantagem da energia limpa não dura para sempre.

artigo.texto: Decreto do Redata tem impasse sobre gás natural e espera decisão de Lula Ministérios se dividem sobre datacenters abastecidos com energia de gás natural, e presidente definirá conteúdo da regulamentação A Esplanada dos Ministérios não chegou a um consenso sobre o conteúdo do decreto que regulamentará o Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center). Versões do texto foram finalizadas e serão entregues ao presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), que tomará a decisão. O principal impasse é a possibilidade de datacenters abastecidos com energia proveniente de usinas de gás natural usufruírem de incentivos tributários — descontos em impostos. Acontece que o Redata estabelece que, para ter os benefícios tributários, as empresas precisam atender à totalidade de sua demanda de energia elétrica por meio de renováveis ou de baixa emissão. O termo "de baixa emissão" foi incluído na reta final da tramitação do PL (projeto de lei) no Congresso, a fim de abranger a fonte. Entre os combustíveis fósseis, o gás natural é o que menos emite gases-estufa e visto como uma fonte complementar à matriz elétrica, assegurando energia firme. O tema divide a Esplanada: o MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) é favorável à inclusão do gás natural; enquanto o MMA (Ministério do Meio Ambiente) e a Fazenda são contrários. Uma ala do Mdic (Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços), pasta que ficou à frente da formulação das versões do decreto, também é favorável à inclusão. O setor de gás natural tem se mobilizado pelo seu pleito. A implementação da política leva em conta ainda as vantagens comparativas do Brasil para atração de Datacenter, como energia renovável a preços competitivos Apesar desse potencial, o Brasil possui uma participação pequena no mercado mundial de Datacenters, ocupando a 10ª participação relativa, atrás de países como Japão e Holanda.

artigo.texto: Um estudo da Universidade Harvard, divulgado no sábado (21 de novembro), mapeou os 403 maiores data centers de inteligência artificial dos Estados Unidos. Juntos, eles emitiram cerca de 26 milhões de toneladas de CO2 em um ano, mais do que países como Guatemala e Quênia. A quantidade é quase a mesma emitida pela Dinamarca em um ano inteiro. Mais de 54% da energia que abastece esses data centers vem de combustíveis fósseis, sendo 38% de gás natural e 15% de carvão, segundo o levantamento. "Pense nisso: estamos falando de emissões de carbono comparáveis às de um país inteiro. Imagine toda a população, todas as indústrias, as casas, os hospitais", disse um pesquisador de Harvard ao Jornal Nacional, da TV Globo, no sábado (21 de novembro). A Virginia é o estado americano com o maior número de data centers. Autoridades locais planejam construir uma torre de energia mais alta que a Estátua da Liberdade para dar conta da demanda. Em 2025, o governo Trump adiou o fechamento da maior parte das usinas a carvão do país para abastecer o mercado de IA. Também retirou os Estados Unidos do Acordo de Paris pela segunda vez. A própria COP31, que terminou nesta semana sem meta de corte de combustíveis fósseis, mostra como o tema ainda divide os países. Enquanto isso, os Estados Unidos ampliam o uso de carvão e gás para sustentar a expansão da IA. Como o Brasil se posiciona na corrida pelos data centers de IA? O Brasil disputa a liderança da América Latina na atração de data centers de IA, segundo a revista The Economist. A capacidade instalada deve mais que dobrar até o fim de 2026, de 826 MW para 1.746 MW, segundo a Associação Brasileira de Data Centers. Publicidade A entidade projeta R$ 560 bilhões em investimentos no setor. O país pode atrair US$ 60 bilhões por ano em data centers até 2050. O programa ReData, do governo federal, exige energia renovável e eficiência hídrica nos projetos habilitados. Segundo levantamento do setor, entre os projetos anunciados estão o Rio AI City, da Elea Data Centers, que deve sair de 1.500 MW para 3.200 MW de capacidade. O Scala AI City, em Eldorado do Sul (RS), mira 5.000 MW até 2033. O RT-One, em Maringá (PR), é apontado como o primeiro data center dedicado a IA da América Latina, com investimento de R$ 6 bilhões. Enquanto o setor avança no Brasil, data centers enfrentam resistência nos próprios Estados Unidos, onde moradores protestam contra novas instalações. "A preocupação ambiental ocorre porque os data centers tendem a se concentrar em certas regiões, o que pode pressionar recursos hídricos locais", disse Rudolf Bühler, do Instituto Mauá, ao SeuDinheiro. A promessa de energia limpa não elimina a pressão sobre a água e a infraestrutura das regiões que concentram os projetos. Um levantamento recente apontou que os data centers de IA em São Paulo consomem 16,1 bilhões de litros de água por ano. O que acontece agora O ReData segue como a régua para medir se os novos projetos vão cumprir a promessa de energia renovável e uso eficiente de água. artigo.texto: A computational study evaluating multi-carrier microgrids has revealed that integrating battery storage into a hybridized renewable infrastructure can reduce daily operating expenditures by approximately 92.97 percent. The investigation, conducted by researchers Dedacus N. Ohaegbuchi, Oliver Dzobo, and Eniafe Festus Ayetiran and published in the journal Sustainable Energy Research, demonstrates how intelligent scheduling can coordinate electricity, thermal energy, and gas networks under volatile market conditions. Focusing on the complex, continuous operational demands of an abattoir facility, the team modeled an integrated framework uniting solar photovoltaics, combined heat and power cogeneration, a biomass-fueled boiler, absorption chilling, and energy storage systems. Using a stochastic optimization framework based on the nature-inspired Firefly Algorithm, the researchers addressed the severe operational challenges caused by solar intermittency and fluctuating time-of-use electricity tariffs. Their simulation outcomes indicate that coordinated scheduling not only curbs reliance on the conventional power grid but also establishes an economically viable pathway for rural and semi-industrial multi-energy hubs. The core research motivation stems from the operational vulnerabilities of conventional centralized power systems when confronted with expanding multi-carrier energy requirements in rural and semi-industrial sectors. Facilities such as commercial abattoirs require simultaneous and dependable supplies of electrical power, high-temperature thermal energy, and active refrigeration. In conventional setups, meeting these disparate loads independently leads to elevated operational expenses, severe fuel dependency, and heightened carbon footprints, particularly under dynamic utility pricing structures. Combined heat and power systems substantially elevate overall energy efficiency through the simultaneous generation of electricity and usable heat, yet their rigid operating envelopes create significant scheduling bottlenecks when deployed in isolation. Coupling cogeneration machinery with intermittent renewable sources, such as solar photovoltaic panels, further complicates dispatch decisions due to weather-induced generation fluctuations. The researchers recognized that managing these cross-carrier dependencies requires an integrated multi-energy system capable of dynamically routing energy vectors, absorbing surplus generation, and shielding rural commercial operations from peak utility electricity tariffs. To evaluate this multi-energy architecture under rigorous conditions, the authors designed a comprehensive technical model reflecting an industrial abattoir facility. The generation and conversion infrastructure incorporates a 3.5-kilowatt solar photovoltaic array covering a surface area of 25 square meters with an operational efficiency of 18.6 percent. Base thermal and electrical baseloads are supported by a 700-kilowatt combined heat and power unit operating with an electrical conversion efficiency of 35 percent and a thermal efficiency of 40 percent. Supplementary heating is provided by an auxiliary biomass-fired boiler rated at 1000 kilowatts with an efficiency of 90 percent, accompanied by a dedicated gasification unit operating at 80 percent efficiency. To address cooling demands, the system incorporates a 200-kilowatt absorption chiller exhibiting a performance efficiency of 90 percent. Thermal management is handled by a 1000-kilowatt heat exchanger operating at 95 percent efficiency with 5-kilowatt charge and discharge capabilities, while electrical flexibility is governed by a 500-kilowatt-hour battery energy storage system with an initial state of charge of 400 kilowatt-hours, a 50-kilowatt-hour lower limit, and 95 percent round-trip efficiency. The daily economic scheduling problem is formulated as a single-objective mathematical optimization over a twenty-four-hour planning horizon divided into hourly time steps. The objective function minimizes total operational expenditure by aggregating electricity procurement costs from the conventional distribution grid, offsetting them with export revenues from surplus electricity sold back to the utility, and factoring in the fuel costs of natural gas and biomass gas consumption. Specifically, the formulation tracks seven hourly decision variables: power imported from the grid, power exported to the grid, photovoltaic generation utilized, fuel inputs to the combined heat and power unit, fuel consumed by the boiler, biomass-derived gas generation, and battery discharge power. Electricity export tariffs are fixed at 0.29 dollars per kilowatt-hour, while operational maintenance for the solar photovoltaic array and battery discharge degradation are each parameterized at 0.01 dollars per kilowatt-hour. Fuel prices reflect long-term contracts, pricing network natural gas at 0.157 dollars per unit and biomass gas at 4.00 dollars, contrasted against hourly dynamic time-of-use tariffs. Enforcing physical feasibility requires a comprehensive suite of equality and inequality constraints governing energy balances, conversion boundaries, and operational logic across all subsystems. The electrical balance equality constraint mandates that total hourly generation—comprising imported utility electricity, efficiency-adjusted solar generation, electrical cogeneration output, and battery discharging—must precisely match the facility electrical demand of 250 kilowatts plus battery charging and grid export quantities. Similarly, the thermal balance equality ensures that total heat supplied by the cogeneration unit and the boiler matches demand, accounting for heat exchanger power, absorption chiller needs, and thermal energy storage flows. A third equality constraint regulates the gas supply balance between network imports and biomass gasification output. artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - Ford Motor Co. has shipped the first lithium iron phosphate cells manufactured at its BlueOval Battery Park Michigan facility, according to a Nov. 18 blog post, a key milestone in its ambitions to build a battery business. - It marks the Marshall, Michigan, factory's first delivery since plans for the $3.5 billion battery plant were announced in 2023. The assembly line can manufacture 40 cells per minute, making it among the fastest LFP battery production lines outside of China, according to Ford. - The batteries are now headed to Ford's Louisville Assembly Plant to power prototypes of the Fathom electric truck, which will be assembled there in Kentucky in 2027. Dive Insight: By manufacturing battery cells at a plant it wholly owns and operates, Ford is both building the expertise it needs to build more affordable electric vehicles and investing in a new battery business. “This milestone is about more than shipping our first cells,” Charles Poon, Ford’s VP of vehicle hardware engineering, wrote in the blog post he authored for Ford. “We’re building the expertise to produce high-quality batteries at scale for more affordable EVs and a new energy storage business.” The company is producing prismatic cells in Michigan, which are rectangular and designed to fit directly into the chassis as a structural component. The battery pack of the Fathom pickup will serve as the truck’s floor. The LFP battery chemistry uses no nickel or cobalt, which further reduces cost, according to Ford. These LFP cells are also durable enough for years of charging and use. Poon said in an August blog post that Ford’s aim is to design electrified powertrains to meet a minimum of 15 years or 225,000-mile service life, with consistent and reliable operation throughout that entire period. To further ensure quality, workers at the BlueOval Battery Park are using AI-powered image recognition and other tools to identify any defects during production. Ford's goal is to reduce defect counts down to a frequency of “per billion cells” rather than millions. Altogether, the efforts to improve battery quality while lowering costs are part of Ford's goal to deliver EVs with the performance customers expect, but with a lower price that entices owners of gas-powered vehicles to make the switch to electric. The Fathom, for example, will start at $28,350 with a destination fee of $1,595, delivering on Ford’s promised starting price of under $30,000, the company announced in August. The next phase for BlueOval Battery Park in Marshall, Michigan, is having the plant up and running in early 2027 ahead of the Fathom's launch. But beyond the Fathom, Ford's investment in a battery plant in Michigan is also part of a larger strategy to vertically integrate its battery supplies while building a new business line. In May, Ford officially launched its new Ford Energy subsidary to manufacture battery energy storage systems for data centers, utilities and large industrial and commercial customers in the U.S. The unit was established to meet the growing demand and generate new revenue streams for the company. Ford Energy is utilizing unused production capacity at the former BlueOval SK joint venture EV battery plant in Glendale, Kentucky, to manufacture the battery energy storage systems. Although the Michigan battery plant is owned by Ford, the automaker reached a licensing agreement to manufacture its LFP cells using technology developed by China’s CATL, a major global producer of batteries for EVs and of energy storage systems that help power data centers. However, Ford’s decision to license technology from CATL to manufacture battery cells in Michigan is controversial. In a Sept. 3 letter to Ford CEO Jim Farley, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the agency remains “deeply alarmed” by the automaker’s reliance on technology from China and its impact on American jobs. Duffy urged Farley to cut the company’s technology ties with China. In response, Ford pointed out that its partnership with CATL in Michigan is a “limited technology-licensing and services agreement,” not a joint venture or foreign-owned manufacturing operation.

artigo.texto: Moradores de Atibaia se mobilizam contra chegada de data center na cidade Moradores questionam falta de transparência e temem possíveis impactos ambientais de instalação de data center no interior de SP De Nicole Braga, no Metrópoles:, lembrando que em janeiro marca dois anos do anúncio de um data center para Maringá, que seria o maior da América Latina: Com pouco mais de 160 mil habitantes, Atibaia, no interior de São Paulo, entrou na mira de grandes empresas de tecnologia. O município deve ser a futura sede de um data center de R$ 3 bilhões, em uma região de divisa entre área rural e área urbana da cidade. Temendo possíveis consequências ambientais, os moradores da cidade passaram a se mobilizar contra o projeto, redigindo uma petição que solicita à prefeitura a proibição de data centers de hiperescala no município. O requerimento do movimento popular Fora Data Center pede o envio à Câmara de Vereadores de um projeto de lei complementar para alterar o código de obras e o plano diretor municipal. Um abaixo-assinado do coletivo reuniu, até meados de novembro de 2026, mais de 4 mil assinaturas. O grupo de moradores reclama de não ter sido avisado sobre o projeto e nem convocado para audiências públicas acerca do tema. Leia mais. Foto: Arquivo

artigo.texto: Publicidade WASHINGTON, 20 Nov (Reuters) – O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou nesta sexta-feira que os EUA vão penalizar empresas norte-americanas queconstruírem data centers fora do país, uma medida que, segundo ele, visa ajudar o setor de inteligência artificial dos EUA a competir com seus equivalentes chineses. “Não vamos permitir que nossas empresas construam data centers fora do nosso país”, disse Trump ao discutir inteligência artificial em uma coletiva de imprensa na Casa Branca após sua visita à Ásia. Ele prometeu aplicar um “imposto altíssimo” às empresas que construírem data centers no exterior. Data centers são fundamentais para o avanço da IA, pois fornecem a capacidade computacional necessária para treinar e executar sistemas de IA cada vez mais complexos. Uma penalidade, portanto, poderia complicar a expansão global da infraestrutura de IA. Os desenvolvedores de data centers costumam instalar essas estruturas perto dos usuários para reduzir atrasos em tarefas sensíveis ao tempo, como o processamento de pagamentos. Além disso, a transmissão de grandes volumes de dados por longas distâncias pode gerar custos significativos. Trump tem sido um defensor fervoroso da construção de data centers nos EUA — uma posição que não é bem vista pelos eleitores. Em diversas comunidades pelo país, a instalação desses centros tem enfrentado resistência devido a preocupações com a demanda por energia elétrica, os custos dos serviços públicos e outros impactos locais. O Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) do Chile recuou 1,8% no terceiro trimestre, em comparação ao período anterior, registrando a maior queda desde 2020. O resultado reflete dificuldades na mineração, desemprego elevado e eventos climáticos severos. A presidente do Banco Central chileno, Rosanna Costa, alertou que a recuperação econômica pode demorar mais que o esperado, diante da baixa confiança empresarial e da ausência de sinais claros de retomada dos investimentos. A Anthropic adotou um modelo incomum em sua oferta pública inicial de ações (IPO), realizada na quinta-feira (19). Assim como a SpaceX, a empresa impôs restrições aos bancos responsáveis pela operação. Entre as exigências estavam limites ao número de profissionais envolvidos, maior controle sobre informações financeiras e cláusulas que restringiam a atuação de banqueiros junto a empresas concorrentes. A Petrobras deve anunciar nesta segunda-feira (23) um novo plano de investimentos para o período de 2027 a 2031. Analistas estimam gastos entre US$ 115 bilhões e US$ 120 bilhões, acima dos US$ 109 bilhões previstos anteriormente. A estatal pretende acelerar projetos de exploração e produção de petróleo, ampliar a fabricação de diesel e investir em biocombustíveis. A meta é reduzir a dependência brasileira de diesel importado. O secretário do Tesouro dos Estados Unidos, Scott Bessent, afirmou neste domingo (22) que o governo Trump busca esclarecimentos sobre as vendas de chips da Nvidia à China. A investigação ocorre após a saída de Jensen Huang da liderança da empresa, em meio a suspeitas de envolvimento com uma suposta espiã chinesa. O presidente Donald Trump sancionou uma lei que oficializa o fim da produção de moedas de um centavo de dólar nos Estados Unidos. A medida busca reduzir gastos, já que cada unidade custava quase quatro centavos para ser fabricada. A fabricação havia sido interrompida em novembro de 2025, mas as moedas existentes continuarão em circulação. A nova legislação também estabelece regras de arredondamento para pagamentos em dinheiro.

artigo.texto: Brasil lidera disputa latino-americana por data centers, destaca The Economist Oferta de eletricidade renovável favorece a atração de investimentos, mas expansão depende de conexões à rede, infraestrutura e segurança regulatória O Brasil ocupa posição de destaque na corrida da América Latina para se tornar um polo global de data centers, impulsionado pela disponibilidade de energia renovável e pelo crescimento da demanda por processamento digital. O tema é abordado pela revista britânica The Economist, que destaca a atratividade regional para empresas de tecnologia interessadas em reduzir custos e emissões de suas operações. A liderança brasileira também aparece em levantamento do Banco da Espanha, publicado em 2026. Segundo o estudo, o Brasil concentrava 44% da capacidade instalada de data centers da América Latina em 2025, à frente do México, com 24%, e do Chile, com 20%. A região encerrou aquele ano com aproximadamente 1,3 gigawatt de capacidade, após uma expansão anual de 20%. Energia renovável como vantagem competitiva Os centros de dados abrigam servidores responsáveis por armazenar informações, executar serviços de computação em nuvem e processar aplicações de inteligência artificial. Sua expansão exige fornecimento elétrico contínuo, tornando a energia um dos principais fatores na escolha de novos locais. Nesse aspecto, o Brasil apresenta uma vantagem: 86,6% da oferta interna de eletricidade veio de fontes renováveis em 2025, segundo o Balanço Energético Nacional 2026, da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE). A fonte hídrica respondeu por 52,2% da oferta, enquanto a geração solar alcançou 88,1 terawatts-hora, crescimento de 24,7% sobre 2024. Essa combinação cria oportunidades para atividades intensivas em eletricidade que buscam reduzir sua pegada de carbono. A disponibilidade de recursos renováveis, contudo, precisa ser acompanhada de investimentos em redes e de condições estáveis para contratação de energia, aponta a análise da OCDE sobre as perspectivas econômicas latino-americanas. Nordeste combina energia e conectividade Embora a infraestrutura brasileira esteja concentrada no Sudeste, o Nordeste ganha relevância para novos projetos. Relatório da BloombergNEF, divulgado em novembro, destaca a combinação entre recursos eólicos e solares e conectividade internacional. O Ceará, em particular, reúne pontos de chegada de cabos submarinos que conectam o Brasil à América do Norte, à Europa e a outros mercados. Segundo o estudo, essa infraestrutura pode favorecer instalações destinadas ao treinamento de modelos de inteligência artificial e a outras tarefas menos sensíveis ao tempo de resposta das conexões. Anúncios ainda precisam virar operações O volume de projetos anunciados indica potencial de crescimento, mas não equivale a capacidade já disponível. A BloombergNEF estima que 87% da capacidade brasileira em desenvolvimento ainda estava em estágio inicial, enquanto apenas 3% se encontrava em construção. O Banco da Espanha identifica o acesso à rede elétrica como um dos principais obstáculos à expansão regional. Também pesam a estabilidade do fornecimento, os prazos de licenciamento, a conectividade, a disponibilidade de água para refrigeração e a formação de profissionais especializados. Para transformar a liderança regional em maior presença global, o desafio brasileiro será converter sua vantagem energética em infraestrutura efetivamente conectada e operacional, capaz de atender à demanda crescente por computação.■

artigo.texto: Washington, 20 – Empresas americanas de tecnologia que construírem data centers para a inteligência artificial (IA) no exterior estarão sujeitas a um “imposto enorme”, afirmou o presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, ontem. “Não vamos permitir que centros de dados sejam instalados em outros países porque a China ficará com todos eles, e não vamos deixar isso acontecer”, disse Trump em entrevista coletiva na Casa Branca. “Vamos impor penalidades severas às empresas que tentarem fazer isso.” O presidente americano não explicou como pretende implementar a medida e afirmou que ainda não havia apresentado o plano nem mesmo a seus assessores. Trump pediu aos americanos que recebam bem a instalação de centros de dados em suas comunidades, mas cobrem contrapartidas das empresas responsáveis pelos projetos. O republicano já havia defendido essa posição antes das eleições de meio de mandato. “Vocês deveriam aproveitar os centros de dados. Façam com que eles paguem a vocês e à comunidade, mas não os impeçam de funcionar”, disse. “Queremos que eles construam aqui.” Diante da crescente resistência de comunidades americanas à instalação de grandes centros de dados, as gigantes de tecnologia têm anunciado mudanças para conquistar apoio local. Entre as iniciativas estão a redução de subsídios públicos, maior transparência e investimentos nas regiões dispostas a receber essas estruturas. Na quinta-feira passada, o Senado, controlado pelos republicanos, aprovou um projeto de lei bipartidário para acelerar a concessão de licenças para usinas de energia, linhas de transmissão e outras obras de infraestrutura. A proposta busca ampliar a oferta de eletricidade para atender à demanda crescente e conter os preços. As mudanças previstas também reduziriam o tempo necessário para tirar grandes projetos de energia do papel e obrigariam os centros de dados a pagar pela eletricidade consumida e pelas melhorias necessárias na rede de transmissão. A insatisfação com essas instalações e com o aumento das tarifas de energia tem impulsionado candidatos democratas a defender medidas para conter a expansão desses empreendimentos, conhecidos pelo alto consumo de eletricidade. Trump elogiou o projeto, que agora será analisado pela Câmara dos Representantes. “Isso vai gerar uma quantidade enorme de novas construções”, afirmou. REGRAS Mesmo que Trump, um dos principais defensores do setor, tente evitar restrições federais, as empresas de inteligência artificial e os desenvolvedores de data centers devem enfrentar um ambiente regulatório mais rigoroso. Apesar do apoio presidencial, as estruturas que sustentam a expansão da IA se tornaram um tema politicamente sensível nos Estados Unidos. As empresas de tecnologia afirmam ter entendido o recado. Em entrevistas à Associated Press, executivos do Google e da Meta disseram que buscam reduzir a desconfiança das comunidades onde pretendem instalar centros de dados, inclusive com mais transparência sobre seus projetos. As companhias também prometem reduzir os impactos ambientais e afirmam que a instalação dessas estruturas pode valorizar os imóveis da região. Ao mesmo tempo, tentam convencer a população de que a inteligência artificial representa uma oportunidade para a economia americana, apesar das críticas ao setor. Na segunda-feira, o governo Trump anunciou novas regras para restringir o acesso remoto a chips e servidores avançados de computação dos Estados Unidos. A medida é mais uma tentativa de limitar o uso de tecnologia americana pela China no treinamento de seus modelos mais avançados de inteligência artificial. INVESTIMENTO No mês passado, a Amazon anunciou que está investindo mais de US$ 1 bilhão nos próximos cinco anos em comunidades onde opera data centers, em projetos de educação, treinamento profissional, preservação de água e energia e outras prioridades locais em resposta à rejeição a essas instalações. De acordo com uma postagem em blog publicada ontem por Matt Garman, CEO da divisão de computação em nuvem da Amazon, a gigante americana não utiliza mais acordos de confidencialidade com agências governamentais com as quais trabalha em seus projetos. Ele afirmou também que realiza encontros abertos à comunidade nas regiões onde atua para compartilhar informações sobre suas atividades. Ele ainda alertou contra a disseminação do que considera desinformação sobre o impacto dos data centers no meio ambiente e nas tarifas de energia. Estadão Conteúdo

artigo.texto: Paris Marx questions how far transparency pledges can ease data-center opposition In a new TechCrunch interview, the Hyperscale author welcomes easier access to project details but argues that electricity, water and noise concerns run deeper. Loading page… Listen to this story In a November 22 TechCrunch interview about his book *Hyperscale*, Paris Marx argued that public disclosure can help residents scrutinize data-center proposals but is unlikely to resolve opposition rooted in local resource costs. He said companies’ commitments to end nondisclosure agreements do not address concerns over electricity bills, water access and noise, and questioned whether the buildout’s promised gains justify its cumulative costs. For developers, transparency may reduce suspicion, but securing community support also means addressing the infrastructure burdens directly. Marx said data centers consume more than 20% of Ireland’s electricity, and Dublin-area grid connections for new facilities have faced a moratorium. In The Dalles, Oregon, Google disclosed that its data centers used 29% of the city’s water as it sought more for expansion. Microsoft, Amazon and OpenAI have committed to ending nondisclosure agreements in local-government negotiations, according to the interview. Technology companies are promising more openness around data-center projects. Journalist Paris Marx argues that disclosure alone will do little to settle the underlying disputes. In a November 22 TechCrunch interview about his book Hyperscale, he welcomed easier access to information but said community resistance reflects concerns about electricity bills, water and noise—not simply secrecy. His criticism reaches beyond how companies negotiate individual developments. Marx described the scale of construction as “fundamentally unsustainable,” arguing that its demands on host communities and cumulative environmental costs are too large. He also challenged the industry’s promised returns, saying benefits in productivity, healthcare and education had not materialized as advertised. Those are his assessments of the buildout, not findings from a new impact study. Marx’s explanation for opposition across political lines starts with proximity. An online service can feel abstract; a large facility proposed nearby brings questions about household expenses and daily life. He pointed to potential effects on water access, power bills and neighborhood noise from rooftop cooling equipment. In his view, those concerns give people with otherwise different politics a shared reason to object. His book examines data centers and generative AI, including the infrastructure behind services that users encounter through screens. Researching it required getting past the perimeter. After visiting the outsides of facilities in northern Virginia and Ireland, Marx traveled to New Zealand to tour one. He described advance passport checks, key-card-controlled doors and a warm server room filled with piercing fan noise and air conditioning. Two earlier resource disputes helped persuade him that data centers deserved a book-length investigation. Both examples, he said, showed communities confronting infrastructure demands before generative AI drove a further construction surge: You can delete an app on your phone, but what difference does that really make to the company? Paris Marx, speaking to TechCrunch TechCrunch’s interviewer cited commitments by Microsoft, Amazon and OpenAI to stop using nondisclosure agreements in negotiations with local governments. These agreements restrict what participants can share publicly. Microsoft’s commitment predates the interview: a September 30 House Judiciary Democrats announcement identified it as a change announced in March 2026. Asked how much difference those commitments would make, Marx answered, “Not a huge difference.” He nevertheless welcomed making project information easier to obtain. He described other company responses as more directly tied to resource concerns: proposals to pay for more electricity infrastructure to reduce pressure on ratepayers, and promises to use different water-based cooling systems to lower electricity consumption. Marx sees the transparency shift as a response to opposition, rather than evidence that the conflict has been resolved. With residents more familiar with data centers, he argued, unanswered questions can strengthen resistance. Keeping negotiations secret can therefore work against the companies seeking permission to build. Loading discussion... artigo.texto: The Somerset Zoning Board of Appeals has approved a large-scale battery energy storage system and a proposed Taco Bell restaurant along Route 6. On Wednesday, the Zoning Board of Appeals voted unanimously to approve a Planned Development application for the Salt Cod Energy Storage facility at 1606 Riverside Avenue, the site of the former Montaup Power Plant. The project, proposed by Somerset Energy Storage, LLC and developed by Flatiron Energy, will store up to 168 megawatts / 672 megawatt-hours of energy. The facility is designed to charge during periods of lower demand and discharge electricity to the grid during peak times, supporting local reliability and connecting to existing National Grid transmission infrastructure along Riverside Avenue. The application underwent months of public hearings and technical review. Topics included fire safety, plume studies, environmental conditions, noise, setbacks, and decommissioning. The Fire Department, third-party reviewers, and other town departments provided input. The board’s written decision is currently being drafted for final endorsement. Construction is expected to begin in mid-to-late 2027, with commercial operations targeted for late 2028, according to project materials. On Thursday, the Zoning Board of Appeals unanimously approved a planned development for a new Taco Bell restaurant at 721 G.A.R. Highway (Route 6). The proposal, submitted by DDO New England, LLC, a Taco Bell franchisee, calls for an approximately 2,165-square-foot quick-serve restaurant with parking, a drive-through, 20 seats, and associated site improvements. The project is part of ongoing commercial development along the Route 6 corridor, near a recently opened Chick-fil-A and a proposed car wash. Hours of operation will be Sunday through Thursday 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 a.m., and Friday/Saturday 9:00 a.m. to 2:00 a.m. The eatery has a landscaping plan in place, and a right turn only sign will be placed when exiting the property. No deliveries will be made from 9:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m. Trash pickup will take place from 9:00 a.m. to noon. An estimated opening for the Taco Bell was not stated during the meeting.

artigo.texto: Fox ESS Delivers a 6MW/14.21MWh Battery Energy Storage Project in Trutnov, Czech Republic TRUTNOV, Czech Republic, Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Fox ESS, a global leader in renewable energy solutions, is further strengthening its strategic partnership with NOBILITY s.r.o. through a new 6MW/14.21MWh battery energy storage project in Trutnov, Czech Republic. Located in Náchodsk, 541 03 Trutnov 3-Poříčí, the project is owned by ZEMKON Stare Buky s.r.o. and developed by NOBILITY s.r.o., with Fox ESS providing an integrated battery energy storage solution designed to support electricity price arbitrage, optimize energy management and unlock greater value from energy assets. Fox ESS was selected for its strong delivery capabilities and comprehensive on-site service support. These strengths provide the customer with greater confidence in project execution and long-term system support. Flexible Energy Trading for Greater Economic Value At the heart of the Trutnov project is electricity price arbitrage. By storing electricity during low-price periods and discharging it when prices rise, Fox ESS’s battery energy storage system enables the customer to take advantage of market price fluctuations, optimize electricity trading strategies and unlock greater economic value from stored energy. This approach also enhances the flexibility and overall utilization of energy assets. Integrated System Configuration for Efficient Deployment The project features a total rated power output of 6MW and an energy storage capacity of 14.21MWh, connected to the grid at 35kV. The system comprises two 5,015kWh battery containers and one 4,180kWh battery container, paired with two power conversion system (PCS) skids rated at 4,000kVA and 2,000kVA, respectively. By integrating independent battery containers and separate PCS skids, Fox ESS provides a coordinated energy storage solution that supports efficient system deployment and streamlined on-site installation. Reliable Delivery and Localized Service Support The equipment was delivered on August 11, 2026, and construction commenced on October 11, 2026. Grid connection and commissioning are preliminarily scheduled for December 30, 2026. With timely delivery and strong on-site service support, Fox ESS is committed to ensuring smooth project implementation and reliable system operation. The Trutnov project marks another step in Fox ESS’s expansion in the Czech energy storage market. By combining integrated energy storage technology with flexible energy management capabilities and dependable service support, Fox ESS continues to empower customers to optimize energy consumption, unlock the economic potential of energy storage and contribute to a smarter, more sustainable energy future. artigo.texto: PG&E makes 20-year solar, battery storage plans with Avantus in California Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E) earlier this week signed 20-year power purchase agreements (PPAs) with Avantus, which develops, owns, and operates utility-scale solar and storage projects across California and in the Southwest United States. The PPAs — which are subject to approval by the California Public Utilities Commission — are for Buttonbush 1A and 1B, the initial phases of the Buttonbush Solar Center in western Kern County, Calif. “The Buttonbush projects will be among the largest clean energy resources in our portfolio and are a part of a historic movement to deliver clean-energy solutions for California and our customers,“ said Gillian Clegg, vice president of energy policy and procurement at PG&E. “Projects like Buttonbush will enable PG&E to meet the growing energy needs across our service area with confidence, and give our customers a dependable, affordable, and clean resource for the next two decades,” Clegg said. The projects will provide a combined 800 megawatts (MW) of solar generation and 3,200 megawatt-hours (MWh) of battery storage to the state’s grid, enough to power roughly 381,000 homes each year, according to PG&E. The agreements are among the largest offtake deals for utility-scale solar and storage in California to date, the companies said Nov. 17. “A commitment of this size from PG&E shows how much California needs clean power that is both reliable and predictable in cost,” said Cliff Graham, CEO of Avantus. “Buttonbush 1A and 1B will put low-cost solar on the grid well into the evening, when demand spikes and the sun sets. “The projects will deliver for Kern County too: union jobs, significant new tax revenue, and steady income for local landowners,” Graham added. “The faster we can bring projects like this online, the sooner families and businesses see the benefits.” Specifically, the projects represent an estimated $3 billion infrastructure investment and are estimated to generate hundreds of millions of dollars in local property tax revenue over their operating life to fund county public services. They also will create some 900 union construction jobs and provide permanent operations and maintenance jobs for decades to come. Construction is expected to start in 2027, with commercial operations in 2029, said PG&E. The projects will be built on water-stressed farmland helping to meet state groundwater requirements, and long-term leases will give farmers a stable revenue stream from their land, while scarce water is preserved for other productive crops in the region. Avantus said it plans to own and operate Buttonbush 1A and 1B, operating as an independent power producer. American Clean Power-California, the Kern Economic Development Corporation, and IBEW Local 428, among others, have endorsed the proposed PPAs.

artigo.texto: Highlights - GMG signed an initial service agreement with the UK Battery Industrialisation Centre in Coventry, England, to manufacture and form its G(R)CELLS battery cells. - Production will start in pouch format, with larger formats to follow, using battery materials supplied from GMG's development centre in Brisbane. - GMG pays for the services and retains all intellectual property; the value of the agreement was not disclosed. Graphene Manufacturing Group Ltd. (TSXV:GMG) Basic Materials Graphene Manufacturing Group Ltd (TSXV:GMG) 1.28 CAD -0.220 14.667% Last Updated at: 2026-11-20T20:37:00Z announced ahead of the North American market open, that it has signed an initial service agreement with the UK Battery Industrialisation Centre (UKBIC) in Coventry, England, to manufacture and form its fast-charging graphene battery cells, known as G(R)CELLS. The update is relevant to readers following Technology Stocks, with the TSX serving as the broad Canadian market backdrop. Under the arrangement, GMG pays for the services provided by UKBIC and retains all intellectual property arising from the G(R)CELLS development work. The battery materials used in the cells will continue to be developed, manufactured and supplied from GMG's Battery Development Centre in Richlands, Brisbane. The company did not disclose the fees or overall value of the service agreement, and it did not attach dates to the production work in the release. Key Details in Context The agreement extends a model GMG had already adopted in the United States. CEO Craig Nicol described the deal as an important step in scaling G(R)CELLS to larger formats, adding that it gives Graphene Manufacturing (TSXV:GMG) Basic Materials Graphene Manufacturing Group Ltd (TSXV:GMG) 1.28 CAD -0.220 14.667% Last Updated at: 2026-11-20T20:37:00Z a manufacturing presence serving the United Kingdom and Europe. For a company whose development base is in Queensland, a European production partner offers proximity to battery developers and potential customers in that region without requiring GMG to build and staff its own facility there. GMG's announcement indicates that its role will cover both manufacturing and formation, the initial charging and conditioning process that prepares a newly assembled cell for use. Graphene and battery materials are made at the Brisbane centre, while cell assembly and formation take place at partner facilities in Indiana and Coventry. That division keeps the company's core materials know-how under its own roof and places the equipment-intensive stages of cell production with established operators. It also explains why shipping and material supply appear among the risks the company flagged, since materials must travel from Australia to sites in North America and Europe. The Capital-Light Route to Larger Cells A central feature of the agreement is that GMG can use UKBIC's equipment rather than invest in its own large-format cell capacity. The company said this approach lets it defer building such capacity until the technology is further de-risked. Chairman Jack Perkowski characterised the strategy as a capital-efficient path toward commercial production through established partners, and said the company's long-term goal is to license its battery technology. That licensing ambition shapes how the partnership should be read. If that demonstration succeeds, the intellectual property retained under the agreement becomes the asset the company intends to commercialise through licences. The approach also limits fixed investment at a stage when the technology's performance in larger formats has yet to be proven, which is relevant for a micro-capitalization issuer on the TSX Venture Exchange. Why Moving Beyond Pouch Cells Is the Real Test Readiness-level scales of this kind track a technology's maturity from early laboratory work through to systems demonstrated in operational environments, with higher levels indicating that a product is closer to commercial deployment. The company did not give dates for reaching those levels. Developments of this kind are a recurring theme in Canadian technology stocks, where pre-commercial companies are often assessed on technical milestones rather than revenue. How GMG Makes Its Graphene The battery program draws on GMG's in-house graphene production. The company produces graphene by decomposing natural gas, or methane, into graphene, hydrogen and residual gases, an approach that differs from processes based on mined graphite. Owning the graphene supply allows GMG to develop its battery materials internally at the Brisbane centre and then ship them to partners such as UKBIC and the Indiana centre for cell manufacturing. Beyond batteries, GMG markets energy-saving products built on the same material. These include a graphene coating for heating, ventilation, air conditioning and refrigeration (HVAC-R) systems, a lubricant additive and a coolant additive. Its energy-storage portfolio covers the G(R)CELLS graphene batteries and a graphene additive slurry intended for use in lithium-ion batteries. The UKBIC agreement relates to the cell side of that portfolio and does not change the company's energy-saving product lines. Risks Flagged Alongside the Agreement GMG's release set out several risks connected with the arrangement. The agreement could be terminated or delayed, and the supply and shipping of battery materials from Australia to England could face disruptions. Because the service fees were not disclosed the financial effect of the agreement on GMG's spending cannot be gauged from the release. What the company has made clear is the structure: it funds the services, keeps the intellectual property and avoids committing capital to a large-format production line of its own at this point. artigo.texto: Colunistas convidados escrevem para a editoria de Opinião do GLOBO. Quem paga a conta e quem se beneficia dos data centers? Comunidades locais questionam um modelo em que os benefícios são apresentados como nacionais ou globais Atualizado Minha família e meus amigos finalmente começaram a entender melhor o que faço. Durante anos, dizer que trabalho para que projetos de conectividade e infraestrutura digital levem em conta o interesse público rendia apenas perguntas protocolares. Nos últimos meses, porém, o tema chegou à mesa do jantar e às urnas americanas. Nas eleições de meio de mandato dos Estados Unidos, os data centers mobilizaram eleitores. Segundo o levantamento da Ballotpedia, em 46 das 47 consultas locais com resultados conhecidos, os eleitores favoreceram maiores restrições a data centers. A resistência se tornou suprapartidária e, embora algumas vozes tentem atribuí-la a uma campanha de influência externa, essa narrativa carece de evidências e desconsidera as preocupações legítimas das populações afetadas. O recado é contundente: comunidades locais questionam um modelo em que os benefícios são apresentados como nacionais ou globais, enquanto os custos recaem sobre elas. A questão central não é simplesmente ser a favor ou contra os data centers, uma vez que eles são essenciais para o desenvolvimento de uma economia digital. Trata-se de discutir em que condições serão construídos, quem participará das decisões e como serão distribuídos seus custos e benefícios. Uma resposta que ganha espaço nos Estados Unidos são os Community Benefits Agreements, acordos de benefícios comunitários, negociados entre empresas e representantes das comunidades afetadas, por vezes com participação de governos locais. Esses instrumentos podem estabelecer compromissos concretos e juridicamente vinculantes para assegurar que as comunidades participem dos benefícios econômicos da infraestrutura. Organizações americanas como a Connect Humanity, que atua com inclusão digital e financiamento de infraestrutura, já contribuem para capacitar comunidades e fortalecer sua posição nessas negociações. A discussão interessa diretamente ao Brasil. Em setembro, foi sancionada a Lei 15.504/2026, que instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), com renúncia fiscal estimada em R$ 5,2 bilhões para 2026. O Redata busca atrair investimentos e fortalecer a infraestrutura digital nacional; e ainda será regulamentado pelo Poder Executivo. O Brasil parte de condições distintas das americanas. Além de contar com matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável, possui projetos recentes de data centers com elevado desempenho energético. Segundo estudo de 2025 do BNDES, as instalações mais modernas no país apresentam índices de eficiência superiores à média mundial. Nos Estados Unidos, parte da infraestrutura mais antiga ainda enfrenta limitações tecnológicas, embora o país também concentre alguns dos data centers mais eficientes do mundo. A experiência americana, de todo modo, sugere que o estabelecimento de salvaguardas socioambientais é essencial para que os projetos possam seguir seu curso e que negligenciar essas questões pode acabar por desacelerar investimentos, produzir conflitos, insegurança e resistência social. A legitimidade de um empreendimento perante as comunidades afetadas tornou-se tão importante quanto a disponibilidade de capital. E essa legitimidade não se conquista com promessas genéricas ou campanhas de comunicação, mas com diálogo, transparência e compromissos concretos. Depois de tantos anos explicando por que infraestrutura digital importa, fico feliz que o assunto tenha chegado à mesa do jantar. Ainda mais importante, porém, é que cheguem à mesa do jantar e ao debate público as perguntas certas: quem pagará a conta e quem se beneficiará? *Nathalia Foditsch é especialista em políticas e regulação de infraestrutura digital e líder de programas internacionais da Connect Humanity
