artigo.texto: QuantumScape today introduced the QS PowerBlock for AI data centers. The modular system can deliver four times the power density and five times the runtime of current data center industry standards. SAN JOSE, Calif. — October 8, 2026 —QuantumScape Corporation (NASDAQ: QS), a global leader in solid-state lithium-metal battery technology, today introduced the QS PowerBlock for AI data centers. The modular system can deliver four times the power density and five times the runtime of current data center industry standards. The QS PowerBlock brings QS solid-state lithium-metal battery technology into AI data centers, supporting safer, higher-performing energy storage and 800VDC architecture. An adaptable reference design, QS PowerBlock can fit a variety of module, shelf, and rack formats, and is designed for deployment in industry-standard power rack configurations. Paired with advanced power system components, it can provide AI data center customers with a compelling combination of power, runtime, and safety to power the 1 MW racks of next-generation data centers. In a demonstration using an expected data center training workload, the QS PowerBlock exceeded key specifications set by the Open Compute Project (OCP), the industry consortium that defines open hardware standards for data centers: - 4x the power density, allowing power-hungry AI systems to integrate into compact and cost-effective data center designs. - 5x longer runtime, giving data center operators more margin to smooth out power fluctuations and improve hardware productivity. - Better safety compared to conventional lithium-ion batteries, helping protect billion-dollar infrastructure investments. QS battery cells have demonstrated thermal stability well over 300 °C in third-party and customer safety testing, compared to conventional lithium-ion cells, which typically go into catastrophic thermal runaway at ~180 °C. “QS solid-state battery technology offers an unmatched combination of energy, power, and safety for many different applications, from electric vehicles to AI data centers and beyond,” said Dr. Siva Sivaram, CEO and president of QS. “With the QS PowerBlock, we are bringing this value proposition to AI data center customers, to enable the 800VDC designs that will power the next phase of AI growth.” QS also announced that it has joined the OCP as a member. As AI workloads push data centers toward unprecedented power density, QS is joining industry leaders to build the open standards that infrastructure providers depend on. The QS PowerBlock performance results were achieved through prototype testing and modeled system configurations under controlled conditions, with comparisons benchmarked against the OCP Open Rack V3 (ORV3) specification. Final QS PowerBlock performance will depend on product design, system configuration and real-world operating conditions. ### About QuantumScape Corporation QuantumScape is on a mission to revolutionize energy storage to enable a sustainable future. The company’s next-generation solid-state lithium-metal battery technology is designed to enable greater energy density, faster charging and enhanced safety to support the transition away from legacy energy sources toward a lower carbon future. artigo.texto: Ampace Highlights AIDC Battery Safety and Semi-Solid-State Technology for AI Data Centres At Data Centre World Paris, Ampace showcased its PU200 UPS battery system, built with semi-solid-state cells. Recent large-scale fire testing of the PU100 provides evidence of the company’s approach to system safety. PARIS, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — At Data Centre World Paris 2026, Ampace showcased how it designs batteries for a critical moment in an AI data centre: when the mains supply fails and the uninterruptible power supply (UPS) must immediately carry the load. Its PU200 battery system combines high-rate discharge capability with a compact cabinet for facilities where space for backup power is limited. Ampace develops the cells, modules and complete battery systems used in its data centre portfolio. Its engineers work from the requirements of the installation back to the cell itself. The power a UPS must deliver guides cell design, the heat generated during discharge informs thermal management, and the space available in the facility shapes the cabinet. Safety and reliability are design priorities at each stage. Battery safety, from cell design to large-scale fire testing A UPS battery can spend long periods on standby before it is called on to deliver high power within seconds. Ampace designs its cells with low internal resistance to limit heat generation during high-rate discharge and support reliable power delivery until an alternative supply takes over. To assess how a complete battery system behaves under fire conditions, Ampace subjected its PU100 UPS battery system to large-scale fire testing under the sixth edition of UL 9540A. The PU100 met the applicable test criteria. For data centre operators evaluating battery fire risk, the results provide evidence of how the tested system performed under those conditions. Semi-solid-state cells for high-power backup The PU200 brings Ampace’s semi-solid-state lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cell technology into a UPS battery cabinet. Its cells support the short, high-power discharge required during a supply interruption, while the compact cabinet gives operators more flexibility when allocating floor space in an existing facility or planning a new modular data centre. A detachable battery management system simplifies access for servicing. artigo.texto: Impacto de custo de data centers ainda é dúvida, diz analista Pesquisa do Bank of America mostra redução da exposição em ações de tecnologia no ritmo mais forte em 20 anos Uma pesquisa do BofA (Bank of America) revelou que os investidores diminuíram sua exposição em ações de tecnologia no ritmo mais forte dos últimos 20 anos. O movimento ocorre em meio ao receio de uma possível desaceleração nos gastos com data centers e ao risco de uma bolha de inteligência artificial. Felipe Cima, analista de renda variável da Manchester, avalia que a pesquisa é um importante indicador do posicionamento dos grandes investidores institucionais. Segundo ele, o mercado estaria atribuindo grande importância ao valor do equity das empresas de inteligência artificial justamente no momento em que o foco se volta para o crédito. "A grande questão que se levanta é qual o retorno sobre os investimentos que têm sido feitos, até quando esses investimentos trilionários vão continuar e qual é a possibilidade de estimar um retorno sobre eles", afirmou. Juros e custo de capital no centro das preocupações O analista destacou que o cenário de juros nos Estados Unidos mudou significativamente. O ano começou com expectativas de cortes nas taxas, mas a perspectiva atual aponta para uma possível nova elevação, sem previsão de queda para o ano seguinte. "Tudo isso impacta o custo de capital dessas empresas no momento em que fica muito difícil para que elas tirem o pé do acelerador", explicou Felipe Cima. Para ele, o risco que chega ao radar é justamente se o capital necessário para financiar investimentos na casa das centenas de bilhões de dólares continuará disponível. IPO da Anthropic e a janela de oportunidade Ao ser questionado sobre o aparente paradoxo entre a apreensão com a inteligência artificial e a expectativa gerada pelo IPO da Anthropic, Felipe Cima afirmou que o movimento faz sentido estratégico. S egundo ele, empresas como Google, Micron e Amazon já investiram na Anthropic via fundos de private equity, o que dispensou a necessidade de uma abertura de capital anterior. "Talvez ela escolher esse momento seja justamente a ideia de que a janela pode se encerrar logo, caso a taxa de juros americana continue subindo", disse. O analista ainda ressaltou que, considerando apenas SpaceX e Anthropic, o volume de arrecadação em IPOs neste ano já deve superar a média anual dos últimos dez anos, que girava em torno de 50 bilhões de dólares. Data centers, política e oportunidades para o Brasil Felipe Cima também comentou sobre a resistência política à construção de data centers nos Estados Unidos, apontando que ainda há incompreensão sobre o impacto desses empreendimentos no custo de energia e no uso da água nas localidades afetadas. "Acho que houve, de certa forma, um exagero por parte dos políticos", avaliou. Para ele, essa resistência pode abrir oportunidades para outros países, incluindo o Brasil, que dispõe de energia e água abundantes. "O Brasil poderia, de uma certa forma ou de outra, acabar se beneficiando dessa diversificação", afirmou. Bolha ou não? Analista descarta comparação com a crise das pontocom Sobre a possibilidade de uma bolha de inteligência artificial semelhante à crise das empresas pontocom dos anos 2000, Felipe Cima foi cauteloso. Ele lembrou que, na época da bolha pontocom, havia empresas negociando a duas mil vezes o preço-lucro, enquanto a Nvidia, por exemplo, apresenta múltiplos bem mais modestos para os próximos anos. "Não é múltiplo de bolha, não é múltiplo de cenário de euforia", afirmou. O analista também ponderou que 90% da economia americana cresce entre 1% e 1,5% ao ano, enquanto os 10% ligados à inteligência artificial crescem entre 25% e 30%. Com base nisso, ele concluiu que é difícil falar em recessão na economia americana nos próximos 18 meses, especialmente se os Estados Unidos conseguirem acomodar a taxa de juros.

artigo.texto: Trump ameaça punir empresas que construírem data centers fora dos Estados Unidos Presidente americano quer concentrar infraestrutura de inteligência artificial no país para conter avanço da China O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou nesta sexta-feira (20) que pretende impor penalidades severas a empresas que construírem centros de dados fora do território americano. A medida busca concentrar no país a infraestrutura necessária ao desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial e impedir que a China amplie sua capacidade tecnológica. A declaração representa uma nova intervenção de Washington na disputa global pelo controle de uma indústria que movimenta centenas de bilhões de dólares. “Não estamos permitindo que centros de dados sejam instalados em outros países porque a China ficará com todos eles, e não vamos deixar isso acontecer”, disse Trump a jornalistas na Casa Branca. “Vamos impor penalidades enormes às empresas que tentarem fazer isso.” O presidente não detalhou quais punições seriam aplicadas, quando entrariam em vigor ou se dependeriam de aprovação do Congresso. Também não esclareceu se as restrições atingiriam todos os investimentos internacionais de empresas americanas ou apenas projetos considerados estratégicos para a segurança nacional. A ameaça ocorre em meio à corrida pela construção de data centers, instalações que abrigam milhares de servidores e processadores utilizados para treinar e operar sistemas de inteligência artificial. Empresas como Microsoft, Amazon, Google e Meta vêm ampliando sua infraestrutura em diferentes países para atender à crescente demanda por serviços digitais. A disputa envolve não apenas a localização desses empreendimentos, mas também o acesso a semicondutores avançados, energia elétrica e redes de transmissão. Quanto maior a capacidade de processamento disponível, maiores são as possibilidades de desenvolver e operar modelos sofisticados de inteligência artificial. A proposta, porém, pode criar dificuldades para as próprias empresas americanas. Grandes operadoras de data centers, como Equinix e Digital Realty, mantêm instalações em diferentes continentes. A proximidade com os usuários reduz o tempo de resposta dos serviços digitais e os custos de transmissão de dados. Em alguns mercados, também é necessária para cumprir exigências legais sobre armazenamento e processamento de informações. Trump não explicou como pretende aplicar a tributação. Nos Estados Unidos, a criação de impostos federais depende, em regra, de legislação aprovada pelo Congresso. O presidente reconheceu que ainda não havia comunicado a proposta aos integrantes de sua própria administração. A iniciativa se soma às restrições americanas à exportação de semicondutores avançados para a China. Nesta semana, o governo também adotou medidas para limitar o acesso remoto a servidores equipados com chips americanos, numa tentativa de impedir que empresas chinesas utilizem infraestrutura instalada em terceiros países para contornar os controles comerciais. Nos Estados Unidos, entretanto, a expansão dos data centers enfrenta resistência de comunidades preocupadas com o consumo de eletricidade, o aumento das tarifas e os impactos ambientais. Trump defendeu que municípios recebam compensações financeiras pela instalação dos empreendimentos, em vez de rejeitá-los. Para o Brasil, a ameaça acrescenta uma incerteza aos esforços para atrair investimentos internacionais em centros de dados, especialmente projetos voltados à inteligência artificial. O país busca aproveitar sua oferta de energia renovável para receber instalações de grande porte. Uma eventual penalização de empresas americanas que investirem no exterior poderia reduzir a atratividade desses projetos, embora ainda não seja possível dimensionar os efeitos sem conhecer as regras propostas. Por enquanto, o anúncio representa uma intenção política, não uma proibição em vigor. A extensão das penalidades, os instrumentos legais necessários e os possíveis efeitos sobre investimentos já anunciados permanecem indefinidos.

artigo.texto: Senate approves bill to speed up permitting reviews, force data centers to pay for energy costs WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate approved bipartisan legislation Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices. The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths. The 62-33 vote is the first major action by Congress since midterm elections that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans. The bill now goes to the House, which approved a more limited, industry-friendly version last year. The Senate bill would overhaul several environmental laws to make it easier to build energy infrastructure, drawing criticism from Democrats and environmental groups about limits on judicial review and changes to bedrock laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act. Trump urged approval of the bill, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a recent social media post. The bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, will ensure the U.S. can build pipelines, mines and power plants more quickly, “lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote. Fifteen Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, voted for the bill. Two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, voted no. Industry groups back bill, but environmentalists fear it would weaken safeguards Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and the oil and gas sector support the bill as a way to deliver more electricity to the grid and avoid delays for infrastructure projects that can stretch a decade or more. However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure, saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals. “Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centers, oil and gas pipelines and (liquefied natural gas) terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the U.S.,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project. Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill “a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America” and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate. Democrats push for amendments A final vote on the measure was held up this week as Oregon’s two Democratic senators pushed to add amendments, including one to ban data centers on public lands. Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden are among several Democrats in both chambers who say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that boosts clean energy, such as solar and wind power, while limiting expansion of oil, natural gas and other fossil fuels. “Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn’t tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that,” Merkley said. Majority Republicans stymied Merkley’s effort to ensure votes on a host of amendments, including one that would block the Trump administration from continuing to cancel clean energy grants and other Democratic priorities for “purely political purposes.” The bill’s sponsors reneged on promises of “a robust amendment process,” he said. In the end, the measure was approved without amendments offered by rank-and-file senators. “I do think that this bill is very consequential to the future of this planet,” Merkley said. Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, oppose the bill, citing concerns about limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved. The current review process often takes five years or more, and shortening that time frame is a key goal of the bill. “In America today, it takes too long and costs too much to build,” said Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso, the No. 2 Republican in the Senate. “Energy projects that would help lower prices remain frozen for years” as they await approval by the federal government. “Construction cannot start without first spending years in the regulatory penalty box,” driving up costs and creating uncertainty, Barrasso said. The bill’s four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — have released a detailed set of amendments designed to bolster support for the legislation. The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal a few weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years. “We are going to make it easier to build in America again, and make life more affordable for American families,” Lee said. artigo.texto: McHenry County has hit the pause button on data centers. The County Board has approved a 12-month moratorium on the controversial projects. The vote was 17-1, with only board member Terri Greeno, R-Crystal Lake, voting no. Greeno said before the vote the county was able to implement battery storage regulations quickly and hoped the county wouldn’t need a year to update its ordinances for data centers. County Board Chair Mike Buehler, R-Crystal Lake, defended the moratorium in response to Greeno’s comments. “I think our goal is to get it right. If it takes us a year to do it, that’s what ... we’re going to do,” Buehler said. Resident Zaynab Ritchie asked the board to implement the moratorium, citing potential pollution, negative health effects, noise and electricity and water consumption. “Please enact the data center moratorium and prioritize your people’s needs over the needs of a machine,” Ritchie said. Board member Joe Gottemoller, another Crystal Lake Republican, was active in pushing for the moratorium and said its approval was a “step in the right direction.” Gottemoller said the county doesn’t have ordinances to regulate data centers and was concerned someone would apply for a data center and be allowed to operate it without regulations. He said data centers are very large buildings and should not have any regulations on them. It was the last meeting for both Gottemoller and Greeno as County Board members, as they lost their reelection bids this month to Democrats Edward “Bud” Bowie Jr. and Austin May, respectively. The data center moratorium is meant to give the county time to come up with regulations for the data projects. No applications are currently active for data centers in the county, officials have said. Adam Wallen, the county’s director of planning and development, previously said the 12-month moratorium is there so the county can develop standards so it’s prepared when a data center applicant comes along. The board can extend, tweak or repeal the moratorium during the 12-month timeframe. McHenry’s is not the first data center moratorium an area county has approved. Neighboring Lake County approved an eight-month pause in September. The counties’ actions only apply to unincorporated areas. Municipalities set their own rules.

artigo.texto: O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump,em discurso nesta sexta-feira (20) na Casa Branca, ameaçou impor "duras sanções" a empresas americanas que construírem seus centros de dados em outros países: "Não permitiremos que os centros de dados sejam instalados em outros países, porque a China se apoderaria de todos eles. Vamos impor duras sanções às empresas que tentarem fazê-lo (...) Vamos impor um tremendo imposto." "Quem vencer na superinteligência, ganha. É preciso tirar proveito dos centros de dados. Façam com que paguem à sua comunidade", disse Trump. "Mas tirem proveito, não os fechem." O presidente também se referiu a outras sanções - sem informais quais - que seu governo poderia impor às empresas que construírem centros de dados no exterior. O discurso de Trump é o primeiro após a cúpula trilateral ocorrida nesta semana. + 'Guerra nuclear não pode ser vencida': Xi, Trump e Putin fazem 'declaração de paz' após cúpula Pedido à Nvidia Trump também pediu à gigante dos chips Nvidia que reincorpore Jensen Huang como diretor-executivo da empresa, após a sua saída devido a um relacionamento com uma suposta espiã chinesa. "Adoraria vê-lo de volta. É uma das mentes mais brilhantes do mundo, e para onde irá? Acho que adoraria que dessem uma segunda chance a Jensen", disse Trump. Putin e a Guerra na Ucrânia O líder americano disse que seu colega russo, Vladimir Putin, garantiu a ele que deseja uma solução diplomática para a guerra na Ucrânia, após Moscou lançar uma onda de ataques contra Kiev. Putin expressou em reunião bilateral "seu desejo de que a guerra entre a Rússia e a Ucrânia termine por meios diplomáticos", informou Trump em entrevista coletiva na Casa Branca, após retornar de uma viagem à China. Eliminação das armas nucleares não é certa Na mesma entrevista, o presidente americano disse que não está certo de que a eliminação das armas nucleares "pode ser alcançada um dia", após se reunir com os líderes da Rússia e da China, as outras duas principais potências nucleares. "Se alguém chega e diz: 'Eu te proponho um acordo. Vamos todos reduzi-las pela metade', é difícil dizer sim, principalmente quando você está no comando", disse Trump, acrescentando que é "muito difícil dizer 'vamos nos desfazer de nossas armas nucleares'". "Relações fantásticas" com Xi e Putin Trump ressaltou suas "relações fantásticas" com os governantes Xi Jinping e Vladimir Putin, e afirmou que esses laços pessoais ajudam a manter os Estados Unidos seguros. "Tenho relações fantásticas com Putin, o que é muito bom. Tenho relações fantásticas com o presidente Xi, o que é algo bom, e nosso país está seguro graças a isso", afirmou Trump na entrevista. Tribunal Penal Internacional Trump declarou, ainda, que o Tribunal Penal Internacional (TPI) está "fora de controle", no momento em que a corte enfrenta questionamentos crescentes por parte de Washington, Moscou e Pequim. Os Estados Unidos prometeram desmantelar o tribunal, contra o qual impuseram novas sanções no mês passado. A China "aceitou, pela primeira vez, condenar os abusos e excessos do Tribunal Penal Internacional", ressaltou Trump. Ele se queixou de que o TPI acredite que "pode chegar e prender os chefes de Estado, e não pode. Podem fazê-lo sem motivo algum, portanto condenamos isso como grupo." O presidente americano criticou a ordem de prisão emitida pelo TPI contra o primeiro-ministro israelense, Benjamin Netanyahu, acusado de crimes de guerra na Faixa de Gaza.

artigo.texto: - Mulilo has secured commercial and financial close for the 77 MW / 308 MWh Leeuwpoort Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) near Carletonville, the first large scale BESS project to reach financial close in Gauteng. - It is the third Mulilo BESS project to close this year, following Mercury and Hartebeesfontein, and will operate under a 15 year power purchase agreement with the National Transmission Company South Africa (NTCSA). - Reatile Group is the strategic empowerment partner, with a local community trust also participating, while Absa, Nedbank and Standard Bank form the lender consortium. Mulilo has announced the successful commercial and financial close of the Leeuwpoort Battery Energy Storage System project, marking a milestone in the delivery of South Africa’s next generation of grid supporting energy infrastructure. Located near Carletonville in the Merafong City Local Municipality, Gauteng, the 77 MW / 308 MWh utility scale facility will connect to the Midas Main Transmission Substation. It is expected to strengthen the resilience and flexibility of the national grid in a strategically important industrial region, where energy demand is shaped by extensive mining activity. As the first large scale battery storage project to reach financial close in the province, Leeuwpoort represents a significant step for Gauteng and for South Africa’s energy transition and grid modernisation. The project was awarded under Bid Window 2 of the Battery Energy Storage Independent Power Producer Procurement Programme (BESIPPPP). It is the third Mulilo BESS project to reach financial close this year, following the Mercury and Hartebeesfontein projects. Leeuwpoort will use the Haohan battery energy storage system supplied by BYD Energy Storage. Once operational, it will provide storage capacity and ancillary services to the transmission system under a 15 year power purchase agreement with NTCSA. Mulilo said the project reflects the strength of its partnership model and its commitment to meaningful participation. Reatile Group is the strategic empowerment partner, while a local community trust will ensure long term community participation and shared socioeconomic benefits. As lead sponsor, Mulilo will also provide construction management, asset management, operations and maintenance oversight, and social impact management services throughout the project’s lifecycle. Mulilo CEO Jan Fourie said: “The financial close of the Leeuwpoort project marks another significant milestone in Mulilo’s commitment to strengthening South Africa’s energy system through utility scale battery energy storage. Projects such as Leeuwpoort play a critical role in enhancing grid stability, unlocking network capacity, and improving energy security. Together with our partners and the support of the South African government, we are proud to deliver lasting value for the country while creating meaningful economic opportunities for local communities.” Sunette Smith, Chief Commercial Officer of Reatile Group, said: “Reatile Group is proud to partner on Leeuwpoort, an important investment in strengthening South Africa’s energy security and enabling the transition to a more resilient and sustainable energy system.” Financial close was made possible by Mulilo’s shareholders, Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) and Norfund, together with close collaboration with Reatile Group, the Department of Electricity and Energy, Eskom, the Independent Power Producers Office, NTCSA and the Merafong City Local Municipality. A lender consortium comprising Absa Bank Limited, Nedbank Limited and Standard Bank of South Africa Limited also backed the project, signalling continued confidence in Mulilo’s development and delivery capability. Key advisers included Arup, Bastion, Bowmans, Deloitte, ENS, Fasken, Marsh and Pepper Tree Capital. Author: Bryan Groenendaal

artigo.texto: Trump ameaça taxar empresas que construírem data centers fora dos EUA Presidente quer concentrar nos Estados Unidos estruturas usadas para processar dados e desenvolver IA O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump (Partido Republicano), ameaçou nesta 6ª feira (20.nov.2026) taxar empresas norte-americanas que construírem data centers fora do país. O republicano afirmou que pretende concentrar nos EUA as estruturas usadas para processar dados e desenvolver inteligência artificial. “Não vamos permitir que nossos data centers sejam construídos em outros países, porque a China vai ficar com todos eles. Não vamos permitir que isso aconteça”, disse Trump em entrevista a jornalistas na Casa Branca. O presidente afirmou que empresas que instalarem data centers no exterior terão de pagar uma “taxa enorme”. Trump citou projetos de data centers na Finlândia e em outros países e disse que quer que essas estruturas sejam construídas nos Estados Unidos. Segundo ele, a instalação de data centers no país produz renda, crescimento econômico e arrecadação. “Eles permitiram que isso [produção fora dos EUA] acontecesse com os chips e tudo mais, e isso foi muito destrutivo para o nosso país”, declarou. A ameaça pode afetar a disputa internacional por investimentos em infraestrutura de inteligência artificial, na qual o Brasil também tenta atrair empreendimentos. O país aprovou em setembro um regime tributário especial para data centers, com incentivos para a instalação e expansão dessas estruturas.

artigo.texto: Kuraray Owns Calgon Carbon, a major producer of granular activated carbon According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Granular Activated Carbon market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global granular activated carbon market is entering a phase of steady expansion as environmental compliance, water scarcity, and industrial purification requirements intensify across both mature and developing economies. Granular activated carbon remains the material of choice in fixed-bed adsorption systems where low pressure drop and thermal reactivation are essential, giving it a durable position in municipal water treatment, air and gas purification, food and beverage processing, pharmaceuticals, and industrial solvent recovery. The 2026-2035 forecast period is shaped by tightening discharge and drinking-water standards, particularly in Asia-Pacific, alongside investments in wastewater reuse and emerging contaminants removal. Supply-side dynamics remain complex: coal-based and coconut shell-based feedstocks face availability and price volatility, while energy-intensive activation and granulation constrain rapid capacity additions. The competitive landscape includes established multinationals and regional specialists investing in reactivation services and impregnated grades. This report provides a data-driven view of market size, segmentation, trade patterns, and the strategic factors likely to define the market through 2035. The baseline scenario for the global granular activated carbon market points to moderate but resilient growth over 2026-2035, with demand rising across municipal water treatment, air purification, and industrial processing. The market is expected to grow at a CAGR of approximately 4.5% in value terms, reaching an index level of about 155 by 2035 (2025=100). This outlook assumes continued enforcement of water and air quality regulations, gradual recovery in industrial capital spending, and steady replacement demand in established fixed-bed systems. Regionally, Asia-Pacific is expected to account for the largest share of incremental demand, supported by public water infrastructure programs and stricter industrial discharge rules. North America and Europe remain mature but benefit from replacement cycles, emerging contaminant regulations, and reactivation service expansion. Latin America and the Middle East & Africa offer smaller but growing opportunities tied to urbanization and desalination. Key uncertainties include raw material price volatility, energy costs, and the pace of regulatory implementation in emerging markets. Overall, the market is not expected to experience explosive growth, but its essential role in environmental compliance and public health supports a stable upward trajectory through 2035. Water treatment remains the largest and most consistent demand segment for granular activated carbon, underpinned by municipal drinking-water facilities and industrial wastewater systems that rely on fixed-bed adsorption for organic contaminant removal. Through 2035, demand is expected to be reinforced by tightening standards for emerging contaminants, including PFAS and disinfection by-product precursors, particularly in North America and Europe, while Asia-Pacific invests heavily in expanding public water infrastructure. Demand-side indicators to watch include municipal capital expenditure on water treatment plants, regulatory timelines for contaminant limits, and the rate of adoption of thermal reactivation services, which can extend media life and influence virgin GAC replacement cycles. Industrial water reuse projects and desalination pre-treatment also support incremental GAC demand. The segment is less cyclical than industrial applications, providing a stable base for overall market growth. Current trend: Growing steadily, supported by stricter drinking-water and wastewater regulations. Major trends: Stricter limits on emerging contaminants driving GAC adoption, Growth in water reuse and desalination pre-treatment, Expansion of reactivation services extending media life, and Increasing municipal infrastructure spending in Asia-Pacific. Representative participants: Calgon Carbon Corporation (Kuraray), Cabot Corporation, Jacobi Carbons, Haycarb PLC, and Carbon Activated Corporation. Air and gas purification represents a significant and growing outlet for granular activated carbon, used in industrial emission control, solvent recovery, and indoor air quality systems. Demand is driven by regulations targeting volatile organic compounds and hazardous air pollutants, as well as by increasing awareness of indoor air quality in commercial and residential buildings. Through 2035, stricter industrial emission standards in Asia-Pacific and Europe are expected to support demand for impregnated and virgin GAC in fixed-bed adsorbers. Key demand-side indicators include industrial production levels in chemicals and coatings, regulatory enforcement intensity, and the adoption of carbon capture and gas separation technologies. The segment is somewhat cyclical, tied to industrial capital spending, but long-term regulatory trends favor steady expansion. Replacement cycles for air purification media also provide recurring demand. Current trend: Expanding with industrial emission controls and indoor air quality concerns. Major trends: Tighter VOC and hazardous air pollutant regulations, Growth in indoor air quality systems, Adoption of GAC in biogas and carbon capture applications, and Increasing use of impregnated grades for specific gas removal. Representative participants: Calgon Carbon Corporation (Kuraray), Donau Carbon GmbH, Silcarbon Aktivkohle GmbH, Jacobi Carbons, and Ingevity Corporation. artigo.texto: Juniper Green Energy Limited has commissioned a 109 MWp solar project in Tuljapur, Maharashtra, and an additional 95 MWh of battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity at its integrated renewable energy facility in Barmer, Rajasthan. The solar project has been developed through Juniper Green ETA Five Private Limited, a subsidiary of Juniper, in Dharashiv district. It is connected to the 220/132/33 kV Tuljapur substation of Maharashtra State Electricity Transmission Company Limited and is backed by a 25-year power purchase agreement with Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited. Meanwhile, the additional BESS capacity at Barmer is connected to the inter-state transmission system through the Fatehgarh-IV (Section-I) pooling station. With these additions, Juniper’s operational portfolio has reached approximately 2.95 GWp of renewable energy capacity and 698 MWh of BESS capacity.

artigo.texto: The Washington County Chamber of Commerce will host a presentation on December 2 at Hagerstown Community College to discuss the opportunities and challenges associated with data center development as the industry continues to generate discussion throughout the region. Joe Kroboth will lead the presentation, which comes amid growing interest in the possibility of a data center development in Washington County. Kroboth is deputy county administrator for Loudoun County, Virginia, where he oversees community development and public safety services. He previously spent seven years as Washington County’s public works director before serving in Loudoun County for 14 years, giving him firsthand experience with the growth of the data center industry. Paul Frey of the Washington County Chamber of Commerce said the presentation will give residents and business owners an opportunity to learn more about the industry and issues surrounding potential development. “We’ve been talking for the last few weeks about data centers, and specifically maybe one in Washington County, and maybe Hagerstown with an annexation opportunity with the Burkholder and McDade properties,” Frey said. The potential development was also discussed during a recent Hagerstown Mayor and Council meeting, where officials considered annexation and possible regulations that could apply if the properties are developed as a data center. Frey said those discussions are important as local officials consider the infrastructure and other requirements associated with such a project. “If it is a data center, what type of energy are they going to use? Will they have water? What are the setbacks?” Frey said. “And so that’s an important topic here in Washington County and frankly in Maryland.” Maryland Senator Paul Corderman has said in the past, “This whole data center conversation has really become a boogeyman, and has really caused a lot of unnecessary division in my mind, where people just need to look at the merits of what’s what’s happening here and make a decision made on facts, not a decision made on a bunch of fear mongering.” Frey said the issue extends well beyond Washington County, as communities across the country consider the growing demand for data centers and the resources needed to support them. The Chamber’s December 2 presentation will address both the challenges and opportunities associated with the industry. “I encourage folks, if you want to know about data centers, the challenges, the opportunities, come see us December 2,” Frey said. Frey said the presentation will tie into discussions taking place locally, throughout Maryland and across the country as communities consider potential data center developments.

artigo.texto: Brasil lidera expansão de data centers na América Latina com avanço de investimentos | Vero NotíciasBrasil lidera expansão de data centers na América Latina com avanço de investimentos O Brasil concentra cerca de 700 megawatts de capacidade em data centers, quase metade do total da América Latina. A disponibilidade de energia renovável e a crescente demanda por serviços digitais impulsionam investimentos de empresas de tecnologia no país. Entre os projetos em expansão estão os da Ascenty, que prevê investimentos de US$ 1,2 bilhão, e da ByteDance, dona do TikTok, com aportes que podem chegar a US$ 39 bilhões. A capacidade brasileira poderá atingir 5 gigawatts até 2030, segundo projeções do setor. Apesar do potencial, a expansão enfrenta desafios relacionados à infraestrutura elétrica, ao licenciamento e àsdisputas comerciais entre Estados Unidos e China. Novas exigências americanas para exportação de semicondutores avançados também podem afetar projetos brasileiros. Dados do The Economist. O Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) do Chile recuou 1,8% no terceiro trimestre, em comparação ao período anterior, registrando a maior queda desde 2020. O resultado reflete dificuldades na mineração, desemprego elevado e eventos climáticos severos. A presidente do Banco Central chileno, Rosanna Costa, alertou que a recuperação econômica pode demorar mais que o esperado, diante da baixa confiança empresarial e da ausência de sinais claros de retomada dos investimentos. A Anthropic adotou um modelo incomum em sua oferta pública inicial de ações (IPO), realizada na quinta-feira (19). Assim como a SpaceX, a empresa impôs restrições aos bancos responsáveis pela operação. Entre as exigências estavam limites ao número de profissionais envolvidos, maior controle sobre informações financeiras e cláusulas que restringiam a atuação de banqueiros junto a empresas concorrentes. A Petrobras deve anunciar nesta segunda-feira (23) um novo plano de investimentos para o período de 2027 a 2031. Analistas estimam gastos entre US$ 115 bilhões e US$ 120 bilhões, acima dos US$ 109 bilhões previstos anteriormente. A estatal pretende acelerar projetos de exploração e produção de petróleo, ampliar a fabricação de diesel e investir em biocombustíveis. A meta é reduzir a dependência brasileira de diesel importado. O secretário do Tesouro dos Estados Unidos, Scott Bessent, afirmou neste domingo (22) que o governo Trump busca esclarecimentos sobre as vendas de chips da Nvidia à China. A investigação ocorre após a saída de Jensen Huang da liderança da empresa, em meio a suspeitas de envolvimento com uma suposta espiã chinesa. O presidente Donald Trump sancionou uma lei que oficializa o fim da produção de moedas de um centavo de dólar nos Estados Unidos. A medida busca reduzir gastos, já que cada unidade custava quase quatro centavos para ser fabricada. A fabricação havia sido interrompida em novembro de 2025, mas as moedas existentes continuarão em circulação. A nova legislação também estabelece regras de arredondamento para pagamentos em dinheiro.

artigo.texto: CATL leads the global EV battery market with a 39.1% share, followed by BYD at 15.2%. Solid-state, sodium-ion and silicon-anode batteries represent major areas of next-generation battery research. Energy storage demand offers new growth opportunities as global battery shipments reach 461.3 GWh in H1 2026. Batteries have quietly become the most contested part of the electric future. They decide what an EV costs, how far it goes, how fast it charges and whether it catches fire. They also decide whether a solar farm can keep running after sunset. China dominates the business, with South Korea, Japan and the United States holding on to real pockets of strength. CATL and BYD are far ahead of other competitors in EV batteries, followed by LG Energy Solution, Panasonic Energy and Samsung SDI vying to keep their place. These are the ten companies shaping the market, and what sets each one apart. CATL, based in Ningde, is the biggest name in EV batteries by a wide margin. From January to September 2026 it supplied 39.1% of the market, or 389.2 GWh of installed capacity. That is roughly two and a half times BYD’s share. Most of its batteries use LFP or NMC chemistry, and it is also pushing into sodium-ion cells, battery swapping and ultra-fast charging. A three-year, 60 GWh storage deal with HyperStrong shows that cars are no longer its only big customer. BYD, in Shenzhen, took 15.2% of EV battery installations in the first nine months of 2026. Its Blade Battery is an LFP design built around safety and low cost. BYD also builds the cars those batteries go into, which means no supplier negotiations and no waiting on anyone else’s schedule. Solid-state is the next target, with first vehicle use aimed at 2027 and mass production around 2030. That control over the whole chain is the main reason rivals struggle to match its costs. LG Energy Solution holds 8.2% of the EV market and is the strongest South Korean player. It makes NMC, NCMA and LFP cells in both cylindrical and pouch formats, and its supply deals with carmakers are spread across the world. Energy storage has been a bright spot, with shipments climbing fast in the first half of 2026, mostly in North America. The company’s next moves are LFP, new chemistries and big storage systems. Gotion, from Hefei, sits fourth with 5.1%. It makes LFP and NMC batteries and has a research team working on solid-state cells. Its roots in battery materials give it more control over its supply than most. Overseas factories and high-energy-density cells are what it is betting on for the next stage. CALB, short for China Aviation Lithium Battery, took 5.0% from January to September 2026. The Changzhou company makes LFP and ternary lithium-ion cells for cars and for energy storage. It is good at producing cells in volume and designing packs for carmakers. With EV and stationary storage demand both rising, CALB is working to build a foothold outside China. Also Read - Ford Enters Battery Manufacturing with First U.S.-Made LFP Cells EVE Energy, based in Huizhou, holds 3.6% of EV installations, but its reach is wider than that figure suggests. Its cells go into cars, consumer electronics and large storage projects, and it ranked second worldwide in energy storage battery shipments in the first half of 2026. Large-format cells and plans for factories abroad are the areas to follow. Panasonic Energy, from Japan, also holds 3.6%. Its name is tied to Tesla, which it has supplied for years with some of the best-regarded cylindrical cells around. Research now covers nickel-rich cathodes, silicon anodes and the 4680 format. Packing more energy into each cell while making it cheaper to build is the company’s primary goal. SK On, from Seoul, has 2.8% of the market. It leans on high-nickel NMC chemistry and advanced cell design. Deals with carmakers and a global network of factories keep it close to the biggest vehicle markets. Cost cutting, solid-state research and better performance drive its long-term plans. Svolt Energy, in Changzhou, held 2.6% in the first nine months of 2026. It makes LFP, high-nickel ternary and cobalt-free batteries. Cobalt is expensive and ethically messy to source, so a good cobalt-free cell is a real prize. Svolt’s European plans give it a route to markets beyond China. REPT BATTERO, based in Wenzhou, took 2.4% of EV installations. Its batteries are mainly LFP and go into cars and big energy storage projects. It focuses on large-format cells and utility-scale storage, the kind of equipment that sits beside a solar farm or substation. Growing overseas and improving cell design are its next priorities. Why this Matters Cleaner energy, electric transport and a stable grid all hang on better batteries. Cheaper cells bring down energy costs and make renewable power easier to rely on, which means less dependence on fossil fuels. The companies on this list will decide how quickly that happens and who profits from it. The next shake-up is likely to come from solid-state cells, sodium-ion chemistry, silicon anodes and recycling. CATL and BYD are far ahead on scale today, but Samsung SDI, Toyota, QuantumScape and Solid Power are attracting attention for their solid-state work. Storage may turn out to be the bigger story. Global energy storage battery shipments hit 461.3 GWh in the first half of 2026, up 71% on a year earlier, with CATL holding 27.1% of that market. Winning EV contracts is no longer enough. Power grids, renewable projects, data centres and advanced electronics all want batteries now. The companies that come out on top will be the ones that get cell performance, cost, safety and factory output right at once, and that can turn lab results into products that work reliably at scale. 1. artigo.texto: A Ford se prepara para comprar créditos de carbono de montadoras concorrentes para assegurar a continuidade das vendas do Mustang com motor V8 na Austrália. O país implementou metas de emissões cada vez mais rígidas que acabam por afetar os fabricantes, mas a Ford não pretende abandonar o clássico esportivo. A alternativa comercial surge com a aplicação do New Vehicle Efficiency Standard (NVES), em vigor desde julho de 2025. O programa estipula limites estritos de emissão de CO2 calculados pela média geral dos automóveis comercializados por cada marca. Fabricantes que ultrapassam o teto compram créditos excedentes de empresas com índices mais favoráveis, evitando multas financeiras. Leia Mais - Vídeo: Verstappen testa Ford Mustang GTD e avalia esportivo - Ford Mustang Mach-E é o Mustang mais vendido pelo segundo ano seguido - Ford confirma Mustang Dark Horse no Brasil; veja detalhes Gestão de portfólio e regras de emissões Essa negociação atende ao catálogo australiano da marca, composto por veículos com altas taxas de emissão. A lista de modelos inclui a picape Ranger a diesel, o SUV Everest e o próprio Mustang V8. Em vez de eliminar esses modelos de maior consumo, a Ford optou por gerenciar a conformidade ecológica em toda a sua frota. Em declaração concedida ao portal australiano Drive, o diretor de marketing da Ford Austrália, Ambrose Henderson, explicou que a questão representa uma demanda global de catálogo e não uma razão para retirar modelos de circulação. Henderson destacou que o Mustang permanece como um elemento fundamental da história da marca, com previsão de vendas contínuas por muitos anos. A estratégia da Ford passa por vender de veículos de baixas emissões com a aquisição de créditos externas quando necessário. A Ford busca não depender exclusivamente das montadoras rivais, apostando na ampliação de opções eletrificadas para compensar os índices gerados pelos carros tradicionais. Henderson admitiu ainda que o programa NVES exerce impacto direto no preço do esportivo. Fatores adicionais também compõem a tabela final ao consumidor: flutuações nas taxas de câmbio e variações no custo de matérias-primas. A necessidade de compra desses créditos restringe-se ao território australiano e não indica risco de descontinuação do Mustang em outros mercados. • Assista aos vídeos do VRUM no YouTube e no Dailymotion!

artigo.texto: Voltwise is building its first large scale battery storage system in Germany in Leopoldshöhe, and hosted a groundbreaking ceremony on 19 November 2026. The system, with an output of 56 MW and a storage capacity of 125 MWh, is scheduled to start operation in 2H27. The new battery storage system provides the flexibility needed to integrate the growing share of renewable energy efficiently into the power system, contributing to a resilient, secure, and affordable energy supply. It uses the SmartStack battery storage system from Fluence, global market leader delivering intelligent energy storage systems, services, and asset optimisation software. The storage system will be connected to the grid via the Bechterdissen substation of Bielefelder Netz at the 110-kV level, which covers an area of around 4000 m2. The plans also include a fire safety concept with a fire-water tank and a 4 m noise barrier to limit noise emissions. Further project partners include Vattenfall and Santander CIB, which acted as arranger, original lender, and original hedge counterparty. “Leopoldshöhe marks a decisive step in building our business in Germany. Starting construction of our first large scale battery storage system shows that we are turning our plans into concrete projects. We want to build on this and develop and deliver further storage sites in Germany,” said Thorsten Klöpper, Managing Director Germany at Voltwise. Alongside Mayor Prof. Dr-Ing. Martin Hoffmann, the groundbreaking in Leopoldshöhe was attended by the landowners, representatives of the project partners, and further guests from politics and the region. Hoffmann added: “The energy transition is not decided at the federal level alone, but also through concrete action at the local level. The new battery energy storage facility in Leopoldshöhe represents an investment in infrastructure that will make our electricity system more flexible and future-proof. I am delighted that our municipality has been chosen as the location for such an investment, allowing us to contribute to the energy supply of tomorrow.” “Germany is one of the most important energy storage markets in Europe. With the Leopoldshöhe project, we are making a concrete contribution to reliability in Germany and laying a foundation on which we intend to build our presence here,” commented John D. Jones, CEO of Voltwise. For more news and technical articles from the global renewable industry, read the latest issue of Energy Global magazine. The new issue begins with a regional report on Asia Pacific, looking at the region’s transition from building capacity to building systems. The issue also explores topics such as offshore wind foundations, solar maintenance, training the new workforce, inspection & maintenance, and more! artigo.texto: POSCO group Strengthens Lithium Supply Partnership with CATL, the World’s Largest Battery Company Signs a long-term lithium supply agreement with CATL, which commands an approximately 40% share of the global EV battery market, covering lithium supply for 2026 through 2028 Extends raw material securing and development expertise from steel to lithium… further solidifying its sales foundation in China, the world’s largest EV battery market. Materializes CEO of POSCO Holdings CHANG In Hwa’s strategy to preemptively secure prime resources and build long-term partnerships with leading global customers, enhancing the competitiveness of the lithium business. POSCO group further strengthens its cooperation with CATL, the world’s largest EV battery company, through a long-term lithium supply agreement. CATL (Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited), which accounts for about 40% of the global EV battery market, leads the industry by supplying batteries to major automakers in China and across the globe. Under the agreement, POSCO group supplies CATL with lithium required for EV battery production for 2026 through 2028. Both companies commit to solidifying their long-term partnership and working together to ensure a stable supply of raw materials. Supply under the agreement is already underway. POSCO group has been expanding its lithium business based on its capabilities in securing and developing raw materials, accumulated through its steel business. Building on its production base established through the preemptive securing of high-quality lithium resources, this agreement is expected to further solidify POSCO group’s sales foundation in China and strengthen its position in the global lithium market. This reflects CEO of POSCO Holdings CHANG In Hwa’s strategic focus on preemptively securing high-quality resources and building long-term partnerships with leading global customers. Moving forward, POSCO group will enhance the production stability and sales competitiveness of its lithium resources to drive profitability. At the same time, as Korea’s flagship supplier of critical resources, the group will contribute to stabilizing the global critical minerals supply chain. artigo.texto: Gerando resumo A Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica (Abeeólica) entrou com uma ação no Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) para tentar derrubar a regra que obriga apenas as empresas geradoras de energia a pagar pelos sistemas de armazenamento em baterias contratados pelo governo. A entidade também pediu a suspensão dos leilões de baterias marcados para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro. A Ação Direta de Inconstitucionalidade (ADI) pede a concessão de uma medida cautelar para suspender a eficácia da norma e impedir sua aplicação, inclusive nos leilões marcados para dezembro. O movimento confirma informação antecipada na última terça-feira, 17, pelo Estadão/Broadcast sobre a iniciativa e ocorre na mesma semana em que a entidade ingressou com uma ação civil pública para suspender a realização dos leilões. A ação questiona um trecho da Lei 15.269/2025, conhecida como Lei da Modernização do Setor Elétrico, que determina que apenas as empresas geradoras de energia dividam os custos da contratação de baterias nos leilões. Para a Abeeólica, a regra desrespeita princípios como igualdade de tratamento, legalidade e segurança jurídica. Leia também - Aeris, fabricante de pás para geradores de energia eólica, pede recuperação extrajudicial - Subsídios criam o modelo Robin Hood às avessas e deixam País com sobra de energia e risco de apagão A ADI foi distribuída ao ministro Cristiano Zanin, que solicitou informações à Presidência da República e ao Congresso Nacional, a serem prestadas no prazo de três dias, especialmente quanto aos fundamentos da medida cautelar. Também intimou o Advogado-Geral da União e o Procurador-Geral da República para manifestação sobre o pedido cautelar, no mesmo prazo. Oficiou ainda a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) e o Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) para que se manifestem sobre o pedido cautelar e prestem informações sobre os leilões e os efeitos de eventual suspensão da regra destacada pela Abeeólica sobre os certames e sobre a alocação do encargo. A Abeeólica buscou a Justiça menos de 15 dias antes da realização do leilão de baterias, em meio à dificuldade de avanço no Congresso Nacional de um projeto de lei que visa alterar a regra sobre o custeamento das baterias. Ocorre também enquanto a Aneel segue na regulamentação do custeamento conforme a norma hoje vigente. As áreas técnicas da autarquia analisam as contribuições de uma consulta pública que apresentou duas propostas de rateio: uma elaborada pelo próprio regulador, para que o pagamento seja modulado em função do chamado Índice de Flexibilidade (IF), e uma apresentada pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), que sugere que o rateio leve em consideração a contribuição de potência de cada gerador durante o período considerado crítico para a operação do sistema, entre o fim da tarde e o início da noite. A definição da regra pode ficar para depois do leilão, o que é considerado pelos empreendedores interessados no certame um risco adicional para o negócio, sobretudo no caso daqueles interessados que também são geradores.

artigo.texto: India’s transition to electric mobility could play a major role in reducing its dependence on fossil fuels and curbing emissions from the transport sector. Accelerated electric vehicle (EV) adoption could potentially reduce the country’s combined oil and battery import bill by 61% by 2050, even if it continues to rely entirely on imported batteries, according to a new study by the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT). The study, titled ‘India’s EV transition: Impact of electric vehicle battery demand on import payments from 2024 to 2050’, highlights the environmental and energy security implications of electrifying India’s road transport fleet. It points out that the reduction in petroleum consumption resulting from faster EV adoption would far outweigh the additional costs associated with battery imports. The findings assume significance as transport remains a major source of oil consumption and associated greenhouse gas emissions. Replacing petrol and diesel vehicles with battery electric vehicles (BEVs) can reduce tailpipe emissions and help limit the sector’s contribution to air pollution and climate change. Under the study’s Ambitious Electrification scenario, India’s combined oil and battery import payments in 2050 could be 61% lower than under the Baseline scenario, even without domestic battery manufacturing. The reduction would be 39% under the Momentum scenario. This is primarily because savings from avoided oil imports would substantially outweigh the additional expenditure on imported batteries. The study estimates that the difference between the least and most favourable scenarios could reach $125 billion by 2050. Of this, $94 billion would result from faster vehicle electrification, while another $31 billion could be saved through greater domestic battery manufacturing. However, the transition also presents growing resource and manufacturing challenges. India’s battery electric vehicle sales recorded a compound annual growth rate of 62.5% between FY 2019-20 and FY 2024-25, but domestic battery cell manufacturing has not kept pace, leaving the country almost entirely dependent on imports to meet its requirements. The study projects that annual battery demand could reach around 340 GWh under the Baseline scenario and 573 GWh under both the Momentum and Ambitious scenarios by 2050. The projections cover two-wheelers, three-wheelers, passenger cars, light commercial vehicles, buses and trucks. Faster electrification would bring a substantial share of this demand forward, particularly before 2040. While domestic battery manufacturing is currently at an early stage, expanding local production could gradually reduce the need for imported batteries, with the differences between manufacturing pathways becoming more pronounced after 2030. From an environmental perspective, the findings underline the need to look beyond replacing internal combustion engine vehicles. Battery manufacturing, electricity generation and the sourcing of raw materials will also determine the overall environmental footprint of electric mobility. While EVs eliminate tailpipe emissions, the climate benefits of electrification depend partly on the energy mix used to charge them. Similarly, responsible sourcing of battery materials, cleaner manufacturing processes and effective battery recycling systems will be essential to ensure that the transition does not shift environmental pressures from roads to mining and manufacturing centres. The study makes a case for pursuing faster electrification alongside investments in domestic battery manufacturing.

artigo.texto: Dürr Provides integrated electrode coating and drying systems for battery production According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Electrode Drying Ovens market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global electrode drying ovens market is entering a transformative phase as battery manufacturing capacity scales at an unprecedented pace. These specialized industrial ovens, critical for solvent removal and binder curing in electrode production, have evolved from niche equipment to essential enablers of the energy transition. The market's trajectory is tightly linked to electric vehicle and stationary energy storage demand, which together account for the majority of consumption. As of 2026, the industry is defined by technological innovation, strategic capacity expansions by oven manufacturers and battery gigafactories, and shifting supply chain dynamics. This report provides a data-driven assessment of the world electrode drying ovens market, examining demand drivers, production capabilities, trade flows, and competitive strategies. The forecast to 2035 anticipates a landscape where operational efficiency, smart factory integration, and adaptability to next-generation battery chemistries will separate leaders from followers. This executive summary distills key insights from a granular examination of market forces, offering a foundational understanding for strategic planning and investment decisions in this high-growth industrial segment. The baseline scenario for the global electrode drying ovens market projects sustained expansion through 2035, with a compound annual growth rate of 8.2% and a market index reaching 220 (2025=100). This outlook is anchored in the accelerating build-out of lithium-ion battery gigafactories across Asia-Pacific, North America, and Europe, where electrode drying ovens represent a critical capital equipment category. Demand is further supported by the transition to continuous conveyor and vacuum drying systems that offer higher throughput and energy efficiency, as battery manufacturers prioritize yield and cost per kilowatt-hour. The market's center of gravity remains East Asia, though North America and Europe are expected to gain share as localization incentives drive new capacity. Technological shifts toward dry electrode processing and next-generation chemistries pose long-term risks, but the baseline assumes widespread adoption remains years away. Supply constraints, including specialized component lead times and skilled installation labor, could temper growth in the near term. Overall, the market is poised for robust, innovation-driven expansion, with opportunities concentrated in automation, process control, and aftermarket services. Lithium-ion battery manufacturing is the largest and fastest-growing end-use sector for electrode drying ovens, accounting for the majority of global demand. These ovens are essential for removing solvents such as NMP from electrode coatings and curing binders to ensure consistent electrochemical performance. The segment is currently characterized by massive capacity additions in Asia-Pacific, with North America and Europe accelerating. Demand-side indicators include gigafactory announcements, EV production targets, and battery cell capacity utilization rates. Through 2035, the shift toward higher-throughput continuous conveyor ovens and vacuum drying systems will intensify, as manufacturers seek to reduce energy consumption per cell and improve yield. The trend toward larger electrode formats and thicker coatings will require ovens with enhanced thermal uniformity and faster drying rates. Additionally, the development of dry electrode processing, while still nascent, could eventually disrupt oven demand, but widespread adoption is not expected before the late 2020s. Overall, the segment's growth is underpinned by the global push for electrification and the resulting need for reliable, high-performance drying equipment. Current trend: Dominant and expanding, driven by EV and storage demand. Major trends: Shift from batch to continuous conveyor ovens for high-volume production, Increasing adoption of vacuum drying ovens for solvent recovery and reduced emissions, Integration of advanced process control and IoT sensors for real-time monitoring, Growing focus on energy efficiency and heat recovery systems, and Development of ovens compatible with next-generation battery chemistries. Representative participants: Despatch Industries, Hengli Eletek, Puhler, Yingkou Jinding, and Shenzhen Kejing Star Technology. Fuel cell production represents a smaller but strategically important end-use sector for electrode drying ovens. These ovens are used to dry catalyst layers and membrane electrode assemblies, where precise temperature and atmosphere control are critical to performance. The segment is currently driven by government-backed hydrogen initiatives and commercial deployment of fuel cells in heavy transport and stationary power. Demand-side indicators include fuel cell stack production volumes, hydrogen infrastructure investment, and policy support. Through 2035, growth is expected to be steady but moderate, as fuel cell technology matures and costs decline. The trend toward higher-volume manufacturing will require ovens with greater throughput and automation, similar to those used in battery production. However, the segment's scale will remain significantly smaller than lithium-ion batteries. Key challenges include the need for specialized atmospheres (e.g., inert gas) and the high cost of platinum catalysts, which may limit adoption. Nonetheless, the push for decarbonization in hard-to-abate sectors supports a positive outlook. Current trend: Steady growth, supported by hydrogen economy initiatives. artigo.texto: Click here to read highlights from the story - Wisconsin once gave the Public Service Commission broad authority to guide utilities’ long-term energy planning, but lawmakers scrapped that system in 1998, shifting more control to utilities. - Ratepayer advocates argue the hands-off approach incentivizes power plant construction over investments in energy efficiency and demand reduction. - A surge in electricity demand from data centers is driving a multibillion-dollar buildout and renewing calls for regulators to take a greater role in planning for future needs. - Regulators say current law limits their ability to compare competing proposals and assess major projects as a package, prompting calls for lawmakers to reconsider the state’s approach. Wisconsin’s electricity needs are on track to skyrocket. Utilities plan to spend billions of dollars to keep up, and ratepayers — residents, businesses and data center operators — will pick up the bill. The three-member Public Service Commission, which regulates utilities, is responsible for guarding ratepayers’ wallets from unreasonable spending, but Wisconsin law gives it relatively little sway over how utilities plan for the future. The commission can review proposed power plants on a case-by-case basis, but not as part of a broader blueprint for keeping the lights on as affordably as possible. That hasn’t always been the case. Bureaucratic gridlock and a near-blackout prompted Wisconsin lawmakers to scrap a more hands-on approach to energy planning three decades ago. Utilities don’t mourn its loss. Ratepayer advocates, however, argue the hands-off approach that followed caused Wisconsin’s electricity prices to climb faster than necessary. A flurry of new power plant projects spurred in part by the data center boom is pushing that once-arcane disagreement into the public eye, and regulators themselves are now taking a side. Wisconsin once gave regulators broad planning power Investor-owned utilities generally operate as regulated monopolies: State and federal commissions grant them exclusive rights to sell electricity to consumers within a defined territory in exchange for government oversight of their rates and infrastructure projects. That basic model dates back more than a century in Wisconsin, which formed its Public Service Commission — among the nation’s first utility regulators — in 1907. The mass adoption of air conditioning and the rise of nuclear power complicated the picture in the mid-20th century. Wisconsin lawmakers responded in the 1970s by empowering the Public Service Commission to take the lead on energy planning, hoping to steer utilities toward the most cost-effective path to meeting skyrocketing electricity demand. Those powers took shape as the “Advanced Plan”: 20-year road maps for utilities to meet electricity needs. Working in two-year cycles alongside consumer advocates and other players, the commission could revise the road map to fit its priorities, and especially to save ratepayers money. “This approach requires that the utilities focus on the most cost effective means of meeting customers’ energy service needs,” the commissioners explained in a 1987 biannual report. Utilities have a strong incentive to build new power plants. Ratepayers pay for newly built plants, along with a commission-approved “rate of return” on every dollar spent on the projects, passed along to the utility’s shareholders. The commission could use the Advanced Plan to reconfigure utilities’ construction plans in search of savings. Later iterations embraced demand-side fixes, trimming future energy needs by incentivizing customers to switch to energy-efficient appliances or run factories at off-peak hours. The PSC used its planning power to chip away at utility monopolies in 1989 by beginning to open utility-owned transmission lines to other power producers. Wisconsin was an early adopter of an open transmission system, hoping to keep prices in check by encouraging competition in the electricity market. State lawmakers later directed utilities to pass control of their transmission infrastructure to a new, independent company to protect other power producers’ access to the grid. That company, now called the American Transmission Company, was the country’s first multi-state, transmission-only utility. The PSC went further in 1993, inviting third-party developers to bid for power plant projects outlined in utilities’ long-term plans. Commissioners awarded a natural gas plant in Whitewater to a New York-based developer later that year, saving We Energies’ customers an estimated $66 million. Other states deregulated their electricity markets entirely. Chaos ensued, most notably in California, where flawed execution, price gouging and a drought caused regional blackouts, a major utility bankruptcy filing and billions of dollars in economic losses. Lawmakers let utilities take the lead Wisconsin didn’t copy California’s experiment. It did, however, scrap the Advanced Plan. Utilities argued comprehensive planning was cumbersome and prone to gridlock, blaming it for a slowdown in power plant and transmission construction in the mid-1990s. Some commission staff also recognized the Advanced Plan’s deficiencies. “It became an anti-utility regulatory mechanism that put electric reliability at risk,” recalled Randel Pilo, the PSC’s chief energy economist through much of the 1990s. A close call in the summer of 1997 pushed Wisconsin’s political and business leaders, and even some ratepayer advocacy groups, to rethink the state’s approach. With nuclear power plants in Wisconsin and Illinois unexpectedly offline for repairs, utilities warned that summertime air conditioning use might stretch the state’s supply past its limits and trigger widespread blackouts. State lawmakers abolished the Advanced Plan the following year. They replaced it with what Pilo called a “regulation-lite” approach, leaving planning for Wisconsin’s energy future mostly in utilities’ hand

artigo.texto: Big private battery project outside Carletonville Various international companies also act as advisers. A big private renewable energy developer and independent power producer, Mulilo, is heading a large project outside Carletonville to build a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS). This company announced on November 16 that the Leeuwpoort Battery Energy Storage System project, a significant milestone in the delivery of South Africa’s next generation of grid-supporting energy infrastructure, has been financially secured. The 77 MW / 308 MWh utility-scale battery energy storage facility will connect to the Midas Main Transmission Substation, strengthening the resilience and flexibility of the national grid in a strategically important industrial and energy-demand region shaped by extensive mining activity. As the first large-scale battery energy storage project to achieve financial close in Gauteng, Leeuwpoort represents a significant milestone for the province and an important step in accelerating South Africa’s energy transition and grid modernisation. The company will now proceed with the project, which was awarded under Bid Window 2 of the Battery Energy Storage Independent Power Producer Procurement Programme, the project is the third Mulilo BESS project to reach financial close this year, building on the successful progression of the Mercury and Hartebeesfontein BESS projects. The project incorporates the Haohan battery energy storage system, supplied by BYD Energy storage. Once operational, Leeuwpoort BESS will provide critical storage capacity and ancillary services to the transmission system under a 15-year power purchase agreement with the National Transmission Company South Africa (NTCSA). According to Eskom, the building of the facility is a direct response to the urgent need to address South Africa’s long-running electricity crisis by adding more generation capacity to the grid and strengthening the grid by adding more storage and transforming capacity megawatt-hours. Currently, the Eskom BESS rollout programme is the largest to be implemented in South Africa. Reaching financial close was made possible through the support of the company’s shareholders, Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) and Norfund, along with the strong collaboration and partnership with the Reatile Group, the Department of Electricity and Energy, Eskom, the Independent Power Producers Office, National Transmission Company of South Africa and the Merafong City Local Municipality. The project was further enabled by a consortium of lenders comprising various South African banks. Various international companies also act as advisers.
