artigo.texto: The 250-megawatt facility is expected to become the Northeast’s largest battery energy storage project and begin operating in late 2027. CHELSEA, Mass. — Flatiron Energy has broken ground on Energizar, a 250-megawatt, 1,200-megawatt-hour battery energy storage project in Chelsea that is expected to become the largest facility of its kind in the Northeast. The groundbreaking ceremony brought together Massachusetts Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll, state and local officials, community and project partners, and construction and labor representatives. When completed, Energizar will store electricity when demand is lower and deliver it during periods of peak demand. The project is designed to strengthen grid reliability and resilience across Greater Boston while providing flexible capacity to support the region’s energy needs. “Projects like Energizar are helping us build a more reliable and affordable energy future,” Driscoll said. “Having the ability to store energy and use it when demand is high will help keep the lights on, lower bills, strengthen our electric grid and better serve families and businesses across the Greater Boston region.” Rebecca Tepper, Massachusetts secretary of energy and environmental affairs, said the project demonstrates the state’s first energy storage procurement is producing results. She also highlighted its community engagement and commitments to local jobs and workforce development. The groundbreaking follows Flatiron’s announcement that it secured approximately $850 million in construction and term financing commitments from financial institutions. The financing includes construction and bridge loans, term loans, letter-of-credit facilities, preferred equity and a tax-credit transfer commitment. “Breaking ground on Energizar represents a major milestone for Flatiron and Massachusetts—and is the culmination of years of planning, collaboration and hard work,” said Jon Poor, Flatiron’s chief operating officer. Consigli Construction Co. is leading construction. The project is expected to reach commercial operation in the fourth quarter of 2027. Flatiron has also committed to investments in Chelsea’s Green New Economy Program, which the city will direct with local and regional partners toward workforce, community and youth development, and community empowerment. The company is working with the city and community organizations to connect Chelsea residents with construction jobs and training opportunities. It has also provided emergency response training to the Chelsea Fire Department. “Energizar represents a significant investment in our city, bringing new economic opportunities and resources to our community while supporting the region’s long-term energy needs,” said Chelsea City Manager Fidel Maltez. Gladys Vega, CEO of La Colaborativa, said the project could help connect residents with workforce training and career opportunities. Roseann Bongiovanni, executive director of GreenRoots, said continued collaboration would be important to ensure Chelsea residents’ needs remain central as the project advances.

artigo.texto: What NVIDIA’s DSX POD Tells Us About the Future of Modular Data Centers Since NVIDIA’s GTC Berlin announcement, ‘modular’ is back in the spotlight for data center builders and operators. DSX POD is a real milestone, but the conversation that followed treats modular as if it were new. Modular has been around for nearly two decades. The real revolution is the factory. Speed is the force reshaping this industry. Speed comes from moving work off the jobsite and onto a production line. Modular is how that work gets packaged and shipped. It matters, but it’s the enabler. The factory is where we save time. Here’s how modular got to this point, what the current conversation gets right, and what it takes to build at gigawatt scale. ‘Modular’ is nothing new: The history of modular in data centers The recent SemiAnalysis deep dive tracked more than 60 GW of capacity using some form of it right now. The past two decades of ‘modular’ data center construction split into three waves. Wave one: modular shells. The industry started with the building. Precast concrete, pre-engineered steel, and factory-made panels got shells up quickly. But the power, cooling, and white space were all still built by hand on site. Wave two: modular power and cooling. Next came switchgear, UPS, and cooling equipment shipped as pre-assembled skids. That’s standard practice now. I worked in this wave at Google, where we broke the infrastructure into blocks we could prefabricate. It helped, but the blocks were not fully integrated or tested. The on-site assembly, wiring, and piping work still left a lot of field testing and Cx open. Wave three: integrated, factory-built blocks. Now the whole white space unit ships finished. The field crew sets it, connects it, and verifies it. This is the wave NVIDIA’s DSX POD belongs to. Each time we see a new wave of ‘modular’ work, the same shift happens: work moves out of the field and into a factory. I’d argue that is the trend that matters. What the ‘modular’ conversation gets right The industry isn’t wrong to be excited about DSX POD. It’s just excited about the wrong part. The speed NVIDIA is talking about with the DSX POD comes from doing most of the work in a factory rather than in the field, not from the unit coming in as a module. With a factory build, the work can run in parallel. On a stick build, every trade waits on the one before it. Concrete, then steel, then electrical, then commissioning. In a factory model, modules are built and tested while the site crew pours foundations. When the pad is ready, the equipment is ready too. A factory is also easily repeatable. I started my career in semiconductor fabs, where the rule was copy-exact. If a process worked in one fab, you reproduced it identically in the next. A factory works the same way. Problems get caught before equipment ships. Fixing a defect in the factory costs a fraction of fixing it in the field. Factory first-pass quality runs above 95%, compared with 60 to 70% in the field. Finally, with a factory build, every unit gets better. Each unit off the line is faster and cleaner than the last because the team learns from each build. When you’re building on the jobsite, you start each project over with a fresh crew. These are all advantages of modular data center builds, but modular is just the enabler. Factory construction is the real engine. Speed is the real revolution, and speed is a manufacturing problem In the AI buildout, the operator who gets capacity online first wins. Stick builds are slow by nature. This slowness comes from electrician shortages, sequential work, and field redesigns. Moving the work into the factory, what the industry calls a ‘modular’ approach, solves these problems. Pre-engineered, factory-built data centers need a fraction of the field labor. Work can run in parallel with site prep, and the repeatable, module-based nature of these builds keeps design consistent and reduces the need for field redesigns. We should be excited about NVIDIA’s announcement because it signals a further shift toward building data centers in the factory, not simply because it’s modular. That shift is why I joined Giga. In the past, we broke data centers into prefab blocks, but those blocks still needed large field crews to connect them. That limited how fast we could build. Giga solves this by building and testing all the power, cooling, and white space equipment in the factory, with standard connections between them, minimizing on-site labor. We also handle engineering, manufacturing, logistics, installation, and commissioning in-house, so one team owns the build from start to finish. That’s how we take full sites from dirt to data in as fast as 9 months. Factory-built data centers will power the future of AI NVIDIA’s announcement is a strong signal for the industry. The next step is applying the same factory-built approach to the whole data center, including power, cooling, and the connections between them, not just compute. Data centers need to be treated more and more like manufactured products and less like construction projects. The builders who keep up will be the ones who own that process from start to finish, from engineering and manufacturing through installation and commissioning. That’s what we’re building at Giga. If you’re planning a campus and want to see what a factory-built approach looks like at scale, explore our GigaBase system. About the Author Angad Sandhu Angad Sandhu is CTO of Giga Energy. He previously led data center engineering at Google through the cloud-to-AI transition and has spent 15+ years delivering power infrastructure at scale. He joined Giga Energy in 2026 to help build a faster, more accountable model for AI infrastructure deployment.

artigo.texto: The National Wealth Fund has announced an equity investment alongside Matrix Renewables UK Limited to support the development of two large-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) projects in Eccles and Kilmarnock, Scotland. The projects will have a combined power capacity of 1 GW and an energy storage capacity of 2 GWh, strengthening the UK’s electricity grid and supporting its transition towards clean energy. The investment will support the development and delivery of both projects, with Matrix Renewables retaining a majority stake in each facility. The partnership is expected to create or support more than 200 jobs across the construction and operational phases, bringing economic benefits to the surrounding areas. Located along important electricity transmission corridors connecting Scotland and England, the two battery storage facilities are expected to play a significant role in improving grid flexibility and managing network constraints. They will also help integrate a larger share of renewable electricity into the power system by storing surplus generation and making electricity available when demand increases. Once operational, the combined storage capacity of the projects will be equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of approximately 520,000 households. The facilities are expected to support the UK’s clean energy ambitions by improving the reliability of electricity supply and making better use of renewable power, particularly wind energy generated across Scotland. Construction work is already underway at the Eccles project, with commercial operations expected to begin in October 2027. Meanwhile, construction at the Kilmarnock project is scheduled to start in December 2026, with commercial operations targeted for September 2028. The investment represents an important step in the National Wealth Fund’s efforts to mobilise private capital for strategic infrastructure and accelerate the UK’s energy transition. It also expands Matrix Renewables’ presence in the British market, marking the company’s first investments in the UK. Matrix has indicated plans to invest further capital in storage and flexible generation projects, with ambitions for additional multi-gigawatt investments as part of its portfolio diversification strategy. Oliver Holbourn, Chief Executive Officer of the National Wealth Fund, said battery storage is essential for developing a cleaner, more secure and flexible electricity system. He highlighted that the investment would help deliver nationally significant infrastructure, strengthen the grid connection between Scotland and England, increase renewable energy storage and support hundreds of jobs. Luis Sabaté, CEO of Matrix Renewables, described the projects as the company’s first investments in one of the world’s most advanced energy storage markets. He said the partnership reflects confidence in the projects and a shared commitment to developing large-scale battery storage infrastructure. Exchequer Secretary and Minister for Growth Dan Tomlinson highlighted Scotland’s importance to Britain’s clean energy future, noting that the investment would support employment, strengthen energy security and encourage economic growth. Minister for Climate Transition Katie White also emphasised the importance of battery storage in capturing and storing Scotland’s growing wind power generation. She said projects of this scale would help improve energy security, maximise renewable electricity utilisation and contribute to reducing energy bills over the long term. The Eccles and Kilmarnock developments underline the growing importance of large-scale battery storage in supporting renewable energy integration and building a more flexible electricity network across the UK. artigo.texto: Accomack County is moving forward with a proposed zoning ordinance change that would make it easier to add battery energy storage systems to certain existing solar facilities. The Board of Supervisors scheduled a public hearing for December 16th on the proposed amendment, which is intended to bring county regulations into compliance with a new Virginia state law. The legislation, Senate Bill 443, allows battery energy storage systems to be installed as an accessory use at solar facilities that already have an approved conditional use permit, without requiring a separate conditional use permit for the battery installation. The proposal applies only to properties with approved solar facilities. Other battery storage projects would remain subject to the county’s existing zoning requirements, including industrial zoning and a conditional use permit. The proposed amendment also requires battery storage systems to comply with existing county regulations covering fire and public safety, environmental protection, flood control, stormwater management and landscaping. The Accomack County Planning Commission held a public hearing on the proposal October 14th. No one spoke for or against the amendment. Commission members voted unanimously, seven to nothing, to recommend approval.

artigo.texto: Andhra Pradesh has opened a tender for the procurement of 1,000 MW / 4,000 MWh of standalone Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) at selected substations across the state. The tender has been issued by the Transmission Corporation of Andhra Pradesh Limited (APTRANSCO) under its Phase-II battery storage procurement programme for 2026-27. The project will have a four-hour storage duration and will be developed under the Build-Own-Operate (BOO) model through Tariff-Based Competitive Bidding (TBCB). The tender, identified as APTRANSCO/BESS/Phase-II/2026-27, carries the tender ID TRANSCO-2026-TN000006. The total planned capacity of 1,000 MW / 4,000 MWh has been divided into two equal portions based on the availability of Viability Gap Funding (VGF) support. The first portion comprises 500 MW / 2,000 MWh of battery storage capacity with VGF support through the Power System Development Fund (PSDF). The remaining 500 MW / 2,000 MWh will be developed without VGF support. Under the procurement structure, selected developers will be responsible for building, owning and operating the standalone battery energy storage facilities. The systems will be installed at locations identified by APTRANSCO across Andhra Pradesh. The tender is expected to create opportunities for battery storage developers, infrastructure companies and equipment suppliers involved in grid-scale energy storage projects. The tender was published on November 19, 2026. APTRANSCO has scheduled the pre-bid meeting for December 2, 2026, at 11:00 AM, providing interested bidders an opportunity to seek clarification on the procurement requirements. The deadline for submitting bids is December 14, 2026, at 5:00 PM, while the opening of bids is scheduled for December 17, 2026, at 11:00 AM. The tender fee has been listed at ₹89,005. The exact order value has not been specified in the available tender information. Similarly, details regarding the Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) and technical and financial qualification requirements need to be verified through the official Request for Selection (RfS) document. The procurement could also generate business opportunities across the battery storage supply chain. Potential suppliers may include manufacturers of battery cells, battery racks, containers, Power Conversion Systems (PCS), Battery Management Systems (BMS) and Energy Management Systems (EMS). Other areas of opportunity include transformers, switchgear, protection systems, HVAC equipment, fire detection and suppression systems, cables, busbars and electrical components. Companies specializing in substation integration, civil construction, testing, commissioning, SCADA and long-term operations and maintenance may also participate in the project supply chain. The 1,000 MW procurement represents another significant step towards strengthening Andhra Pradesh’s grid-scale energy storage infrastructure and supporting the integration of renewable energy into the state’s electricity network. artigo.texto: Trina Storage, a China-based BESS integrator, used RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas to unveil the Elementa Hybrid Genset, which it had previewed at Data Center World Power. The plant has been built for data center developers who need on-site power while their grid interconnection is delayed, limited or unavailable. AI workloads can make demand fluctuate faster than gas generators alone may follow, Trina Storage has said, while a battery is not designed to cover an extended outage by itself. Both are therefore combined, with reciprocating gas engines of up to 2.5 MW coming from qualified partners and Trina Storage acting as the system integrator. The company supplies the Elementa DC battery systems and the Electra AC platform in blocks of 5 MW/10 MW. Under a hybrid plant controller, the BESS takes a sudden increase in load immediately, while the gas generators are ramped up gradually. Further tests of the grid-forming function are ongoing, alongside certification. Trina Storage launches a gas-and-BESS power plant for AI data centers The Elementa Hybrid Genset from Trina Storage pairs gas engines of up to 2.5 MW with battery storage, and it is aimed at data centers that are short of grid power. artigo.texto:
A Agência Internacional de Energia, a AIE, emitiu um alerta global sobre o impacto ambiental da expansão da inteligência artificial. Segundo o relatório, as emissões de carbono geradas pelos data centers vão disparar 70% até 2030. Essas instalações reúnem os servidores que sustentam o funcionamento da IA e exigem uma infraestrutura enorme, com processamento ininterrupto e sistemas pesados de refrigeração.
O consumo de eletricidade desses locais vai dobrar até o final desta década em comparação com os níveis atuais. A inteligência artificial responde por três quartos desse crescimento projetado. O documento da AIE aponta que as novas instalações focadas em IA vão consumir 350 terawatts-hora adicionais por ano até 2030, volume que supera toda a demanda elétrica anual do Reino Unido.
As grandes empresas de tecnologia investem em fontes renováveis, mas o ritmo não acompanha a necessidade de processamento. Com isso, os combustíveis fósseis ganham espaço. O próprio relatório da AIE afirma que o carvão e o gás ganham espaço imediato no abastecimento por causa do ritmo acelerado de expansão dos servidores de IA.
Na China, as usinas a carvão vão fornecer metade da eletricidade consumida pelos data centers até 2030, com fontes limpas, nuclear e gás cobrindo o restante. Nos Estados Unidos, o gás natural vai responder por 60% da eletricidade destinada a essas instalações. Até agosto de 2026, os EUA já registravam 180 gigawatts em projetos de novas usinas a gás vinculadas exclusivamente a data centers.

artigo.texto: A Finnish battery startup facing sustained accusations from industry rivals that its technology is overstated or outright fraudulent has released new independent test data showing its solid-state cells deliver more than their rated capacity at temperatures that would degrade or destroy a conventional lithium-ion battery. Donut Lab, which has previously claimed its cells can charge in minutes and offer high energy density, commissioned a second evaluation by VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland, the country’s state-run research institute. The results, published by Donut Lab this week, focus specifically on thermal performance, examining how the battery behaves at 80°C and 100°C, temperatures at which standard lithium-ion cells begin to suffer serious performance loss and pose safety risks. Standard lithium-ion batteries are very sensitive to heat, with an upper operating temperature limit of typically around 60 to 70 degrees Celsius. High temperatures increase the risk of damage to battery cells and shorten their service life. High temperatures can also cause accelerated reactions inside the cell, and in the worst case, the risk of thermal runaway increases significantly. The Donut Battery does not use flammable liquid electrolytes, the component most responsible for thermal runaway in conventional cells. That difference in architecture is what VTT’s tests were designed to quantify under real thermal stress. The methodology was straightforward. Engineers placed the cell on an aluminium profile, secured a steel plate on top to apply light pressure and reduce hot spots, then measured capacity in stages at each temperature. At 176°F, the battery delivered about 110% of its rated capacity, showed better efficiency than at room temperature, and the cell showed no visible changes after the test. At 212°F, the battery used roughly 107% of its capacity and recharged back to 4.15 volts with the same capacity as at room temperature. Although the pouch lost vacuum at that temperature, the active materials remained fully functional. The efficiency gain at elevated temperatures is explained by basic electrochemistry. Heat reduces the internal resistance of a cell, which in turn reduces the voltage drop during discharge, allowing more of the stored energy to be extracted as usable output. In a liquid-electrolyte battery, that benefit is overwhelmed by accelerating degradation chemistry. In Donut Lab’s solid-state design, the degradation mechanism is largely absent, allowing the efficiency benefit to dominate instead. “The battery’s full capacity was utilised with excellent results at both 80 and 100 degrees Celsius, and it was possible to discharge it at a 1C discharge rate at 80 degrees and a 0.5C discharge rate at 100 degrees without any increase in temperature. The battery’s properties did not change even at 100 degrees, and it functioned normally when recharged, which demonstrates the convincing performance of the Donut Battery even in extremely hot conditions. This confirms that the battery is exceptional not only in terms of performance but also in terms of safety,” said Ville Piippo, CTO at Donut Lab. The results carry practical implications beyond the laboratory. Batteries that tolerate extreme heat without cooling system support could reduce the weight, complexity, and cost of thermal management in electric vehicles, particularly relevant for markets in desert climates where ambient temperatures routinely exceed the operating ceiling of conventional packs. Industrial applications including grid storage, aerospace, and military systems have similarly been constrained by the thermal sensitivity of existing battery chemistry. The tests also represent a deliberate shift in how Donut Lab is managing its public credibility. After bold claims generated skepticism rather than investment interest, the company is now building its case incrementally through third-party data published openly, letting the numbers do the work that press releases could not. For automakers in the US and companies focused on energy storage, having batteries that can handle extreme heat is absolutely essential. Batteries that can endure high temperatures not only lessen the strain on cooling systems but also enhance safety in sweltering regions like Arizona, Texas, and Nevada. Whether the technology proves durable at manufacturing scale remains the central unanswered question, but on the narrow question of what the cells do under extreme heat, the independent record now says they perform better than anything currently in mass production.
